$$\det\begin{bmatrix} a - \lambda & b \\ c & d - \lambda\end{bmatrix} = (a - \lambda)(d - \lambda) - bc = \lambda^2 - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc).$$

The coefficient $a + d$ is the **[[trace]]** of $A$ (the sum of the diagonal entries), written
$\operatorname{tr} A$. So for $2 \times 2$ matrices the characteristic polynomial is
$\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$. Two consequences that hold for all $n$: the
eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity, and including any complex ones) add up to the trace and
multiply to the determinant. For example, the $90^\circ$ rotation matrix has eigenvalues $\pm i$:
their sum $0$ is its trace and their product $1$ is its determinant.

### Example 1

Find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & -6\end{bmatrix}$.

1. $\operatorname{tr} A = 2 + (-6) = -4$ and $\det A = -12 - 9 = -21$.
2. Characteristic equation: $\lambda^2 + 4\lambda - 21 = 0$.
3. Factor: $(\lambda + 7)(\lambda - 3) = 0$, so $\lambda = 3$ or $\lambda = -7$.
4. Check: $3 + (-7) = -4 = \operatorname{tr} A$ and $3(-7) = -21 = \det A$. ✓

For eigenvectors, row-reduce $A - 3I = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -9\end{bmatrix}$: $x_1 = 3x_2$,
giving $(3, 1)$. And $A + 7I = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}$: $x_2 = -3x_1$, giving
$(1, -3)$.

### Example 2

Find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}$.

1. Expand $\det(A - \lambda I)$ down column 3, which has only one nonzero entry:
$$\det(A - \lambda I) = (4 - \lambda)\begin{vmatrix} 1 - \lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 1 - \lambda\end{vmatrix} = (4 - \lambda)\big[(1 - \lambda)^2 - 4\big].$$
2. $(1 - \lambda)^2 - 4 = 0$ gives $1 - \lambda = \pm 2$, so $\lambda = -1$ or $\lambda = 3$.
3. The eigenvalues are $4$, $3$ and $-1$. Their sum is $6 = 1 + 1 + 4$, the trace. ✓

The graph of the characteristic polynomial shows the three eigenvalues as the places where it crosses the horizontal axis:

```plot
{"x": [-2, 5], "y": [-12, 14], "xLabel": "λ", "yLabel": "det(A - λI)", "functions": [{"f": "(4 - x)*((1 - x)^2 - 4)"}], "points": [{"at": [-1, 0]}, {"at": [3, 0]}, {"at": [4, 0]}], "labels": [{"at": [2.6, 10], "text": "(4 - λ)[(1 - λ)² - 4]"}, {"at": [-1.5, -4], "text": "λ = -1"}, {"at": [2.3, 3.5], "text": "λ = 3"}, {"at": [4.45, 3.5], "text": "λ = 4"}], "caption": "The eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial"}
```

For $3 \times 3$ and larger matrices, finding roots of the characteristic polynomial by hand is
only practical when the matrix has structure (zeros, triangular blocks) or the roots are
nice. Software finds eigenvalues by entirely different iterative methods, because polynomial
roots are numerically unstable to compute from coefficients.

Which method to use by hand depends on the matrix:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which method finds the eigenvalues
  accDescr: First ask what kind of matrix A is. If it is triangular, read the eigenvalues off the diagonal. If it is 2 by 2, solve lambda squared minus the trace times lambda plus the determinant equals zero. If it is larger with no special structure, expand det of A minus lambda I along the row or column with the most zeros and factor the characteristic polynomial. In every case, check that the eigenvalues add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
  S{"What kind of matrix is A?"}
  S -- "triangular" --> T["Read the diagonal entries"]
  S -- "2 × 2" --> Q["Solve λ² - (tr A)λ + det A = 0"]
  S -- "larger" --> X["Expand det(A - λI) along the row or column with the most zeros"]
  X --> F["Factor the characteristic polynomial"]
  T --> C["Check: sum = trace, product = det A"]
  Q --> C
  F --> C
```

## Multiplicity

The **[[algebraic multiplicity]]** of an eigenvalue is its multiplicity as a root of the
characteristic polynomial. For instance if the characteristic polynomial is
$(\lambda - 2)^2(\lambda - 5)$, the eigenvalue 2 has algebraic multiplicity 2 and 5 has
multiplicity 1. (Up to an overall sign, that's the polynomial of the matrix $B$ in the last lesson: for a $3 \times 3$ matrix, $\det(A - \lambda I)$ has leading term $-\lambda^3$.) For a
triangular matrix, the characteristic polynomial is $\prod(a_{ii} - \lambda)$, so repeated
diagonal entries give repeated eigenvalues.

A real matrix can have complex eigenvalues: $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ has
characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2 + 1$, with no real roots. That's the subject of a later
lesson.

## Similar matrices

$A$ and $B$ are **[[similar]]** if there is an invertible $P$ with $B = P^{-1}AP$. Similar matrices
describe the same transformation in different coordinates, and:

> *Theorem.* Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial, hence the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities.

Proof: $B - \lambda I = P^{-1}AP - \lambda P^{-1}P = P^{-1}(A - \lambda I)P$, so by the product
rule $\det(B - \lambda I) = \det P^{-1}\det(A - \lambda I)\det P = \det(A - \lambda I)$.

The converse is false: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ have the same characteristic polynomial but
aren't similar (the only matrix similar to $2I$ is $2I$ itself). Also, "similar" is not the
same as "row equivalent".

### Example 3

For what value of $h$ is 3 an eigenvalue of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & h \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}$? What is the other eigenvalue then?

1. 3 is an eigenvalue exactly when $\det(A - 3I) = 0$: $\det\begin{bmatrix} -1 & h \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} = -3 - 3h = 0$, so $h = -1$.
2. The eigenvalues add up to the trace, $2 + 6 = 8$, so the other one is $8 - 3 = 5$.
3. Check with the determinant: with $h = -1$, $\det A = 12 - (-1)(3) = 15 = 3 \cdot 5$. ✓

Using the trace and determinant this way saves solving the quadratic when one eigenvalue is already known.

## Common mistakes

- *Sign of the middle term.* For $2 \times 2$, it's $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$; with $\operatorname{tr} A = -4$ the term is $+4\lambda$.
- *Computing $\det A - \lambda$* instead of $\det(A - \lambda I)$.
- *Expecting real roots always.* Real matrices can have complex eigenvalues.
- *Assuming same eigenvalues means similar.*
- *Dropping a factor* like $(4 - \lambda)$ when expanding, and missing an eigenvalue.

## Key points

- Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.
- For $2 \times 2$: $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A = 0$.
- The eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant (with multiplicity).
- Algebraic multiplicity is the multiplicity as a root.
- Similar matrices ($B = P^{-1}AP$) share characteristic polynomials and eigenvalues.

lessons.title: Diagonalization
lessons.body:
## A matrix in its own best coordinates

Diagonal matrices are as simple as matrices get: they scale each coordinate separately, and
their powers are just powers of the diagonal entries. Diagonalization rewrites a matrix as a
diagonal matrix in disguise, $A = PDP^{-1}$, where $P$ changes to a basis of eigenvectors.
In that basis $A$ simply stretches each coordinate by an eigenvalue. This lesson says when
that's possible and how to do it, and uses it to compute powers $A^k$ quickly.

## The factorization $A = PDP^{-1}$

A square matrix $A$ is **[[diagonalizable]]** if $A = PDP^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and
diagonal matrix $D$; that is, if $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix.

> *Diagonalization theorem.* An $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if $A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors. In that case $A = PDP^{-1}$, where the columns of $P$ are $n$ independent eigenvectors and the diagonal entries of $D$ are the corresponding eigenvalues, in the same order.

Why: $AP = PD$ says, column by column, $A\mathbf{p}_j = d_{jj}\mathbf{p}_j$. So $AP = PD$ holds
exactly when each column of $P$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $d_{jj}$, and $P$ is
invertible exactly when those eigenvectors are independent. Then multiply $AP = PD$ on the
right by $P^{-1}$.

A matrix with an eigenvector basis for $\mathbb{R}^n$ (an **[[eigenvector basis]]**) is exactly a
diagonalizable matrix.

*Diagonalization as a change of coordinates.* Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the basis formed by the
columns of $P$, so $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = P^{-1}\mathbf{x}$. The $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates of
$A\mathbf{x}$ are $P^{-1}A\mathbf{x} = (P^{-1}AP)\,P^{-1}\mathbf{x} = D\,[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$.
So $D$ is the *matrix of the transformation* $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ *relative to the basis*
$\mathcal{B}$ (often called the $\mathcal{B}$-matrix): in eigenvector coordinates the map just
multiplies coordinate $i$ by $\lambda_i$. The same calculation works for any basis of
$\mathbb{R}^n$: $P^{-1}AP$ is always the matrix of $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ in the coordinates
given by the columns of $P$. That is the precise sense in which similar matrices describe the
same transformation.

The diagram shows the two routes from $\mathbf{x}$ to $A\mathbf{x}$: directly, or by changing to eigenvector coordinates, scaling, and changing back.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A equals P D P inverse as a change of coordinates
  accDescr: Two routes lead from x to Ax. The direct route multiplies by A. The indirect route first multiplies x by P inverse to get its coordinates in the eigenvector basis, then multiplies by the diagonal matrix D, which scales each coordinate by its eigenvalue, giving the eigenvector coordinates of Ax, and finally multiplies by P to return to standard coordinates. Both routes give the same result, which is why A equals P D P inverse.
  X["x"] -- "A" --> AX["Ax"]
  X -- "P⁻¹" --> XB["coordinates of x in the eigenvector basis"]
  XB -- "D: scale coordinate i by λi" --> AXB["coordinates of Ax in the eigenvector basis"]
  AXB -- "P" --> AX
```

## Powers

If $A = PDP^{-1}$, the inner factors cancel in products:

$$A^2 = PDP^{-1}PDP^{-1} = PD^2P^{-1}, \qquad A^k = PD^kP^{-1}.$$

And $D^k$ is diagonal with entries $\lambda_i^k$. Computing $A^{100}$ takes no more work than
$A^2$.

### Example 1

Diagonalize $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and find a formula for $A^k$.

1. Eigenvalues: $\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 6 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 3)$, so $\lambda = 2, 3$.
2. Eigenvectors (from the eigenvalues lesson): $(1, 1)$ for 2 and $(2, 1)$ for 3.
3. $P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}$, $P^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$.
4. $A^k = PD^kP^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2^k & 0 \\ 0 & 3^k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2\cdot3^k - 2^k & 2^{k+1} - 2\cdot3^k \\ 3^k - 2^k & 2^{k+1} - 3^k\end{bmatrix}.$
5. Check $k = 1$: $\begin{bmatrix} 6 - 2 & 4 - 6 \\ 3 - 2 & 4 - 3\end{bmatrix} = A$. ✓ For $k = 3$: $A^3 = \begin{bmatrix} 46 & -38 \\ 19 & -11\end{bmatrix}$.

The order of columns in $P$ must match the order of eigenvalues in $D$. Swapping both gives
another valid diagonalization.

## When is a matrix diagonalizable?

> *Theorem.* An $n \times n$ matrix with $n$ distinct real eigenvalues is diagonalizable.

That follows because eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent. Distinct
eigenvalues are sufficient but not necessary. With repeated eigenvalues, count eigenvectors:
the **[[geometric multiplicity]]** of $\lambda$ is $\dim\operatorname{Nul}(A - \lambda I)$, the number of
independent eigenvectors for $\lambda$. It's always between 1 and the algebraic multiplicity.

> $A$ is diagonalizable exactly when its eigenvalues are all real (counted with multiplicity, there are $n$ of them) and, for every eigenvalue, the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity. Equivalently, the eigenspace dimensions add up to $n$.

The "all real" part matters because we are building $P$ and $D$ from real numbers. A $3 \times 3$ matrix with eigenvalues $1$ and $\pm i$ has a 1-dimensional eigenspace for $1$ that matches its multiplicity, but only one real eigenvector, so it is not diagonalizable with real matrices. (Complex eigenvalues are the subject of the next lesson.)

Put together, the tests give a decision chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Deciding whether a matrix is diagonalizable
  accDescr: Find the eigenvalues of the n by n matrix A with their algebraic multiplicities. If some eigenvalue is not real, A is not diagonalizable with real matrices. If all are real and there are n distinct eigenvalues, A is diagonalizable. If some eigenvalue is repeated, find the dimension of each eigenspace, the null space of A minus lambda I. If every eigenspace dimension equals the algebraic multiplicity, A is diagonalizable, with eigenvectors as the columns of P and eigenvalues on the diagonal of D; if any is smaller, A is not diagonalizable.
  A["Find the eigenvalues and their algebraic multiplicities"] --> B{"Are they all real?"}
  B -- "no" --> N1["Not diagonalizable with real matrices"]
  B -- "yes" --> C{"n distinct eigenvalues?"}
  C -- "yes" --> Y["Diagonalizable: P holds eigenvectors, D the eigenvalues"]
  C -- "no" --> E["For each repeated λ, find dim Nul(A - λI)"]
  E --> F{"Every dimension equals the algebraic multiplicity?"}
  F -- "yes" --> Y
  F -- "no" --> N2["Not diagonalizable: too few eigenvectors"]
```

### Example 2

$B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 2 (algebraic multiplicity 2) and 5.

1. The eigenspace for 2 has basis $\{(-1, 1, 0), (-1, 0, 1)\}$: dimension 2, matching the multiplicity.
2. For 5: $B - 5I = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has null space spanned by $(1, 1, 1)$.
3. Three independent eigenvectors, so $B$ is diagonalizable: $P = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}$.

### Example 3

Is $S = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ diagonalizable?

1. Triangular, so the only eigenvalue is 2, with algebraic multiplicity 2.
2. $S - 2I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$: one pivot, one free variable, so the eigenspace is 1-dimensional (spanned by $(1, 0)$).
3. Only one independent eigenvector in $\mathbb{R}^2$: *not* diagonalizable.

Geometrically $S$ is a shear followed by scaling: the only direction it doesn't turn is the
$x$-axis. Not every matrix has enough eigenvectors.

A useful check on any diagonalization is to verify $AP = PD$ rather than computing $P^{-1}$:
multiply $A$ by each column of $P$ and confirm you get the corresponding eigenvalue times that
column. It catches mismatched orders and arithmetic slips at once.

## Common mistakes

- *Mismatched order.* Column $j$ of $P$ must be an eigenvector for the $j$th diagonal entry of $D$.
- *Thinking repeated eigenvalues rule out diagonalization.* $B$ in Example 2 is diagonalizable. Check eigenspace dimensions.
- *Confusing diagonalizable with invertible.* $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ is diagonalizable but singular; $S$ in Example 3 is invertible but not diagonalizable.
- *Writing $A^k = P^kD^kP^{-k}$.* The $P$ and $P^{-1}$ appear once each: $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$.

## Key points

- $A = PDP^{-1}$ with eigenvectors as the columns of $P$ and eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$.
- $A$ is diagonalizable ⟺ it has $n$ independent eigenvectors; $n$ distinct real eigenvalues guarantee it.
- With repeated eigenvalues, diagonalizable ⟺ all eigenvalues are real and each eigenspace's dimension equals the eigenvalue's algebraic multiplicity.
- $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, where $D^k$ just raises each eigenvalue to the $k$th power.

lessons.title: Complex eigenvalues
lessons.body:
## When no direction stays put

A rotation of the plane by $90^\circ$ turns *every* nonzero vector, so it has no real
eigenvectors. Its characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2 + 1$ has no real roots. But it does
have complex roots, $\pm i$, and those complex eigenvalues carry exactly the information
that describes the motion: an angle of rotation and a scaling factor. This lesson shows how
to read rotation and scaling from complex eigenvalues of a real $2 \times 2$ matrix.

## Complex numbers, briefly

A complex number is $z = a + bi$ with $i^2 = -1$; $a$ is its real part and $b$ its imaginary
part. Its **[[complex conjugate]]** is $\bar z = a - bi$, and its modulus (absolute value) is
$|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. Every quadratic with real coefficients has two roots in the complex
numbers, given by the quadratic formula; if the discriminant is negative, they form a
conjugate pair $a \pm bi$.

The definitions of eigenvalue and eigenvector carry over with complex scalars and vectors in
$\mathbb{C}^n$. A **[[complex eigenvalue]]** of a real matrix is a non-real root of its characteristic
polynomial.

## Complex eigenvalues of real matrices come in pairs

If $A$ is real and $A\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x}$, then taking conjugates of everything,
$A\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \bar\lambda\bar{\mathbf{x}}$. So when $\lambda$ is a complex eigenvalue with
eigenvector $\mathbf{x}$, its conjugate $\bar\lambda$ is also an eigenvalue, with eigenvector
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}$.

## Rotation–scaling matrices

The model example is

$$C = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}.$$

Its characteristic polynomial is $(a - \lambda)^2 + b^2$, so $\lambda = a \pm bi$. Write
$r = |\lambda| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and let $\varphi$ be the angle of the point $(a, b)$ measured
from the positive $x$-axis. Then $a = r\cos\varphi$, $b = r\sin\varphi$ and

$$C = r\begin{bmatrix} \cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi\end{bmatrix}.$$

So $C$ is a **[[rotation–scaling matrix]]**: a rotation by $\varphi$ followed by scaling by $r$. The
modulus of the eigenvalue is the scale factor and its angle is the rotation angle. Repeated
multiplication by $C$ makes points spiral: outward if $r > 1$, inward if $r < 1$, around a
circle if $r = 1$.

In the complex plane, the eigenvalue $a + bi$ sits at the point $(a, b)$; its distance from 0 is the scale factor and its angle is the rotation angle:

![The complex plane with the eigenvalue λ = a + bi plotted as a point. The segment from 0 to λ has length r = |λ|, the angle φ between that segment and the positive real axis is the rotation angle, the real part a is measured along the real axis and the imaginary part b vertically. The conjugate a - bi is the mirror image below the real axis.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```plot
{"x": [-4, 5], "y": [-3, 4], "equal": true, "segments": [{"from": [4.0, 0.0], "to": [3.12, 1.8], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3.12, 1.8], "to": [1.62, 2.81], "arrow": true}, {"from": [1.62, 2.81], "to": [0.0, 2.92], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0.0, 2.92], "to": [-1.31, 2.27], "arrow": true}, {"from": [-1.31, 2.27], "to": [-2.05, 1.18], "arrow": true}, {"from": [-2.05, 1.18], "to": [-2.13, 0.0], "arrow": true}, {"from": [-2.13, 0.0], "to": [-1.66, -0.96], "arrow": true}, {"from": [-1.66, -0.96], "to": [-0.86, -1.49], "arrow": true}, {"from": [-0.86, -1.49], "to": [0.0, -1.55], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0.0, -1.55], "to": [0.7, -1.21], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0.7, -1.21], "to": [1.09, -0.63], "arrow": true}, {"from": [1.09, -0.63], "to": [1.13, 0.0], "arrow": true}], "points": [{"at": [4.0, 0.0], "label": "x₀"}], "caption": "Iterates of a rotation–scaling matrix with r = 0.9 and angle 30°: an inward spiral"}
```

### Example 1

Find the eigenvalues of $C = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt3 & -1 \\ 1 & \sqrt3\end{bmatrix}$ and describe the transformation.

1. Here $a = \sqrt3$, $b = 1$, so $\lambda = \sqrt3 \pm i$.
2. $r = \sqrt{3 + 1} = 2$, and $(\sqrt3, 1)$ is at angle $\varphi = 30^\circ$.
3. So $C$ rotates by $30^\circ$ counterclockwise and doubles lengths. Applying it 12 times rotates by $360^\circ$ and scales by $2^{12}$: $C^{12} = 4096I$.

## Every real $2 \times 2$ matrix with complex eigenvalues is a disguised rotation–scaling

> *Theorem.* Let $A$ be a real $2 \times 2$ matrix with a complex eigenvalue $\lambda = a - bi$ ($b \neq 0$) and associated eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$. Then $A = PCP^{-1}$, where
> $$P = [\,\operatorname{Re}\mathbf{v} \;\; \operatorname{Im}\mathbf{v}\,] \quad\text{and}\quad C = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}.$$

In the coordinates given by the columns of $P$, $A$ acts as a rotation–scaling. The picture
is an elliptical spiral rather than a circular one, but the scale factor per step is still
$r = |\lambda|$.

### Example 2

Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$. Find the eigenvalues, the scale factor, and a factorization $A = PCP^{-1}$.

1. $\operatorname{tr} A = 4$, $\det A = 3 + 2 = 5$: $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 5 = 0$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 20}}{2} = 2 \pm i$.
2. Scale factor $r = |2 \pm i| = \sqrt5 \approx 2.24$, so iterates spiral outward. The rotation angle of $C$ is that of $(2, 1)$: $\tan^{-1}(1/2) \approx 26.6^\circ$.
3. Eigenvector for $\lambda = 2 - i$: row 2 of $A - (2 - i)I$ is $[\,1 \;\; 1 + i\,]$, so $x_1 = -(1 + i)x_2$. Take $\mathbf{v} = (-1 - i,\ 1)$.
4. $\operatorname{Re}\mathbf{v} = (-1, 1)$, $\operatorname{Im}\mathbf{v} = (-1, 0)$. So $P = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$.
5. Check $AP = PC$: both equal $\begin{bmatrix} -3 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}$. ✓

(With $\lambda = a - bi$, the matrix $C$ has $-b$ in the top right; here $b = 1$.)

### Example 3

Check that $\mathbf{v} = (1, -i)$ is an eigenvector of the $90^\circ$ rotation $R = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, and find its eigenvalue.

1. $R\mathbf{v} = (0 \cdot 1 + (-1)(-i),\ 1 \cdot 1 + 0) = (i, 1)$.
2. Compare with $i\mathbf{v} = (i, -i^2) = (i, 1)$. They match, so $R\mathbf{v} = i\mathbf{v}$: eigenvalue $i$.
3. By conjugation, $\bar{\mathbf{v}} = (1, i)$ is an eigenvector for $-i$.

Here $a = 0$ and $b = 1$, so $r = 1$ and the angle is $90^\circ$: exactly the rotation we started with. Complex arithmetic is just a bookkeeping device; the real content is "rotate by $90^\circ$, don't scale".

## Common mistakes

- *Concluding there are no eigenvalues* when the discriminant is negative. There are two complex ones.
- *Forgetting the pair.* If $2 + i$ is an eigenvalue of a real matrix, so is $2 - i$.
- *Using $a$ instead of $r$ as the scale factor.* The scaling per step is $|\lambda| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
- *Mixing up the sign convention* in $A = PCP^{-1}$: it pairs $\lambda = a - bi$ with $C = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}$.

## Key points

- Real matrices can have complex eigenvalues; they come in conjugate pairs $a \pm bi$, with conjugate eigenvectors.
- $\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}$ rotates by the angle of $(a, b)$ and scales by $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
- Any real $2 \times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ is similar to that rotation–scaling matrix: $A = PCP^{-1}$ with $P = [\,\operatorname{Re}\mathbf{v} \;\; \operatorname{Im}\mathbf{v}\,]$.
- Iterates spiral outward if $|\lambda| > 1$, inward if $|\lambda| < 1$.

lessons.title: Discrete dynamical systems and Markov chains
lessons.body:
## Systems that step forward in time

Many processes update a state vector by the same rule at every step: populations from one
year to the next, market shares from one month to the next, rental cars moving between
locations each day. When the rule is linear, the state evolves by $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A\mathbf{x}_k$,
and eigenvalues and eigenvectors predict the long-run behavior without computing hundreds of
steps. Markov chains are the most important special case. (The next lesson treats quantities
that change continuously in time, $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$.)

## Discrete dynamical systems

A **[[discrete dynamical system]]** is a sequence of vectors with $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A\mathbf{x}_k$
for $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, starting from an initial state $\mathbf{x}_0$. Then
$\mathbf{x}_k = A^k\mathbf{x}_0$.

Suppose $A$ is $n \times n$ with an eigenvector basis $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ and
eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$. Write $\mathbf{x}_0 = c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{v}_n$.
Because $A^k\mathbf{v}_i = \lambda_i^k\mathbf{v}_i$,

$$\mathbf{x}_k = c_1\lambda_1^k\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\lambda_2^k\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_n\lambda_n^k\mathbf{v}_n.$$

Each eigen-direction grows or decays on its own. Terms with $|\lambda_i| < 1$ fade away;
terms with $|\lambda_i| > 1$ grow; the term with the largest $|\lambda_i|$ eventually dominates,
so (if its weight $c_i \neq 0$) $\mathbf{x}_k$ lines up with that eigenvector and grows by a
factor of about $\lambda_i$ per step.

For $2 \times 2$ systems the origin is classified by the eigenvalues:

| Eigenvalues | Name | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| both $\lvert\lambda\rvert < 1$ | **[[attractor]]** | every trajectory tends to $\mathbf{0}$ |
| both $\lvert\lambda\rvert > 1$ | **[[repeller]]** | trajectories move away from $\mathbf{0}$ |
| one $\lvert\lambda\rvert > 1$, one $\lvert\lambda\rvert < 1$ | **[[saddle point]]** | attracted along one direction, repelled along the other |

The pictures show typical trajectories of each kind, with diagonal matrices so that the eigenvectors lie along the axes. Each dot is one step.

![Three panels of trajectories near the origin. Attractor: both eigenvalues less than 1 in absolute value, and every trajectory steps in toward the origin. Repeller: both eigenvalues greater than 1, and trajectories step away from the origin. Saddle point: one eigenvalue greater than 1 and one less than 1, and trajectories come in along the vertical axis and then leave along the horizontal axis.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1

Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.85 & 0.25 \\ 0.25 & 0.85\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x}_0 = (3, 1)$. Describe $\mathbf{x}_k$.

1. Eigenvectors: $A(1, 1) = (1.1, 1.1)$, so $\lambda_1 = 1.1$ with $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 1)$; $A(1, -1) = (0.6, -0.6)$, so $\lambda_2 = 0.6$ with $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1)$.
2. Decompose: $(3, 1) = 2(1, 1) + 1(1, -1)$.
3. So $\mathbf{x}_k = 2(1.1)^k(1, 1) + (0.6)^k(1, -1)$.
4. As $k$ grows, $(0.6)^k \to 0$, so $\mathbf{x}_k \approx 2(1.1)^k(1, 1)$: the two components become equal and grow 10% per step. The origin is a saddle point.

```plot
{"x": [-1, 8], "y": [-1, 8], "equal": true, "functions": [{"f": "x", "dashed": true, "label": "eigenvector line (λ = 1.1)"}], "points": [{"at": [3, 1], "label": "x₀"}, {"at": [2.8, 1.6]}, {"at": [2.78, 2.06]}, {"at": [2.88, 2.45]}, {"at": [3.06, 2.8]}, {"at": [3.3, 3.14]}, {"at": [3.59, 3.5]}, {"at": [3.93, 3.87]}, {"at": [4.3, 4.27]}, {"at": [4.73, 4.71]}, {"at": [5.19, 5.18]}], "caption": "The trajectory from x₀ = (3, 1) bends onto the line of the dominant eigenvector"}
```

## Markov chains

A **[[probability vector]]** has nonnegative entries that add up to 1. A **[[stochastic matrix]]** is a
square matrix whose columns are probability vectors. A **[[Markov chain]]** is a dynamical system
$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = P\mathbf{x}_k$ with $P$ stochastic and $\mathbf{x}_0$ a probability vector;
each $\mathbf{x}_k$, called a **[[state vector]]**, is then also a probability vector. Entry $p_{ij}$
is the probability of moving *to* state $i$ *from* state $j$ in one step.

### Example 2

A rental company has two lots, A and B. Each day, 80% of the cars at A stay at A and 20% are
returned to B; 30% of the cars at B end up at A and 70% stay at B. Today half the fleet is at
each lot. Find the distribution tomorrow and the day after.

1. Columns are "from", rows are "to": $P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7\end{bmatrix}$. Each column sums to 1.
2. $\mathbf{x}_1 = P\mathbf{x}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8(0.5) + 0.3(0.5) \\ 0.2(0.5) + 0.7(0.5)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.55 \\ 0.45\end{bmatrix}$.
3. $\mathbf{x}_2 = P\mathbf{x}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.44 + 0.135 \\ 0.11 + 0.315\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.575 \\ 0.425\end{bmatrix}$.

A transition diagram shows the numbers of $P$: an arrow for each move, labeled with its probability. The arrows leaving each lot add up to 1.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Transition diagram for the rental cars
  accDescr: Two lots, A and B. Each day 80 percent of the cars at lot A stay at A and 20 percent move to B. Of the cars at lot B, 30 percent move to A and 70 percent stay at B. The probabilities leaving each lot add up to 1, which is why each column of the stochastic matrix sums to 1.
  A(("Lot A")) -- "0.2" --> B(("Lot B"))
  B -- "0.3" --> A
  A -- "0.8" --> A
  B -- "0.7" --> B
```

## Steady states

A **[[steady-state vector]]** (or equilibrium) of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a probability vector
$\mathbf{q}$ with $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$: an eigenvector for eigenvalue 1, scaled so its entries
add to 1. Every stochastic matrix has eigenvalue 1 (the rows of $P - I$ add to the zero row, so
$P - I$ is singular). A stochastic matrix is **[[regular]]** if some power $P^k$ has all entries
strictly positive.

> *Theorem.* If $P$ is a regular stochastic matrix, it has a unique steady-state vector $\mathbf{q}$, and for every initial probability vector, $\mathbf{x}_k \to \mathbf{q}$.

To find $\mathbf{q}$: solve $(P - I)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, then divide by the sum of the entries.

### Example 3

Find the steady state for the rental cars.

1. $P - I = \begin{bmatrix} -0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & -0.3\end{bmatrix}$. Row 2 is $-1$ times row 1, so $-0.2x_1 + 0.3x_2 = 0$: $x_1 = 1.5x_2$.
2. Take $x_2 = 2$: $(3, 2)$. Divide by $3 + 2 = 5$: $\mathbf{q} = (0.6, 0.4)$.
3. Check: $P\mathbf{q} = (0.48 + 0.12,\ 0.12 + 0.28) = (0.6, 0.4)$. ✓

In the long run 60% of the cars are at lot A, whatever the starting split. The other
eigenvalue of $P$ is $0.5$ (from $\operatorname{tr} P = 1.5 = 1 + 0.5$), so the distance to the
steady state halves each day: $0.5 \to 0.55 \to 0.575 \to \cdots \to 0.6$.

## Common mistakes

- *Rows vs columns.* In this convention the *columns* of a stochastic matrix sum to 1, and $p_{ij}$ is the chance of going from $j$ to $i$.
- *Forgetting to normalize* the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$ into a probability vector.
- *Assuming every trajectory follows the dominant eigenvector.* If $\mathbf{x}_0$ has zero weight on it, it never appears.
- *Calling a system with eigenvalues 1.2 and 0.5 an attractor.* One eigenvalue bigger than 1 in absolute value makes the origin a saddle.

## Key points

- $\mathbf{x}_k = A^k\mathbf{x}_0 = \sum c_i\lambda_i^k\mathbf{v}_i$ when $\mathbf{x}_0 = \sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i$ in an eigenvector basis.
- The largest $|\lambda|$ dominates in the long run; $|\lambda| < 1$ terms die out. Attractor, repeller and saddle describe $2 \times 2$ cases.
- A stochastic matrix has probability-vector columns; a Markov chain is $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = P\mathbf{x}_k$.
- A steady state solves $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$ with entries summing to 1; for regular $P$ every chain converges to it.

lessons.title: Systems of differential equations
lessons.body:
## From steps to continuous time

The last lesson followed a state vector that jumps forward one step at a time,
$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A\mathbf{x}_k$. Many quantities change continuously instead: the temperatures
of connected rooms, the amounts of a drug in blood and tissue, the currents in a circuit, the
positions and velocities of masses joined by springs. When each rate of change is a linear
combination of the current values, the model is

$$\mathbf{x}'(t) = A\mathbf{x}(t),$$

a **[[system of linear differential equations]]**. Here $\mathbf{x}(t)$ is a vector of functions, the
prime means the derivative of every entry, and $A$ is a constant $n \times n$ matrix. Eigenvalues
and eigenvectors solve it in almost the same way they solved the discrete system; the only change
is that $\lambda^k$ becomes $e^{\lambda t}$. This lesson uses one fact from calculus: the
derivative of $e^{\lambda t}$ is $\lambda e^{\lambda t}$.

## Eigenvector solutions

For one equation, $x' = ax$ has the solutions $x(t) = ce^{at}$. For a system, try a solution that
keeps a fixed direction and changes only in size: $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$. Its
derivative is $\lambda e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$, and $A\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}A\mathbf{v}$. These
agree for every $t$ exactly when $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$:

> If $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, then $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$ solves $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$.

The system is linear, so sums and scalar multiples of solutions are again solutions. If $A$ has
an eigenvector basis $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$,
every solution has the form

$$\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2e^{\lambda_2t}\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_ne^{\lambda_nt}\mathbf{v}_n.$$

At $t = 0$ every exponential equals 1, so the weights come from the initial state:
$c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{x}(0)$, that is, $P\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{x}(0)$ with
$P = [\,\mathbf{v}_1 \;\cdots\; \mathbf{v}_n\,]$.

The steps, in order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Solving x prime equals A x with an eigenvector basis
  accDescr: Find the eigenvalues of A from the characteristic equation. Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. Solve P c equals x of 0 for the weights, where the columns of P are the eigenvectors. Write x of t as the sum of c i times e to the lambda i t times v i. Check that the formula gives x of 0 at t equals 0. Read off the long-run behavior from the signs of the real parts of the eigenvalues.
  A["Find the eigenvalues from det(A - λI) = 0"] --> B["Find an eigenvector vi for each λi"]
  B --> C["Solve Pc = x(0) for the weights"]
  C --> D["x(t) = c1 e^(λ1 t) v1 + ... + cn e^(λn t) vn"]
  D --> E["Check: t = 0 gives x(0)"]
  E --> F["Long run: signs of the real parts of the λi"]
```

### Example 1

Solve $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x}(0) = (3, 2)$.

1. Eigenvalues: $\operatorname{tr} A = 3$ and $\det A = -4$, so $\lambda^2 - 3\lambda - 4 = (\lambda - 4)(\lambda + 1) = 0$, giving $\lambda = 4$ and $\lambda = -1$.
2. Eigenvectors: $A - 4I = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ gives $\mathbf{v}_1 = (2, 3)$; $A + I = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ gives $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1)$.
3. Weights: $c_1(2, 3) + c_2(1, -1) = (3, 2)$ means $2c_1 + c_2 = 3$ and $3c_1 - c_2 = 2$. Adding, $5c_1 = 5$, so $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 1$.
4. Solution: $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{4t}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} + e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$.
5. Check: at $t = 0$ this is $(2 + 1, 3 - 1) = (3, 2)$. ✓ For large $t$ the $e^{-t}$ term dies away and $\mathbf{x}(t)$ runs off along the line through $(2, 3)$.

```plot
{"x": [-5, 5], "y": [-5, 5], "equal": true, "vectorField": {"u": "x + 2*y", "v": "3*x + 2*y", "step": 1}, "functions": [{"f": "1.5*x", "dashed": true, "label": "λ = 4"}, {"f": "-x", "dashed": true, "label": "λ = -1"}], "curves": [{"x": "2*exp(4*t) + exp(-t)", "y": "3*exp(4*t) - exp(-t)", "t": [-1.4, 0.2]}], "points": [{"at": [3, 2], "label": "x(0)"}], "caption": "A saddle: the solution comes in along the λ = -1 line and leaves along the λ = 4 line"}
```

## Decoupling

Why does this work? Change variables to eigenvector coordinates, $\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{y}$. Then
$P\mathbf{y}' = AP\mathbf{y}$, so

$$\mathbf{y}' = P^{-1}AP\,\mathbf{y} = D\mathbf{y}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad y_1' = \lambda_1y_1,\ \dots,\ y_n' = \lambda_ny_n.$$

In the original variables every rate depends on every other variable; in the new ones each
equation involves a single unknown. The system is **[[decoupled]]** into $n$ separate one-variable
equations, solved by $y_i = c_ie^{\lambda_it}$. Multiplying back by $P$ gives the general solution
above. This is the same idea as diagonalization, now applied to rates of change.

### Example 2

Two rooms share a wall. Let $x_1$ and $x_2$ be how many degrees each room is above the outdoor
temperature, with $t$ in hours. Each room loses heat outdoors at rate $2x_i$ and gains heat from
the other room at rate $x_j - x_i$, so $x_1' = -3x_1 + x_2$ and $x_2' = x_1 - 3x_2$. Room 1
starts $4^\circ$ above outside and room 2 at the outdoor temperature. Find $\mathbf{x}(t)$.

1. $A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}$. $A(1, 1) = (-2, -2)$ and $A(1, -1) = (-4, 4)$, so $\lambda_1 = -2$ with $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 1)$ and $\lambda_2 = -4$ with $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1)$.
2. Weights: $c_1(1, 1) + c_2(1, -1) = (4, 0)$ gives $c_1 = c_2 = 2$.
3. $\mathbf{x}(t) = 2e^{-2t}(1, 1) + 2e^{-4t}(1, -1)$, so $x_1 = 2e^{-2t} + 2e^{-4t}$ and $x_2 = 2e^{-2t} - 2e^{-4t}$.
4. Read the decoupled pieces: the average $\tfrac12(x_1 + x_2) = 2e^{-2t}$ decays at rate 2 (heat leaving the house), and the difference $x_1 - x_2 = 4e^{-4t}$ decays faster, at rate 4 (the rooms evening out).
5. Room 2 warms at first, then cools: $x_2' = -4e^{-2t} + 8e^{-4t} = 0$ when $e^{-2t} = \tfrac12$, at $t = \tfrac12\ln 2 \approx 0.35$ hours, where $x_2 = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5^\circ$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 2.5], "y": [0, 4.2], "xLabel": "t (hours)", "yLabel": "degrees above outside", "functions": [{"f": "2*exp(-2*x) + 2*exp(-4*x)", "color": "#2c5e8f"}, {"f": "2*exp(-2*x) - 2*exp(-4*x)", "dashed": true, "color": "#c2570c"}], "points": [{"at": [0.347, 0.5], "label": "peak"}], "labels": [{"at": [0.45, 2.3], "text": "room 1: x₁(t)"}, {"at": [1.1, 0.95], "text": "room 2: x₂(t), dashed"}], "caption": "Both rooms approach the outdoor temperature; room 2 first warms, then cools"}
```

## The matrix exponential

For one equation the solution is $x(t) = e^{at}x(0)$. The same formula works for systems once
$e^{At}$ is defined, using the power series of $e^x$:

$$e^{At} = I + At + \frac{(At)^2}{2!} + \frac{(At)^3}{3!} + \cdots$$

This **[[matrix exponential]]** always converges. Differentiating term by term gives
$\frac{d}{dt}e^{At} = A + A^2t + \frac{A^3t^2}{2!} + \cdots = Ae^{At}$, and $e^{A\cdot0} = I$, so

> $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}(0)$ is the solution of $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with initial state $\mathbf{x}(0)$.

You never sum the series by hand for a diagonalizable matrix. Since $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, every term
has the form $P(\cdots)P^{-1}$, and the diagonal series sums entry by entry:

$$e^{At} = Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}, \qquad e^{Dt} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{\lambda_1t} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & e^{\lambda_nt}\end{bmatrix}.$$

### Example 3

Find $e^{At}$ for the rooms matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}$.

1. From Example 2, $P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ and $D = \operatorname{diag}(-2, -4)$. Then $P^{-1} = \tfrac12\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$.
2. $Pe^{Dt} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{-2t} & e^{-4t} \\ e^{-2t} & -e^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}$.
3. $e^{At} = \dfrac12\begin{bmatrix} e^{-2t} + e^{-4t} & e^{-2t} - e^{-4t} \\ e^{-2t} - e^{-4t} & e^{-2t} + e^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}$.
4. Check: at $t = 0$ this is $I$. ✓ And $e^{At}(4, 0)$ is 4 times the first column, $(2e^{-2t} + 2e^{-4t},\ 2e^{-2t} - 2e^{-4t})$, matching Example 2.

Two cautions. First, $e^{At}$ is *not* the matrix of exponentials of the entries: in Example 3
the entries of $At$ are $-3t$ and $t$, and nothing like $e^{-3t}$ appears. Second, the series
also handles matrices that can't be diagonalized. For $N = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$,
$N^2 = 0$, so the series stops: $e^{Nt} = I + Nt = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.
For $\begin{bmatrix} \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda\end{bmatrix} = \lambda I + N$, the result is
$e^{\lambda t}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, so a missing eigenvector shows up as a
factor $t$. (The rule $e^{X + Y} = e^Xe^Y$ used here needs $XY = YX$, which holds because
$\lambda I$ commutes with everything.)

## Complex eigenvalues: spirals

For the rotation–scaling matrix $C = \begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}$ (eigenvalues
$a \pm bi$), the series gives

$$e^{Ct} = e^{at}\begin{bmatrix} \cos bt & -\sin bt \\ \sin bt & \cos bt\end{bmatrix}.$$

Every solution turns through the angle $bt$ (counterclockwise when $b > 0$) while its length is
multiplied by $e^{at}$: it spirals in if $a < 0$, spirals out if $a > 0$, and goes around a
closed loop if $a = 0$. A general real $2 \times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ is
$PCP^{-1}$, so its solutions are the same spirals viewed through the change of coordinates $P$.

```plot
{"x": [-4.5, 4.5], "y": [-4, 4], "equal": true, "vectorField": {"u": "-x - 2*y", "v": "2*x - y", "step": 1}, "curves": [{"x": "4*exp(-t)*cos(2*t)", "y": "4*exp(-t)*sin(2*t)", "t": [0, 6]}], "points": [{"at": [4, 0], "label": "x(0)"}], "caption": "x′ = Cx with a = -1, b = 2: eigenvalues -1 ± 2i, a spiral sink"}
```

## Stability

Each term $c_ie^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i$ decays when $\lambda_i < 0$ and grows when $\lambda_i > 0$,
and for complex $\lambda = a \pm bi$ the size is controlled by $e^{at}$. So the test is the *sign
of the real part*, not the size of $|\lambda|$:

> The origin is **[[asymptotically stable]]** (every solution tends to $\mathbf{0}$) exactly when every eigenvalue of $A$ has negative real part.

For $2 \times 2$ systems:

| Eigenvalues of $A$ | Origin | Solutions |
|---|---|---|
| real, both negative | **[[sink]]** (attractor) | approach $\mathbf{0}$ |
| real, both positive | **[[source]]** (repeller) | move away from $\mathbf{0}$ |
| real, opposite signs | saddle point | in along one eigenvector, out along the other |
| $a \pm bi$ with $a < 0$ | spiral sink | spiral in |
| $a \pm bi$ with $a > 0$ | spiral source | spiral out |
| $\pm bi$ (real part 0) | **[[center]]** | closed loops around $\mathbf{0}$ |

Because $\operatorname{tr} A = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2$ and $\det A = \lambda_1\lambda_2$ (complex
eigenvalues included), a $2 \times 2$ system is asymptotically stable exactly when
$\operatorname{tr} A < 0$ and $\det A > 0$. Example 1 ($\det A = -4$) is a saddle; Example 2
($\operatorname{tr} = -6$, $\det = 8$) is a sink.

The trace–determinant plane collects the whole table in one picture. The parabola $\det A = (\operatorname{tr} A)^2/4$ is where the discriminant $(\operatorname{tr} A)^2 - 4\det A$ is zero: above it the eigenvalues are complex (spirals and centers), below it they are real. Points exactly on the parabola or on the horizontal axis are borderline cases (a repeated eigenvalue, or an eigenvalue 0) not covered by the table.

![The trace-determinant plane, with trace on the horizontal axis and determinant on the vertical axis. Everything below the horizontal axis (negative determinant) is a saddle point. Above the axis, a dashed parabola det = tr²/4 separates regions: outside it on the left are sinks and on the right sources; inside it on the left are spiral sinks and on the right spiral sources; the positive vertical axis between them is the center.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The discrete and continuous tests fit together. Sampling a solution once per time unit gives
$\mathbf{x}(k + 1) = e^{A}\mathbf{x}(k)$, a discrete system whose matrix $e^A$ has eigenvalues
$e^{\lambda}$. Since $|e^{\lambda}| = e^{\operatorname{Re}\lambda}$, the condition $|e^{\lambda}| < 1$
is the same as $\operatorname{Re}\lambda < 0$.

## Common mistakes

- *Using the discrete test.* For $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$, eigenvalues $0.5$ and $0.8$ give a source, not an attractor: $e^{0.8t}$ grows. Look at the sign of the real part, not whether $|\lambda| < 1$.
- *Exponentiating entries.* $e^{At}$ is $Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}$ (or the series), never the matrix of $e^{a_{ij}t}$. Even for a diagonal matrix only the diagonal entries are exponentiated; the zeros stay 0.
- *Using $\mathbf{x}(0)$ as the weights.* The weights solve $P\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{x}(0)$; they equal the entries of $\mathbf{x}(0)$ only when the eigenvectors are the standard basis.
- *Pairing a weight with the wrong exponential.* $c_i$ and $e^{\lambda_it}$ go with the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_i$ for that same $\lambda_i$.

## Key points

- If $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, then $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$ solves $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$; with an eigenvector basis, $\mathbf{x}(t) = \sum c_ie^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i$ where $P\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{x}(0)$.
- The substitution $\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{y}$ decouples the system into $y_i' = \lambda_iy_i$.
- $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}(0)$, with $e^{At} = \sum (At)^k/k!$; for diagonalizable $A$, $e^{At} = Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}$.
- Asymptotically stable ⟺ every eigenvalue has negative real part ($2 \times 2$: $\operatorname{tr} A < 0$ and $\det A > 0$). Complex eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ give spirals, and $a = 0$ gives a center.

lessons.title: The Cayley–Hamilton theorem and the minimal polynomial
lessons.body:
## A matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation

In the characteristic equation lesson, the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$
was a tool for *finding* eigenvalues: plug in numbers, look for zeros. This lesson plugs in
something else: the matrix $A$ itself. The surprising result, the **[[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]]**, is
that the answer is always the zero matrix. It turns high powers of $A$ into low ones, gives a
formula for $A^{-1}$ without row reduction, and leads to the *minimal polynomial*, which
decides whether a matrix is diagonalizable without finding a single eigenvector.

## Polynomials in a matrix

If $q(t) = c_0 + c_1t + c_2t^2 + \cdots + c_mt^m$ is an ordinary polynomial and $A$ is square,
the **[[matrix polynomial]]** $q(A)$ is

$$q(A) = c_0I + c_1A + c_2A^2 + \cdots + c_mA^m.$$

The constant term becomes $c_0I$, not $c_0$: you can't add a number to a matrix. Two facts make
matrix polynomials easy to work with.

- *They factor like ordinary polynomials.* Powers of the same matrix commute, so if
  $q(t) = (t - 2)(t - 5)$ then $q(A) = (A - 2I)(A - 5I)$, in either order.
- *They act on eigenvectors by plugging in the eigenvalue.* If $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, then
  $A^k\mathbf{v} = \lambda^k\mathbf{v}$ for every $k$, so
  $$q(A)\mathbf{v} = q(\lambda)\mathbf{v}.$$
  So every eigenvector of $A$ is an eigenvector of $q(A)$, with eigenvalue $q(\lambda)$.

## The Cayley–Hamilton theorem

> *Cayley–Hamilton theorem.* If $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ is the characteristic polynomial of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, then $p(A) = 0$, the $n \times n$ zero matrix.

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix the characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$, so
the theorem says

$$A^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\,A + (\det A)\,I = 0.$$

You can check this directly for $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$: the top-left entry of $A^2$ is
$a^2 + bc$, and $a^2 + bc - (a + d)a + (ad - bc) = 0$. The other three entries cancel the same way.

*Why it's true when $A$ is diagonalizable.* Write $A = PDP^{-1}$. Then $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$ for every $k$,
so $p(A) = P\,p(D)\,P^{-1}$, and $p(D)$ is diagonal with entries $p(\lambda_1), \dots, p(\lambda_n)$. Each
$\lambda_i$ is a root of $p$, so $p(D) = 0$ and $p(A) = 0$. Equivalently: $p(A)$ sends every vector of an
eigenvector basis to $p(\lambda_i)\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{0}$, so it is the zero matrix.

*The general case (proof sketch).* Not every matrix is diagonalizable, so a different argument
is needed. Let $M(\lambda) = \operatorname{adj}(A - \lambda I)$, the adjugate. Its entries are cofactors of
$A - \lambda I$, polynomials of degree at most $n - 1$, so $M(\lambda) = B_0 + B_1\lambda + \cdots + B_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}$
for some constant matrices $B_j$. The adjugate formula from the Cramer's rule lesson says
$(A - \lambda I)M(\lambda) = p(\lambda)I$ for every $\lambda$. Expanding the left side and matching the
coefficient of each power of $\lambda$ gives $n + 1$ matrix equations; multiplying the one for
$\lambda^j$ on the left by $A^j$ and adding them all, the left side telescopes to $0$ and the right
side is $p(A)$. (Filling in every step is a good exercise, but it isn't needed in this course.)

*A tempting wrong proof.* "Substitute $\lambda = A$: $p(A) = \det(A - AI) = \det 0 = 0$." This mixes
up two different things. $\det(A - \lambda I)$ is a *number* for each number $\lambda$; putting a
matrix inside the determinant this way gives the number $0$, while $p(A)$ is a *matrix* built from
powers of $A$. The real theorem says that matrix is zero, which is much more.

*History.* William Rowan Hamilton proved a special case in 1853, phrased in terms of quaternions.
Arthur Cayley stated the result in his 1858 memoir on matrices, checked it for $2 \times 2$ matrices,
said he had verified the $3 \times 3$ case, and saw no need for a general proof. Ferdinand Georg
Frobenius gave the first general proof in 1878.

### Example 1

Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}$. Verify Cayley–Hamilton, then use it to find $A^{-1}$ and $A^3$.

1. $\operatorname{tr} A = 7$ and $\det A = 12 - 2 = 10$, so $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10$ (eigenvalues 2 and 5).
2. $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 7 \\ 14 & 18\end{bmatrix}$, and $A^2 - 7A + 10I = \begin{bmatrix} 11 - 21 + 10 & 7 - 7 \\ 14 - 14 & 18 - 28 + 10\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$. ✓
3. *Inverse.* Rewrite $A^2 - 7A = -10I$ as $A(7I - A) = 10I$. So $A^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{10}(7I - A) = \tfrac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}$. (This is the familiar $2 \times 2$ inverse formula in disguise: $7I - A$ swaps the diagonal and negates the rest.)
4. *Cube.* $A^2 = 7A - 10I$, so $A^3 = A \cdot A^2 = 7A^2 - 10A = 7(7A - 10I) - 10A = 39A - 70I$.
5. $A^3 = 39\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} - 70I = \begin{bmatrix} 47 & 39 \\ 78 & 86\end{bmatrix}$. Multiplying $A^2$ by $A$ directly gives the same matrix. ✓

The pattern in step 4 works for any power: each time a power higher than $n - 1$ appears, the
theorem replaces it with lower powers. *Every power of an $n \times n$ matrix is a combination of
$I, A, \dots, A^{n-1}$.*

## High powers by remainders

That last fact can be made efficient. Divide $t^k$ by $p(t)$ (ordinary polynomial division):
$t^k = Q(t)p(t) + r(t)$, with a remainder $r$ of degree less than $n$. Replace $t$ by $A$: since
$p(A) = 0$, we get $A^k = r(A)$. To find $r$ without long division, plug in the eigenvalues:
$p(\lambda_i) = 0$, so $\lambda_i^k = r(\lambda_i)$. With $n$ distinct eigenvalues that is $n$ equations for
the $n$ coefficients of $r$.

### Example 2

$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 2 and 3. Write $A^k = \alpha A + \beta I$ and find $A^{10}$.

1. The remainder $r(t) = \alpha t + \beta$ must agree with $t^k$ at both eigenvalues: $2\alpha + \beta = 2^k$ and $3\alpha + \beta = 3^k$.
2. Subtract: $\alpha = 3^k - 2^k$. Then $\beta = 2^k - 2\alpha = 3\cdot2^k - 2\cdot3^k$.
3. So $A^k = (3^k - 2^k)A + (3\cdot2^k - 2\cdot3^k)I$. The top-left entry is $4(3^k - 2^k) + 3\cdot2^k - 2\cdot3^k = 2\cdot3^k - 2^k$, matching the formula found by diagonalization in the Diagonalization lesson. ✓
4. For $k = 10$: $\alpha = 59049 - 1024 = 58025$ and $\beta = 3072 - 118098 = -115026$, so
   $A^{10} = 58025A - 115026I = \begin{bmatrix} 117074 & -116050 \\ 58025 & -57001\end{bmatrix}$.

No eigenvectors and no $P^{-1}$ were needed, only the eigenvalues.

## The minimal polynomial

The characteristic polynomial is one polynomial that sends $A$ to zero, but it may not be the
smallest. Call $q$ an **[[annihilating polynomial]]** of $A$ if $q(A) = 0$. A polynomial is *monic* if
its leading coefficient is 1. The **[[minimal polynomial]]** $m(t)$ of $A$ is the monic polynomial of
smallest degree with $m(A) = 0$. Three facts about it:

1. *It divides every annihilating polynomial.* Divide: $q = Qm + r$ with $\deg r < \deg m$. Then
   $r(A) = q(A) - Q(A)m(A) = 0$, and a nonzero $r$ would beat $m$'s degree, so $r = 0$.
   In particular $m$ divides the characteristic polynomial (Cayley–Hamilton), so $\deg m \le n$.
2. *Its roots are exactly the eigenvalues.* If $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$,
   then $\mathbf{0} = m(A)\mathbf{v} = m(\lambda)\mathbf{v}$, so $m(\lambda) = 0$. And every root of $m$ is a root
   of the characteristic polynomial, since $m$ divides it. Only the *multiplicities* can differ.
3. *It detects diagonalizability.*

> *Theorem.* A real square matrix $A$ is diagonalizable (with real $P$ and $D$) exactly when its minimal polynomial is a product of distinct real linear factors, $m(t) = (t - \lambda_1)(t - \lambda_2)\cdots(t - \lambda_s)$ with $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_s$ different.

One direction is short. If $A$ is diagonalizable with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_s$,
let $q(t) = (t - \lambda_1)\cdots(t - \lambda_s)$. For an eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, the
factor $A - \lambda_iI$ sends it to $\mathbf{0}$ (the factors commute, so put that one last), so $q(A)$ kills
an entire eigenvector basis and $q(A) = 0$. Then $m$ divides $q$, and since every $\lambda_i$ must be a
root of $m$, $m = q$. The other direction (no repeated factor forces enough eigenvectors) takes
more machinery; we state it without proof.

So to test diagonalizability: list the distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_s$ and compute the
single product $(A - \lambda_1I)\cdots(A - \lambda_sI)$. Zero means diagonalizable; nonzero means not.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Testing diagonalizability with the minimal polynomial
  accDescr: Start from the characteristic polynomial. If some eigenvalue is not real, the matrix is not diagonalizable with real matrices. Otherwise list the distinct eigenvalues lambda 1 to lambda s and compute the product of A minus lambda i times I over all of them. If the product is the zero matrix, the minimal polynomial has no repeated factor and A is diagonalizable. If it is not zero, the minimal polynomial has a repeated factor and A is not diagonalizable.
  A["Find the characteristic polynomial and its roots"] --> B{"All roots real?"}
  B -- "no" --> N1["Not diagonalizable with real matrices"]
  B -- "yes" --> C["List the distinct eigenvalues λ1, ..., λs"]
  C --> D["Compute (A - λ1 I)(A - λ2 I)...(A - λs I)"]
  D --> E{"Is the product the zero matrix?"}
  E -- "yes" --> Y["m(t) has no repeated factor: diagonalizable"]
  E -- "no" --> N2["m(t) has a repeated factor: not diagonalizable"]
```

### Example 3

Find the minimal polynomials of $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ and $S = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}$. Both have characteristic polynomial $-(\lambda - 2)^2(\lambda - 5)$.

1. The candidates are the monic divisors that contain every eigenvalue: $(t - 2)(t - 5)$ or $(t - 2)^2(t - 5)$.
2. For $B$: $B - 2I$ is the all-ones matrix $J$, and $B - 5I = J - 3I$. Since $J^2 = 3J$, $(B - 2I)(B - 5I) = J^2 - 3J = 0$. So $m_B(t) = (t - 2)(t - 5)$, and $B$ is diagonalizable, as the Diagonalization lesson found by counting eigenvectors.
3. For $S$: $(S - 2I)(S - 5I) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \ne 0$.
4. So $m_S(t) = (t - 2)^2(t - 5)$, the full characteristic polynomial up to sign. The repeated factor means $S$ is not diagonalizable: its eigenvalue 2 has only one independent eigenvector.

### Example 4

Use Cayley–Hamilton to find $B^{-1}$ for the matrix $B$ of Example 3.

1. For a $3 \times 3$ matrix, $\det(\lambda I - B) = \lambda^3 - (\operatorname{tr} B)\lambda^2 + c\lambda - \det B$, where $c$ is the sum of the three products of pairs of eigenvalues. With eigenvalues $2, 2, 5$: $\operatorname{tr} B = 9$, $c = 4 + 10 + 10 = 24$, $\det B = 20$.
2. Cayley–Hamilton: $B^3 - 9B^2 + 24B - 20I = 0$, so $B(B^2 - 9B + 24I) = 20I$ and $B^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{20}(B^2 - 9B + 24I)$.
3. $B^2$ has 11 on the diagonal and 7 elsewhere. Diagonal of $B^2 - 9B + 24I$: $11 - 27 + 24 = 8$; off-diagonal: $7 - 9 = -2$.
4. $B^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix} 8 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 8 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}$. Check one entry of $BB^{-1}$: row 1 times column 1 is $\tfrac{1}{20}(24 - 2 - 2) = 1$. ✓

(The minimal polynomial gives an even shorter route here: $(B - 2I)(B - 5I) = 0$ means $B^2 - 7B + 10I = 0$, so $B^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{10}(7I - B)$, which is the same matrix.)

## Common mistakes

- *Writing the constant term as a number.* In $A^2 - 7A + 10I$ the last term is $10I$; "$A^2 - 7A + 10$" is meaningless.
- *The determinant "proof".* Substituting $\lambda = A$ inside $\det(A - \lambda I)$ proves nothing; the theorem is about the matrix $p(A)$.
- *Thinking $p(A) = 0$ makes $A$ zero.* It is a relation among the powers of $A$, not a statement about $A$ alone.
- *Dropping an eigenvalue from the minimal polynomial.* Every eigenvalue is a root of $m$; only multiplicities can shrink.
- *Assuming $m = p$ always.* For $B$ above, $m$ has degree 2 while $p$ has degree 3. For $I$, the minimal polynomial is $t - 1$.

## Key points

- For a polynomial $q$, $q(A) = c_0I + c_1A + \cdots$, and $q(A)\mathbf{v} = q(\lambda)\mathbf{v}$ for each eigenvector.
- Cayley–Hamilton: $p(A) = 0$. For $2 \times 2$: $A^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)A + (\det A)I = 0$.
- Consequences: every power of $A$ is a combination of $I, \dots, A^{n-1}$; for invertible $2 \times 2$ $A$, $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det A}\big((\operatorname{tr} A)I - A\big)$; $A^k = r(A)$ where $r$ matches $t^k$ at the eigenvalues.
- The minimal polynomial is the monic annihilating polynomial of least degree; it divides $p$ and has the same roots.
- $A$ is diagonalizable ⟺ its minimal polynomial has only distinct real linear factors.

lessons.title: Defective matrices and the Jordan form
lessons.body:
## When there aren't enough eigenvectors

The Diagonalization lesson ended with a warning: $S = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ has the
eigenvalue 2 twice but only one independent eigenvector, so it can't be written as $PDP^{-1}$. And
in the differential equations lesson, the matrix exponential of $\begin{bmatrix} \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda\end{bmatrix}$
contained a strange factor $t$. This lesson explains both. A matrix without an eigenvector basis
is called **[[defective]]**: some eigenvalue has geometric multiplicity smaller than its algebraic
multiplicity. Defective matrices can't be made diagonal, but they can always be made *almost*
diagonal: eigenvalues on the diagonal and a few 1s just above it. That is the Jordan form.

## Generalized eigenvectors and Jordan chains

If $\lambda$ has too few eigenvectors, look one step further. Eigenvectors are the nonzero
solutions of $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. A **[[generalized eigenvector]]** for $\lambda$ is a
nonzero $\mathbf{v}$ with $(A - \lambda I)^k\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for some $k \ge 1$. Every eigenvector is
one (with $k = 1$); the new ones need $k \ge 2$.

The useful way to find them is a chain. Start with an eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1$ and solve

$$(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1, \qquad (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{v}_2, \qquad \dots$$

as long as these systems are consistent. The vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$ form a
**[[Jordan chain]]**: $A - \lambda I$ pushes each one down to the previous one and sends $\mathbf{v}_1$ to $\mathbf{0}$.
Rearranged, the chain equations say

$$A\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda\mathbf{v}_1, \qquad A\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_1, \qquad A\mathbf{v}_3 = \lambda\mathbf{v}_3 + \mathbf{v}_2, \ \dots$$

So $A$ doesn't keep $\mathbf{v}_2$ on its own line: it stretches it by $\lambda$ and then shifts it by
$\mathbf{v}_1$. The vectors of a Jordan chain are linearly independent (apply $(A - \lambda I)^{k-1}$ to a
dependence relation and only the coefficient of $\mathbf{v}_k$ survives; repeat).

## Jordan blocks

Put a chain into the columns of $P = [\,\mathbf{v}_1 \;\cdots\; \mathbf{v}_k\,]$. Column by column, $AP = PJ$ where

$$J = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda & 1 & & \\ & \lambda & \ddots & \\ & & \ddots & 1 \\ & & & \lambda\end{bmatrix}$$

has $\lambda$ on the diagonal, 1s on the superdiagonal, and zeros elsewhere: column $j$ of $PJ$ is
$\lambda\mathbf{v}_j + \mathbf{v}_{j-1}$, exactly $A\mathbf{v}_j$. This $k \times k$ matrix is a **[[Jordan block]]**.
A $1 \times 1$ Jordan block is just $[\lambda]$, so a diagonal matrix is made of $1 \times 1$ blocks.

Write a block as $J = \lambda I + N$, where $N$ has 1s on the superdiagonal. $N$ shifts coordinates
($N\mathbf{e}_1 = \mathbf{0}$, $N\mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{e}_1$, ...), so $N^k = 0$ for a $k \times k$ block.
A matrix with some power equal to zero is called **[[nilpotent]]**.

> *Jordan form theorem.* If every eigenvalue of the $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is real, there is an invertible real $P$ with $A = PJP^{-1}$, where $J$ is block diagonal with Jordan blocks on its diagonal. $J$, the **[[Jordan form]]** of $A$, is unique except for the order of the blocks. (Allowing complex numbers, every square matrix has a Jordan form.)

The proof, which builds a basis out of Jordan chains, belongs to a second course. What you can
read off $J$:

- the eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, each repeated by its algebraic multiplicity;
- the number of blocks for $\lambda$ equals the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda$ (each block contributes one eigenvector, the first vector of its chain);
- $A$ is diagonalizable exactly when every block is $1 \times 1$;
- the size of the largest block for $\lambda$ is the power of $(t - \lambda)$ in the minimal polynomial.

The block sizes can be found from ranks: the number of blocks for $\lambda$ of size at least $j$ is
$\operatorname{rank}(A - \lambda I)^{j-1} - \operatorname{rank}(A - \lambda I)^{j}$, where $(A - \lambda I)^0 = I$ has rank $n$.

The form is named for Camille Jordan, who described it in his 1870 treatise on permutation groups
and equations. Karl Weierstrass's theory of elementary divisors (1868) contains an equivalent
classification, and in 1874 the two approaches led to a public dispute between Jordan and Leopold
Kronecker.

### Example 1

Find the Jordan form of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and a formula for $A^k$.

1. $\operatorname{tr} A = 4$, $\det A = 3 + 1 = 4$: $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 4 = (\lambda - 2)^2$. One eigenvalue, $\lambda = 2$, with algebraic multiplicity 2.
2. $A - 2I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ has rank 1, so the eigenspace is 1-dimensional: $A$ is defective. Eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, -1)$.
3. Chain: solve $(A - 2I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1$, i.e. $x_1 + x_2 = 1$ (the second equation is the negative of the first). Take $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, 0)$.
4. $P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, $J = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$. Check $AP = PJ$: both are $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}$. ✓
5. Powers: $J^k = (2I + N)^k$, and since $N^2 = 0$ the binomial expansion stops after two terms (allowed because $2I$ and $N$ commute): $J^k = 2^kI + k2^{k-1}N = \begin{bmatrix} 2^k & k2^{k-1} \\ 0 & 2^k\end{bmatrix}$.
6. $A^k = PJ^kP^{-1}$ with $P^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ gives $A^k = 2^{k-1}\begin{bmatrix} k + 2 & k \\ -k & 2 - k\end{bmatrix}$. Check $k = 1$: $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ ✓; $k = 2$: $2\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix} = A^2$. ✓

The vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ is not unique: $(0, 1)$, or $\mathbf{v}_2$ plus any multiple of $\mathbf{v}_1$, works too, giving a different $P$ but the same $J$.

```plot
{"x": [-2.5, 3.8], "y": [-1.8, 1.5], "equal": true, "functions": [{"f": "-x", "dashed": true}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [1, -1], "arrow": true, "label": "v₁"}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [1, 0], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [2, 0], "dashed": true, "arrow": true}, {"from": [2, 0], "to": [3, -1], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [3, -1], "arrow": true, "label": "Av₂"}], "labels": [{"at": [-1.9, 0.4], "text": "eigenvector line"}, {"at": [3.2, -0.55], "text": "+ v₁"}, {"at": [0.5, 0.22], "text": "v₂"}, {"at": [1.5, 0.22], "text": "2v₂"}], "caption": "A stretches v₂ by 2 and then shifts it by v₁: Av₂ = 2v₂ + v₁"}
```

In general, for a $k \times k$ block the powers are
$J^m = \lambda^mI + \binom{m}{1}\lambda^{m-1}N + \binom{m}{2}\lambda^{m-2}N^2 + \cdots$, so the entries one, two, ...
places above the diagonal are $m\lambda^{m-1}$, $\binom{m}{2}\lambda^{m-2}$, and so on. For example, with
$\lambda = 2$ and a $3 \times 3$ block, $J^4$ has 16 on the diagonal, $4 \cdot 2^3 = 32$ just above it, and
$\binom{4}{2}2^2 = 24$ in the corner. Polynomial factors like $m$ and $\binom{m}{2}$ are the signature of a
defective matrix. In a dynamical system $\mathbf{x}_{m+1} = A\mathbf{x}_m$ with $|\lambda| < 1$ they don't change
the long-run verdict ($m\lambda^{m-1} \to 0$ still), but they can make the state grow for a while
before it decays.

### Example 2

A $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $-(\lambda - 5)^3$. List its possible Jordan forms, and find the one for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}$.

1. The block sizes for 5 must add up to 3: $1 + 1 + 1$, $2 + 1$, or $3$. The number of blocks equals $\dim\operatorname{Nul}(A - 5I) = 3 - \operatorname{rank}(A - 5I)$.

| $\operatorname{rank}(A - 5I)$ | Eigenspace dimension | Blocks | Minimal polynomial |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3 | three $1 \times 1$ ($A = 5I$) | $t - 5$ |
| 1 | 2 | one $2 \times 2$, one $1 \times 1$ | $(t - 5)^2$ |
| 2 | 1 | one $3 \times 3$ | $(t - 5)^3$ |

2. For the given matrix, $A - 5I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ has rank 1, so there are two blocks: $J = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}$.
3. Check with the rank formula: blocks of size at least 2 number $\operatorname{rank}(A - 5I) - \operatorname{rank}(A - 5I)^2 = 1 - 0 = 1$, since $(A - 5I)^2 = 0$. ✓ One block of size 2, and the remaining size is a $1 \times 1$ block.

## The exponential of a Jordan block

The same splitting $J = \lambda I + N$ solves $\mathbf{x}' = J\mathbf{x}$. Because $\lambda I$ and $N$ commute,
$e^{Jt} = e^{\lambda t}e^{Nt}$, and the series for $e^{Nt}$ stops once $N^k = 0$:

$$e^{Jt} = e^{\lambda t}\Big(I + tN + \tfrac{t^2}{2!}N^2 + \cdots + \tfrac{t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}N^{k-1}\Big).$$

For a $2 \times 2$ block, $e^{Jt} = e^{\lambda t}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, the formula from the
differential equations lesson. In terms of a chain $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2$ of $A$, the solutions of
$\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ are

$$\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2e^{\lambda t}\big(t\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2\big),$$

with the weights again from $P\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{x}(0)$. (Check the second piece: its derivative is
$\lambda e^{\lambda t}(t\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2) + e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1$, and $A$ times it is
$e^{\lambda t}(t\lambda\mathbf{v}_1 + \lambda\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_1)$, the same.)

### Example 3

Solve $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ for the matrix of Example 1 with $\mathbf{x}(0) = (1, 2)$.

1. From Example 1: $\lambda = 2$, $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, -1)$, $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, 0)$.
2. Weights: $c_1(1, -1) + c_2(1, 0) = (1, 2)$. The second entries give $-c_1 = 2$, so $c_1 = -2$; then $c_2 = 1 - c_1 = 3$.
3. $\mathbf{x}(t) = -2e^{2t}(1, -1) + 3e^{2t}\big(t(1, -1) + (1, 0)\big) = e^{2t}(1 + 3t,\ 2 - 3t)$.
4. Check: at $t = 0$ this is $(1, 2)$. ✓ The derivative of the first entry is $e^{2t}(2 + 6t + 3) = e^{2t}(5 + 6t)$, and row 1 of $A\mathbf{x}$ is $e^{2t}\big(3(1 + 3t) + (2 - 3t)\big) = e^{2t}(5 + 6t)$. ✓

## A fragile form

The Jordan form is a theoretical tool more than a computational one. It jumps under tiny changes:
$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ \varepsilon & 2\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $2 \pm \sqrt{\varepsilon}$, distinct for every small
$\varepsilon > 0$, so it is diagonalizable, while at $\varepsilon = 0$ it is a single Jordan block. A
computer working with rounded numbers can't reliably tell these apart, so numerical software
avoids the Jordan form and uses other factorizations, such as the Schur form (a unitary change of basis to a triangular matrix;
for a real matrix with real eigenvalues the change of basis can be taken orthogonal). Exact matrices with small integer entries, like the ones in this
lesson, are where the Jordan form is computed by hand.

## Common mistakes

- *Assuming a repeated eigenvalue means a Jordan block.* $5I$ has eigenvalue 5 three times and is diagonal. Count eigenvectors (or ranks) first.
- *Solving $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{0}$ again.* The second chain vector solves $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1$, with $\mathbf{v}_1$ on the right.
- *Putting the chain in the wrong order.* The eigenvector goes in the first column of $P$; then the 1 sits above the diagonal.
- *Computing $J^k$ entrywise.* $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}^k$ has $k2^{k-1}$ in the corner, not $1^k = 1$.
- *Forgetting the factor $t$.* For a $2 \times 2$ block the solutions include $te^{\lambda t}$, not just $e^{\lambda t}$.

## Key points

- A matrix is defective when some eigenvalue has fewer independent eigenvectors than its algebraic multiplicity.
- A Jordan chain solves $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{0}$, $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v}_{j+1} = \mathbf{v}_j$; then $A\mathbf{v}_{j+1} = \lambda\mathbf{v}_{j+1} + \mathbf{v}_j$.
- Every matrix with real eigenvalues is $PJP^{-1}$ with $J$ made of Jordan blocks $\lambda I + N$; one block per independent eigenvector.
- $J^m$ and $e^{Jt}$ follow from the binomial expansion and the series, which stop because $N$ is nilpotent: factors $m\lambda^{m-1}$ and $te^{\lambda t}$ appear.
- The Jordan form is exact but fragile; software uses other factorizations.

lessons.title: Population models and the Perron–Frobenius theorem
lessons.body:
## Why do population models settle down?

The dynamical systems lesson showed that $\mathbf{x}_k = A^k\mathbf{x}_0$ is eventually dominated by
the eigenvalue of largest absolute value, *if* there is a single such eigenvalue and the starting
vector has some weight on its eigenvector. For Markov chains, the steady-state theorem promised
that a regular stochastic matrix always has a probability vector it settles into. Why are those
"ifs" so reliably true in models of populations, probabilities and rankings? Because those
matrices have no negative entries, and nonnegative matrices obey a remarkable theorem of Oskar
Perron and Georg Frobenius. This lesson builds the classic age-structured population model and
uses it to see the theorem at work.

## The Leslie model

Split a population of females into age classes of equal width (say 0–1, 1–2 and 2–3 years for a
short-lived bird) and count them once per time step of the same width. Two kinds of numbers drive
the model:

- the *fecundity* $f_i$: average number of newborn daughters (counted at the next census) per female in class $i$;
- the *survival rate* $s_i$: fraction of class $i$ alive one step later, and therefore in class $i + 1$.

Newborns all enter class 1, and survivors move up one class, so for three classes

$$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = L\mathbf{x}_k, \qquad L = \begin{bmatrix} f_1 & f_2 & f_3 \\ s_1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$$

A matrix of this shape (fecundities across the top row, survival rates just below the diagonal,
zeros elsewhere) is a **[[Leslie matrix]]**, after P. H. Leslie, who published the model in
*Biometrika* in 1945. Every entry is nonnegative, and survival rates are between 0 and 1.
(Real studies have to decide which sex to count and exactly when births are recorded; counting
females only is the usual simplification.)

### Example 1

A bird population has three age classes with
$L = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 1.5 \\ 0.9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 0\end{bmatrix}$. Starting from $\mathbf{x}_0 = (90, 60, 30)$, find $\mathbf{x}_1$. Then find the long-run growth rate and age distribution.

1. One step: $\mathbf{x}_1 = (2 \cdot 60 + 1.5 \cdot 30,\ 0.9 \cdot 90,\ 0.5 \cdot 60) = (165, 81, 30)$. The total went from 180 to 276, a factor of about 1.53.
2. Characteristic equation. Expanding $\det(L - \lambda I)$ along the first row gives $-\lambda^3 + f_1\lambda^2 + f_2s_1\lambda + f_3s_1s_2 = 0$; here $f_1 = 0$, so (multiplying by $-1$) $\lambda^3 - 1.8\lambda - 0.675 = 0$.
3. Try $\lambda = 1.5$: $3.375 - 2.7 - 0.675 = 0$. ✓ Dividing out $(\lambda - 1.5)$ leaves $\lambda^2 + 1.5\lambda + 0.45$, with roots $\frac{-1.5 \pm \sqrt{0.45}}{2} \approx -0.415$ and $-1.085$. So 1.5 is the eigenvalue of largest absolute value.
4. Eigenvector for 1.5: the second row says $0.9x_1 = 1.5x_2$, so $x_2 = 0.6x_1$; the third says $0.5x_2 = 1.5x_3$, so $x_3 = x_2/3 = 0.2x_1$. With $x_1 = 5$: $\mathbf{v} = (5, 3, 1)$. Check row 1: $2 \cdot 3 + 1.5 \cdot 1 = 7.5 = 1.5 \cdot 5$. ✓
5. In the long run the population grows by a factor of 1.5 per step (50%), with the age classes in the ratio $5 : 3 : 1$, that is $\tfrac59 \approx 56\%$, $\tfrac39 \approx 33\%$ and $\tfrac19 \approx 11\%$.

The eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, scaled so its entries add to 1, is the
**[[stable age distribution]]**. The pattern in step 4 works for every Leslie matrix: the eigenvector
for $r$ is $\big(1,\ \tfrac{s_1}{r},\ \tfrac{s_1s_2}{r^2},\ \dots\big)$, so it is automatically positive.

```plot
{"x": [0, 16], "y": [0, 2.8], "xLabel": "step k", "yLabel": "growth factor of the total", "functions": [{"f": "1.5", "dashed": true, "label": "r = 1.5"}], "points": [{"at": [1, 0.9]}, {"at": [2, 2.5]}, {"at": [3, 1.02]}, {"at": [4, 2.029]}, {"at": [5, 1.213]}, {"at": [6, 1.758]}, {"at": [7, 1.34]}, {"at": [8, 1.629]}, {"at": [9, 1.414]}, {"at": [10, 1.566]}, {"at": [11, 1.454]}, {"at": [12, 1.534]}, {"at": [13, 1.476]}, {"at": [14, 1.518]}, {"at": [15, 1.487]}], "caption": "Starting with 100 newborns only, the step-to-step growth factor swings and then settles at 1.5"}
```

The swings in the picture come from the eigenvalue $-1.085$: it is negative, so its term flips
sign every step, and $|{-1.085}|/1.5 \approx 0.72$ says how much of the swing survives each step.
The closer that ratio is to 1, the slower the population settles.

## The Perron–Frobenius theorem

Write $\rho(A)$ for the largest absolute value of an eigenvalue of $A$ (its *spectral radius*). An
eigenvalue equal to $\rho(A)$ and strictly larger in absolute value than every other eigenvalue is a
*dominant eigenvalue*. A square matrix $A$ with nonnegative entries is a **[[primitive matrix]]** if
some power $A^k$ has all entries strictly positive. (A regular stochastic matrix is exactly a
primitive stochastic matrix.) The **[[Perron–Frobenius theorem]]** describes the eigenvalues of primitive matrices:

> *Perron–Frobenius theorem (for primitive matrices).* If $A$ is primitive, then:
> 1. $r = \rho(A)$ is a positive real eigenvalue of $A$, and it is dominant: $|\lambda| < r$ for every other eigenvalue $\lambda$.
> 2. $r$ is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial, so its eigenspace is a line.
> 3. That line contains a vector with all entries positive.
> 4. No other eigenvalue has an eigenvector with all entries nonnegative.

Perron proved this for matrices with all entries positive in 1907; Frobenius extended it to
nonnegative matrices in 1912. (The full theorem also covers *irreducible* matrices, which may have
several eigenvalues of absolute value $r$; this lesson uses only the primitive case.)

What it buys: if $A$ is primitive and $\mathbf{x}_0$ is nonnegative and nonzero, then $\mathbf{x}_0$ has
positive weight on the positive eigenvector $\mathbf{v}$, and

$$\mathbf{x}_k = A^k\mathbf{x}_0 \approx c\,r^k\,\mathbf{v} \quad\text{for large } k, \text{ with } c > 0.$$

The shares $\mathbf{x}_k / (\text{sum of entries})$ approach $\mathbf{v}$ scaled to sum 1, whatever the start.
Two familiar results are special cases:

- *Markov chains.* Every column of a stochastic matrix sums to 1, which forces $\rho(P) = 1$ (a
  bound below makes this precise). For a regular $P$, Perron–Frobenius gives a unique positive
  steady state that every chain approaches: the steady-state theorem.
- *Leslie models.* A Leslie matrix whose last class reproduces and whose survival rates are all positive is
  primitive if, for example, two neighboring age classes both have positive fecundity (as in Example 1, classes 2 and 3).

A quick bound on $r$ without solving anything: for a nonnegative matrix, $r$ lies between the
smallest and largest *row* sums, and also between the smallest and largest *column* sums ($A$ and
$A^T$ have the same eigenvalues). For a stochastic matrix every column sum is 1, so $r = 1$.

Repeatedly multiplying by $A$ and rescaling, as in the plot above, is also how $r$ and $\mathbf{v}$
are computed for very large matrices; numerical analysts call it the *power method*.

### Example 2

Why primitivity matters. A species breeds only in its second year: $L = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ 0.25 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, starting from $\mathbf{x}_0 = (100, 0)$.

1. $\mathbf{x}_1 = (0, 25)$, $\mathbf{x}_2 = (100, 0)$, $\mathbf{x}_3 = (0, 25)$, ... The population alternates forever and never settles into a fixed age distribution.
2. Eigenvalues: $\lambda^2 - 4(0.25) = 0$, so $\lambda = \pm1$. Two eigenvalues share the largest absolute value, so there is no dominant eigenvalue.
3. $L$ is not primitive: $L^2 = I$, and every power is either $L$ or $I$, each with zero entries.
4. If even a few first-year birds breed, say $f_1 = 0.2$, then $L^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1.04 & 0.8 \\ 0.05 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is positive, the matrix is primitive, and the oscillation dies out. The eigenvalues become $\frac{0.2 \pm \sqrt{0.04 + 4}}{2} \approx 1.105$ and $-0.905$.

## Growth or decline: the net reproductive number

Ecologists often want just one thing: will the population grow or shrink? Let
$\ell_1 = 1$, $\ell_2 = s_1$, $\ell_3 = s_1s_2$, ... be the chance that a newborn survives to reach
class $i$. The **[[net reproductive number]]**

$$R_0 = f_1\ell_1 + f_2\ell_2 + f_3\ell_3 + \cdots$$

is the expected number of daughters a newborn female produces over her whole life.

> For a Leslie matrix whose last class reproduces, $r > 1$ exactly when $R_0 > 1$, $r = 1$ exactly when $R_0 = 1$, and $r < 1$ exactly when $R_0 < 1$.

*Why.* Divide the characteristic equation by $\lambda^n$; it becomes
$g(\lambda) = \dfrac{f_1\ell_1}{\lambda} + \dfrac{f_2\ell_2}{\lambda^2} + \cdots = 1$ (the discrete Euler–Lotka equation).
For $\lambda > 0$, $g$ is strictly decreasing, so it equals 1 at exactly one positive $\lambda$, which
is $r$. Since $g(1) = R_0$: if $R_0 > 1$ then $g(1) > 1 = g(r)$, which forces $r > 1$, and similarly
for the other cases.

### Example 3

For the birds of Example 1, find $R_0$, and find the first-year survival $s_1$ that would make the population exactly stationary.

1. $\ell_1 = 1$, $\ell_2 = 0.9$, $\ell_3 = 0.9 \cdot 0.5 = 0.45$.
2. $R_0 = 0 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 0.9 + 1.5 \cdot 0.45 = 1.8 + 0.675 = 2.475 > 1$: growth, consistent with $r = 1.5$.
3. With unknown $s_1$: $R_0 = 2s_1 + 1.5 \cdot 0.5\,s_1 = 2.75s_1$. Setting $R_0 = 1$ gives $s_1 = 1/2.75 \approx 0.364$.
4. Check: with $s_1 = 4/11$, the characteristic equation $\lambda^3 = 2s_1\lambda + 0.75s_1$ at $\lambda = 1$ reads $1 = \tfrac{8}{11} + \tfrac{3}{11}$. ✓ So $r = 1$: if fewer than about 36% of first-year birds survived, this population would decline.

Note what $R_0$ and $r$ measure differently: $R_0$ is per *generation* and $r$ is per *time step*.
They agree on the verdict (above or below 1) but not on the size.

## Common mistakes

- *Putting survival rates on the diagonal.* Survivors move *up* a class, so $s_i$ sits in row $i + 1$, column $i$.
- *Expecting every nonnegative matrix to have a dominant eigenvalue.* Example 2 is nonnegative but not primitive, and it oscillates.
- *Reading the growth rate as $R_0$.* $R_0 = 2.475$ in Example 1, but the population grows by 1.5 per step.
