Row-equivalent matrices usually have different entries; column 2 of $A$ is twice column 1, so it is not a pivot column; size, not squareness, is all that matters.

questions.stem: A $3 \times 3$ matrix has columns with $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ not multiples of each other and $\mathbf{a}_3 = 4\mathbf{a}_1 + 5\mathbf{a}_2$. Without row-reducing, column 3 of its RREF is $(\;$___, ___, $0)$.
questions.explanation: Columns 1 and 2 are pivot columns ($\mathbf{a}_1 \ne \mathbf{0}$, and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is not a multiple of $\mathbf{a}_1$), so in the RREF they are $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$. The relation $\mathbf{a}_3 = 4\mathbf{a}_1 + 5\mathbf{a}_2$ holds in the RREF too, so column 3 is $4\mathbf{e}_1 + 5\mathbf{e}_2 = (4, 5, 0)$.

questions.stem: In mathematics, an invariant of a process is:
choices: A step of the process that can be undone
A quantity or property that the process never changes
The final result the process produces
A quantity that changes by the same amount at every step
questions.explanation: An invariant is something the process leaves unchanged; for row operations, the column relations (equivalently the solutions of the homogeneous system). Reversibility is a different property of row operations, and the RREF is the result, not an invariant.

questions.stem: Which of these can an elementary row operation change?
choices: Whether column 3 equals column 1 plus column 2
The solution set of the homogeneous system with coefficient matrix $A$
questions.explanation: Row operations change entries all the time; for example $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - R_1$ changes every column whose first two entries differ. The other three are all fixed by the column relations, which no row operation can change.

questions.stem: The RREF of $A$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$. Which statements about the columns of $A$ are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The pivot columns are 1 and 3. Column 2 of the RREF is $2\mathbf{e}_1$, so $\mathbf{a}_2 = 2\mathbf{a}_1$. Column 4 is $-\mathbf{e}_1 + 3\mathbf{e}_2$, and $\mathbf{e}_2$ is the second pivot column, which is column 3, so $\mathbf{a}_4 = -\mathbf{a}_1 + 3\mathbf{a}_3$. Column 1 is a pivot column, so it is nonzero. Column 3 is a pivot column, so it is not a combination of the columns to its left. The last choice uses column 2 instead of the second pivot column.

questions.stem: Why is comparing echelon forms (not reduced) a poor test of whether two matrices are row equivalent?
choices: Echelon forms never exist for non-square matrices
Comparing them takes more arithmetic than the RREF
One matrix can have many different echelon forms, so different echelon forms prove nothing
Echelon forms change the solution set of the system
questions.explanation: The same matrix can reduce to different echelon forms (the lesson's example gave $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 5 \\ 0 & -6 & -12\end{bmatrix}$), so two different echelon forms could still come from row-equivalent matrices. The RREF is unique, so comparing RREFs settles the question. Every matrix has echelon forms, and row operations never change solution sets.

questions.stem: The columns of a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ have no column relation except $c_1 = c_2 = c_3 = 0$. What is the RREF of $A$?
choices: It depends on the row operations used
questions.explanation: With no nontrivial relation, no column is a combination of the columns to its left (column 1 is not even zero), so all three columns are pivot columns: $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3$. That is the identity matrix. The RREF never depends on the row operations used.

questions.stem: Apply one Jacobi sweep to $4x + y = 9$, $x + 3y = 5$, starting from $(x_0, y_0) = (1, 1)$. What is $(x_1, y_1)$?
questions.explanation: Jacobi uses only the old values: $x_1 = \tfrac14(9 - y_0) = \tfrac14(9 - 1) = 2$ and $y_1 = \tfrac13(5 - x_0) = \tfrac13(5 - 1) = \tfrac43$. $(2, 1)$ is the Gauss–Seidel result (it uses the new $x_1 = 2$ for $y$); $\left(\tfrac94, \tfrac53\right)$ starts from $(0, 0)$; $(8, 4)$ forgets to divide by the diagonal coefficients.

questions.stem: Apply one Gauss–Seidel sweep to $4x + y = 9$, $x + 3y = 5$, starting from $(x_0, y_0) = (1, 1)$. Then $x_1 =$ ___ and $y_1 =$ ___.
questions.explanation: First $x_1 = \tfrac14(9 - y_0) = \tfrac14(9 - 1) = 2$. Gauss–Seidel uses this new value at once: $y_1 = \tfrac13(5 - x_1) = \tfrac13(5 - 2) = 1$. So $(x_1, y_1) = (2, 1)$, which happens to be the exact solution.

questions.stem: Which matrices are strictly diagonally dominant? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Compare each diagonal entry's absolute value with the sum of the absolute values of the rest of its row. $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}$: $4 > 1$, $5 > 2$. The first $3 \times 3$: $3 > 2$, $4 > 3$, $3 > 2$. The second $3 \times 3$: $|-6| = 6 > 5$, $3 > 2$, $4 > 2$. $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ fails in row 1 ($2$ is not greater than $2$), and $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ fails in both rows.

questions.stem: The edges of this plate are held at the temperatures shown. For each numbered interior point, choose the sum of its neighbors that lie on the edge.

image.alt: A square plate with four numbered interior points in a 2 by 2 grid: 1 top left, 2 top right, 3 bottom left, 4 bottom right. Edge points above the top row are at 80 degrees, below the bottom row at 20 degrees, left of the left column at 40 degrees and right of the right column at 60 degrees.

questions.explanation: Point 1 (top left) touches the top edge (80) and the left edge (40): 120. Point 2 touches top (80) and right (60): 140. Point 3 touches left (40) and bottom (20): 60. Point 4 touches right (60) and bottom (20): 80. These sums are the right-hand sides of $4T_i - (\text{interior neighbors}) = \text{sum}$. No point touches both the top and the bottom edge, so no sum is $80 + 20 = 100$.

questions.stem: In the plate of the lesson, $T_4$ (bottom right) has neighbors $T_2$ (above), $T_3$ (left), 60 (right) and 20 (below). Which equation does the averaging rule give?
questions.explanation: $T_4 = \tfrac14(T_2 + T_3 + 60 + 20)$. Multiply by 4 and move the unknowns left: $4T_4 - T_2 - T_3 = 80$. 45 is the value of $T_4$, not the right side; $T_1$ is diagonal to $T_4$, not a neighbor; 20 uses only one edge neighbor.

questions.stem: Put the steps of one Gauss–Seidel sweep for three unknowns in order.
choices: Compute the new $x_1$ from equation 1, using the old $x_2$ and $x_3$
Compute the new $x_2$ from equation 2, using the new $x_1$ and the old $x_3$
Compute the new $x_3$ from equation 3, using the new $x_1$ and $x_2$
Compare with the previous guess to decide whether to stop
questions.explanation: Gauss–Seidel updates the unknowns in turn, each time using the newest values available, so $x_2$ needs the new $x_1$ and $x_3$ needs both. The stopping test compares the finished sweep with the previous guess, so it comes last.

questions.stem: Jacobi on $x + 2y = 3$, $3x + y = 4$ produces $(3, 4)$, $(-5, -5)$, $(13, 19)$, … Why does it fail?
choices: In the order written, the coefficient matrix is not diagonally dominant
Jacobi only works for systems with more than two unknowns
The starting guess $(0, 0)$ is too far from the solution
questions.explanation: Row 1 has diagonal 1 against 2, and row 2 has 1 against 3, so the guesses can (and do) blow up. The system has the solution $(1, 1)$. Swapping the equations gives $3x + y = 4$, $x + 2y = 3$, which is strictly diagonally dominant, and then Jacobi converges from any start, including $(0, 0)$.

questions.stem: Match each term with its description.
choices: Reaches the exact answer in a fixed number of steps
Improves a guess sweep by sweep
Most of its entries are zero
Each diagonal entry outweighs the rest of its row
questions.explanation: Row reduction is a direct method; Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel are iterative. Grid models give sparse matrices. "Outweighs" means the diagonal entry's absolute value is larger than the sum of the absolute values of the other entries in its row. A matrix with every entry nonzero is called dense.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel methods is true?
choices: Jacobi uses each new value as soon as it is computed
Both need the exact solution as their starting guess
Gauss–Seidel uses each new value as soon as it is computed
They always produce the same guesses after each sweep
questions.explanation: That is the only difference between them: Gauss–Seidel uses new values immediately, while Jacobi waits for the next sweep. Their guesses therefore differ (in the lesson, $y_1 \approx 1.6667$ for Jacobi and $0.9167$ for Gauss–Seidel). Any starting guess works when the matrix is strictly diagonally dominant.

questions.stem: In the equilibrium model, an interior point has neighbors at 70°, 50°, 62° and 58°. What is its temperature, in degrees? Give only the number: ___
questions.explanation: Each interior temperature is the average of its four neighbors: $\tfrac14(70 + 50 + 62 + 58) = \tfrac{240}{4} = 60$.

questions.stem: Which change makes the Jacobi method for $2x + 7y = 9$, $5x - y = 4$ certain to converge?
choices: Keep the equations in the order given
Start from the guess $(1, 1)$ instead of $(0, 0)$
questions.explanation: Reordered, the matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ 2 & 7\end{bmatrix}$: $5 > 1$ and $7 > 2$, so it is strictly diagonally dominant and Jacobi converges from any start. As given, row 1 has $2 < 7$. Multiplying a row by 10 scales the diagonal entry and the rest of the row alike, so the comparison doesn't change. A different starting guess doesn't create a guarantee. (The exact solution is $(1, 1)$, but you rarely know it in advance.)

questions.stem: A plate model on a $1000 \times 1000$ grid has a million unknowns. Why are iterative methods attractive for it?
choices: Each sweep uses only the few nonzero coefficients, so it is cheap and the matrix stays sparse
They give the exact answer in fewer steps than row reduction
They converge for every linear system
questions.explanation: Each equation has at most 5 nonzero coefficients, so a sweep costs a few operations per unknown, while plain row reduction would take on the order of $n^3$ operations and fill in many zeros. Iterative methods give approximations, need a stopping rule, and can diverge (as in the lesson's Example 4).

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: If the coefficient matrix is strictly diagonally dominant, Jacobi converges from any starting guess
A system that is not diagonally dominant can never be solved by Gauss–Seidel
Swapping two equations can change whether Jacobi converges
A small change between two sweeps proves that the answer is accurate
A system with a strictly diagonally dominant matrix has exactly one solution
questions.explanation: The convergence theorem gives the first and last statements, and Example 4 shows a swap turning divergence into convergence. Diagonal dominance is sufficient, not necessary: some other systems still converge (larger plate grids, for example). A small change between sweeps is only a practical stopping rule, not a proof of accuracy.

questions.stem: Apply one Jacobi sweep to $2x - y = 6$, $x + 4y = 8$, starting from $(0, 0)$. Then $x_1 =$ ___ and $y_1 =$ ___.
questions.explanation: Solve equation 1 for $x$: $x = \tfrac12(6 + y)$, and equation 2 for $y$: $y = \tfrac14(8 - x)$. With the old values $x_0 = y_0 = 0$: $x_1 = 3$ and $y_1 = 2$. (The next sweep gives $x_2 = \tfrac12(6 + 2) = 4$ and $y_2 = \tfrac14(8 - 3) = 1.25$.)

questions.stem: The picture shows vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ lying in a shaded plane, a long line through the origin in the direction of a vector $\mathbf{w}$, and a dark arrow $\mathbf{b}$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A shaded plane in three-dimensional space with two blue arrows lying in it from a common point, a long red line crossing the plane at that point, and a dark arrow pointing up out of the plane from the same point. Four numbered markers: on the common point, on an empty part of the plane, on the red line, and on the dark arrow.

choices: A vector not in Span{u, v}
A line not through the origin
questions.explanation: Every span contains $\mathbf{0}$, so the plane and the line both pass through the origin (1), where all the arrows start. Two vectors that are not multiples of each other span a plane (2); one nonzero vector spans a line (3). The arrow $\mathbf{b}$ (4) leaves the plane, so it is not a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$. A line not through the origin can never be a span.

questions.stem: Let $\mathbf{v}_1 = (2, 1)$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = (-1, 2)$. Fill in the weights: $(3, 4)$ equals ___ times $\mathbf{v}_1$ plus ___ times $\mathbf{v}_2$. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: Solve $x_1(2, 1) + x_2(-1, 2) = (3, 4)$: $2x_1 - x_2 = 3$ and $x_1 + 2x_2 = 4$. From the first, $x_2 = 2x_1 - 3$; then $x_1 + 4x_1 - 6 = 4$, so $x_1 = 2$ and $x_2 = 1$. Check: $2(2, 1) + (-1, 2) = (3, 4)$. ✓ This is the combination drawn in the lesson.

questions.stem: Put the steps for deciding whether $\mathbf{b}$ is in $\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1, \dots, \mathbf{a}_n\}$, and finding the weights if it is, in order.
choices: Row-reduce it to an echelon form
Check whether the last column has a pivot
If it has none, finish the reduced echelon form and read off the weights
Check the weights by computing the linear combination
questions.explanation: The given vectors become columns, with $\mathbf{b}$ last. An echelon form already shows whether there is a pivot in the last column (inconsistent, so $\mathbf{b}$ is not in the span). Only a consistent system has weights to read off, and the check comes once you have them.

questions.stem: Which vectors are in $\operatorname{Span}\{(1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 2)\}$? Select all that apply.
In $\mathbb{R}^3$, match each span to its shape. Here $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are nonzero and not multiples of each other.
choices: A line that misses the origin
questions.explanation: The only combination of $\mathbf{0}$ is $\mathbf{0}$. One nonzero vector spans a line through the origin, and adding a multiple of it ($2\mathbf{u}$) adds nothing new. Two non-parallel vectors span a plane through the origin. The standard basis vectors reach every $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = x_1\mathbf{e}_1 + x_2\mathbf{e}_2 + x_3\mathbf{e}_3$. No span misses the origin.

questions.stem: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$, the first entry of $A\mathbf{x}$ is ___ and the second entry is ___.
questions.explanation: Row–vector rule: $1(2) + 2(-1) = 0$ and $3(2) + (-1)(-1) = 7$. Column view: $2\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}$.

questions.stem: Match each fact about row reduction to what it tells you.
left: $A$ has a pivot position in every row
An echelon form of $A$ has a row of zeros
An echelon form of $[\,A \;\; \mathbf{b}\,]$ has a pivot in the last column
An echelon form of $[\,A \;\; \mathbf{b}\,]$ has no pivot in the last column
choices: Ax = b is consistent for every b
Some b make Ax = b inconsistent
This particular system has no solution
This particular system has at least one solution
This particular system has exactly one solution
questions.explanation: Pivots in every row of the coefficient matrix $A$ rule out a row $[\,0 \;\cdots\; 0 \;\; d\,]$ for every $\mathbf{b}$. A zero row of $A$'s echelon form lets you choose $\mathbf{b}$ so that row ends in a nonzero number. For one particular $\mathbf{b}$, a pivot in the last column of the augmented matrix means inconsistent, and no pivot there means consistent. "Exactly one solution" also needs a pivot in every column of $A$, which none of the facts says.

questions.stem: $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix. Which statements are equivalent to "the columns of $A$ span $\mathbb{R}^m$"? Select all that apply.
choices: $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a solution for every $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$
$A$ has a pivot position in every row
$A$ has a pivot position in every column
Every $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ is a linear combination of the columns of $A$
questions.explanation: The theorem in this lesson makes spanning, solvability for every $\mathbf{b}$, every $\mathbf{b}$ being a combination of the columns, and a pivot in every row all equivalent. A pivot in every column (equivalently, only the trivial solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$) is a different property: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ has a pivot in its only column but its column spans just a line in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

questions.stem: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \\ 3 & 7 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is consistent exactly when $b_3 = b_1 + b_2$. If $b_1 = 2$ and $b_2 = -5$, the system is consistent only when $b_3 =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $b_3 = b_1 + b_2 = 2 + (-5) = -3$. For any other $b_3$, row 3 of the reduced augmented matrix is $[\,0 \;\; 0 \;\; 0 \;\; b_3 - b_1 - b_2\,]$ with a nonzero last entry.

questions.stem: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}$, for which $\mathbf{b}$ is $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ consistent?
questions.explanation: $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 + 2R_1$ turns $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -2 & b_1 \\ -2 & 4 & b_2\end{array}\right]$ into $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -2 & b_1 \\ 0 & 0 & b_2 + 2b_1\end{array}\right]$. $A$ has no pivot in row 2, so not every $\mathbf{b}$ works; the system is consistent exactly when $b_2 + 2b_1 = 0$, that is, $b_2 = -2b_1$. Both columns are multiples of $(1, -2)$, so their span is that line.

questions.stem: The picture shows the solution sets of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ and $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ (with $\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{0}$) for a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ with two free variables. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two parallel shaded planes, one above the other. A point on the lower plane has a blue arrow lying in the lower plane and a red arrow rising from it to a point on the upper plane; a dashed blue arrow on the upper plane runs from that point to another point. Five numbered markers: on the starting point in the lower plane, on the red arrow, on an empty part of the lower plane, on an empty part of the upper plane, and on the end of the dashed arrow.

questions.explanation: The homogeneous solutions form a plane through the origin (1, 3). A particular solution $\mathbf{p}$ (2) reaches the parallel plane of solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ (4). Adding a homogeneous solution $\mathbf{v}_h$ to $\mathbf{p}$ gives another solution $\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}_h$ (5). The vector $\mathbf{b}$ lives in the codomain, not among the solutions $\mathbf{x}$, so it is not drawn here.

questions.stem: Put the steps for writing the solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ in parametric vector form in order.
choices: Solve for the basic variables in terms of the free variables
Write $\mathbf{x}$ as a single column of those expressions
Split the column into a constant vector plus one vector times each free variable
questions.explanation: You can only solve for basic variables after the RREF shows which they are; the column is built from those solved expressions; and splitting it is the last step, giving $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + s\mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v} + \cdots$.

questions.stem: The solutions of $x_1 - 4x_2 + 2x_3 = 0$ are $\mathbf{x} = x_2\mathbf{u} + x_3\mathbf{v}$, where $\mathbf{u}$ = (___, 1, 0) and $\mathbf{v}$ = (___, 0, 1). Fill in the two missing first entries.
questions.explanation: Solve for the basic variable: $x_1 = 4x_2 - 2x_3$, with $x_2, x_3$ free. So $\mathbf{x} = (4x_2 - 2x_3, x_2, x_3) = x_2(4, 1, 0) + x_3(-2, 0, 1)$. A common slip is keeping the signs from the original equation ($-4$ and $2$); moving the terms across flips them.

questions.stem: $\mathbf{p} = (1, 2, 0)$ solves $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ (with $\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{0}$), and the solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ are exactly the multiples $t(1, -1, 1)$. Which vectors solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
The solutions are $\mathbf{p} + t(1, -1, 1) = (1 + t, 2 - t, t)$.
- $(1, 2, 0)$: $t = 0$. ✓
- $(2, 1, 1)$: $t = 1$. ✓
- $(0, 3, -1)$: $t = -1$. ✓
- $(1, -1, 1)$: this is a homogeneous solution, so $A$ sends it to $\mathbf{0}$, not $\mathbf{b}$. ✗
- $(2, 3, 1)$: the third entry forces $t = 1$, but then the second entry would be 1, not 3. ✗

questions.stem: $A$ is a $3 \times 5$ matrix with 2 pivot positions. The solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ in parametric vector form is the span of how many vectors?
questions.explanation: Each free variable contributes one vector. With 5 columns and 2 pivot columns there are $5 - 2 = 3$ free variables, so the solution set is the span of 3 vectors. (2 is the number of pivots, not free variables.)

questions.stem: Match each set of vectors to whether it is linearly independent or dependent.
questions.explanation: $(2, 4) = 2(1, 2)$, so the first pair is dependent. The standard basis vectors are independent (their matrix is $I_3$). Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ are always dependent. Any set containing $\mathbf{0}$ is dependent. One nonzero vector is independent. All five follow from the quick tests, with no row reduction needed.

questions.stem: The vectors $(1, 2, -1)$, $(2, 5, 1)$ and $(0, 1, h)$ are linearly dependent exactly when $h =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Row-reduce $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & h\end{bmatrix}$. $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ gives $[\,0 \;\; 1 \;\; 1\,]$; $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 + R_1$ gives $[\,0 \;\; 3 \;\; h\,]$; $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 3R_2$ gives $[\,0 \;\; 0 \;\; h - 3\,]$. Column 3 lacks a pivot exactly when $h = 3$. (Then $(0, 1, 3) = (2, 5, 1) - 2(1, 2, -1)$.)

questions.stem: $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\mathbb{R}^4$. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
choices: No vector in the set is a linear combination of the others
None of the three vectors is $\mathbf{0}$
The matrix $[\,\mathbf{v}_1 \;\; \mathbf{v}_2 \;\; \mathbf{v}_3\,]$ has a pivot in every row
questions.explanation: A dependent set has a vector that is a combination of the others, so an independent one doesn't. A dependence relation among $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2$ would also be one for all three (weight 0 on $\mathbf{v}_3$), so the smaller set is independent. A set containing $\mathbf{0}$ is dependent. But the $4 \times 3$ matrix has at most 3 pivots, so it can't have one in each of its 4 rows: three vectors never span $\mathbb{R}^4$.

questions.stem: In the left panel, $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ all lie in one plane through the origin, and $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ are not parallel. What follows?

image.alt: Two panels. Left, labeled dependent: vectors u, v and w all lie in one shaded plane. Right, labeled independent: u and v lie in the plane and w points out of it.

choices: The set is dependent, because $\mathbf{w}$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$
The set is independent, because no two of the vectors are parallel
The set is dependent, because it has more vectors than $\mathbb{R}^3$ has entries
Independence can't be decided from a picture in $\mathbb{R}^3$
questions.explanation: Two non-parallel vectors span their plane, so any $\mathbf{w}$ in that plane equals $a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v}$, giving the nontrivial relation $a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}$. "No two parallel" is not enough for three or more vectors. Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is not "more vectors than entries" (that would need four).

questions.stem: $[\,\mathbf{v}_1 \;\; \mathbf{v}_2 \;\; \mathbf{v}_3\,]$ has reduced echelon form $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$. Complete the dependence relation: ___ $\mathbf{v}_1 +$ ___ $\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0}$.
questions.explanation: The RREF says $x_1 - 3x_3 = 0$ and $x_2 + 2x_3 = 0$, so $x_1 = 3x_3$ and $x_2 = -2x_3$. With $x_3 = 1$: $3\mathbf{v}_1 - 2\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0}$. Reading the entries $-3$ and $2$ straight from the matrix gives the signs backwards.

questions.stem: Which of these is an affine combination of points $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$?
questions.explanation: The weights of an affine combination add to 1: $3 + (-2) = 1$. The others have weight sums $2$, $0$ and $\tfrac34$. (Negative weights are allowed; $3\mathbf{p} - 2\mathbf{q}$ is the point at $t = -2$ on the line through $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$.)

questions.stem: $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are different points in $\mathbb{R}^3$. What is the set of all their affine combinations?
questions.explanation: $(1 - t)\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{p} + t(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p})$ for all real $t$ is the whole line through the two points. The segment needs $0 \le t \le 1$ (convex combinations); the plane comes from linear combinations; the line through $\mathbf{0}$ is $\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}\}$, the affine hull shifted back to the origin.

questions.stem: With $\mathbf{p} = (1, 1)$ and $\mathbf{q} = (5, 3)$, the point $(7, 4)$ equals $(1 - t)\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{q}$ for $t =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $(1 - t)\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{p} + t(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}) = (1 + 4t, 1 + 2t)$. Setting $1 + 4t = 7$ gives $t = 1.5$, and then $1 + 2(1.5) = 4$. ✓ Since $t > 1$, the point lies on the line beyond $\mathbf{q}$, outside the segment.

questions.stem: $\mathbf{y}$ is an affine combination of $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3$ exactly when:
questions.explanation: With weights adding to 1, $\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{v}_1 = c_2(\mathbf{v}_2 - \mathbf{v}_1) + c_3(\mathbf{v}_3 - \mathbf{v}_1)$, and the steps reverse. Being in the span of the $\mathbf{v}_i$ ignores the sum condition, and the span of the differences without subtracting $\mathbf{v}_1$ from $\mathbf{y}$ describes the flat moved to the origin, not the flat itself.

questions.stem: With $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 0, 2)$, $\mathbf{v}_2 = (3, 1, 1)$, $\mathbf{v}_3 = (0, 2, 4)$, which weights $(c_1, c_2, c_3)$ write $\mathbf{y} = (2, 3, 3)$ as an affine combination?
questions.explanation: $-\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 = (-1 + 3 + 0, 0 + 1 + 2, -2 + 1 + 4) = (2, 3, 3)$, and $-1 + 1 + 1 = 1$. ✓ The others give $(4, -1, -1)$, $(3, 3, 5)$ (and weights adding to 2) and $(-2, 1, 5)$. Since the three points are affinely independent, these weights are the only ones.

questions.stem: Which sets of points are affinely independent? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
Test the differences from the first point.
- $(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$: independent, a triangle. ✓
- $(1, 1)$, $(2, 2)$: parallel, the points are collinear. ✗
- $(1, 1)$: one nonzero difference; any two distinct points are affinely independent. ✓
- Four points in $\mathbb{R}^2$: at most $2 + 1 = 3$ can be affinely independent. ✗
- $(-1, 1, 0)$, $(-1, 0, 1)$: not parallel, so the three points form a triangle. ✓ (As vectors these three points are also linearly independent, but that is a different test.)

questions.stem: What is the largest number of affinely independent points in $\mathbb{R}^3$?
questions.explanation: Lifted to $(\mathbf{v}_i, 1)$ the points become vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$, and at most 4 vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$ are independent. Four is reached by the corners of a tetrahedron, such as $\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3$. The answer 3 is the largest number of linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

questions.stem: For each numbered point, describe its barycentric coordinates relative to triangle $\mathbf{v}_1\mathbf{v}_2\mathbf{v}_3$.

image.alt: A shaded triangle with corners v1 (bottom left), v2 (right) and v3 (top). Four numbered markers: one inside the triangle, one on the edge from v2 to v3, one outside the triangle beyond that edge, and one on the corner v1.

choices: One is zero, the other two positive
Two are zero and one is 1
questions.explanation: Inside the triangle all three coordinates are positive (1). On the edge $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbf{v}_3$ the weight on $\mathbf{v}_1$ is 0 (2). Across that edge, outside, the weight on $\mathbf{v}_1$ is negative (3). At the corner $\mathbf{v}_1$ the coordinates are $(1, 0, 0)$ (4). Barycentric coordinates always add to 1, so they can't all be negative or add to 0.

questions.stem: The centroid of a triangle is the average $\tfrac13(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3)$ of its corners. Each of its three barycentric coordinates equals ___. Give an exact fraction.
questions.explanation: $\tfrac13\mathbf{v}_1 + \tfrac13\mathbf{v}_2 + \tfrac13\mathbf{v}_3$ has weights adding to 1, and barycentric coordinates are unique, so they are $(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$: equal masses at the corners balance at the centroid.

questions.stem: Find the barycentric coordinates $(c_1, c_2, c_3)$ of $(1, 2)$ relative to $\mathbf{v}_1 = (0, 0)$, $\mathbf{v}_2 = (4, 0)$, $\mathbf{v}_3 = (0, 4)$.
questions.explanation: $c_1(0, 0) + c_2(4, 0) + c_3(0, 4) = (4c_2, 4c_3) = (1, 2)$ gives $c_2 = \tfrac14$, $c_3 = \tfrac12$, and then $c_1 = 1 - \tfrac14 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. The choice $(0, \tfrac14, \tfrac12)$ forgets that the weights must add to 1; the others mix up which weight goes with which corner.

questions.stem: Match each kind of combination $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_p\mathbf{v}_p$ to the condition on its weights.
choices: Weights add to 1, and none is negative
questions.explanation: Linear combinations allow any weights. Affine combinations require $c_1 + \cdots + c_p = 1$. Convex combinations also require every $c_i \ge 0$, so they are mixtures. Equal weights $\tfrac1p$ give one particular convex combination, the average.

questions.stem: Alloy A is 10% copper and alloy B is 30% copper by mass. What fraction of a mix should be alloy B to get 25% copper?
questions.explanation: With fraction $t$ of B, the copper content is the convex combination $(1 - t)(10) + t(30) = 10 + 20t$. Setting $10 + 20t = 25$ gives $t = \tfrac34$: three parts B to one part A. ($\tfrac14$ is the fraction of A.)

questions.stem: Solving for a mixture of three blends gives the weights $c_1 = \tfrac{17}{15}$, $c_2 = -\tfrac{7}{15}$, $c_3 = \tfrac13$, and these are the only weights that work. What does this mean?
choices: Use 17 parts of the first blend, 7 of the second and 5 of the third
The target is not in the plane of the three blends
The target is outside the triangle of blends, so no mixture produces it
The three blends are affinely dependent
questions.explanation: The weights add to 1, so the target is an affine combination: it lies in the plane. But a negative weight would mean adding a negative amount of the second blend. The only weights are not all nonnegative, so the target is outside the convex hull of the blends and no real mixture reaches it. Unique weights also show the blends are affinely independent.

questions.stem: In the picture, $\mathbf{p} = (4, 4)$ is inside the triangle, $\mathbf{m}$ is on the edge $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbf{v}_3$, and $\mathbf{q}$ is beyond that edge. Order the four points by their first barycentric coordinate $c_1$ (the weight on $\mathbf{v}_1$), smallest first.

image.alt: A triangle with corners v1, v2, v3 labeled (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1); an inside point p labeled (1/4, 3/8, 3/8); a point m on edge v2v3 labeled (0, 1/2, 1/2); and an outside point q labeled (−1/2, 1, 1/2).

questions.explanation: The first coordinates are $-\tfrac12$ for $\mathbf{q}$, $0$ for $\mathbf{m}$, $\tfrac14$ for $\mathbf{p}$ and $1$ for $\mathbf{v}_1$. The weight on $\mathbf{v}_1$ grows as you move from the far side of the opposite edge toward $\mathbf{v}_1$; it equals the signed area of triangle $\mathbf{y}\mathbf{v}_2\mathbf{v}_3$ as a fraction of the area of the whole triangle, negative when the point is across edge $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbf{v}_3$.
Add entry by entry with $1 + 1 = 0$: $(1 + 1, 0 + 1, 1 + 0, 1 + 1) = (0, 1, 1, 0)$. The entry 2 doesn't exist in GF(2); it is 0.
Mod 2, $1 + 1 = 2$ leaves remainder 0. The negative of 1 is the number you add to 1 to get 0, which is 1 itself; so subtracting is the same as adding.

questions.stem: Four linearly independent vectors in $\text{GF}(2)^6$ span how many vectors?
questions.explanation: A combination is the sum of a subset of the four vectors, and there are $2^4 = 16$ subsets. Because the vectors are independent, different subsets give different sums, so the span has exactly 16 vectors. ($2^6 = 64$ is the size of the whole space.)

questions.stem: Which of these number systems are fields? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A field needs a reciprocal for every nonzero element. The rationals and reals have them; in GF(2) the only nonzero element is 1, and $1 \cdot 1 = 1$. The integers fail (2 has no integer reciprocal), and so do the integers mod 4, where $2 \cdot 2 = 0$ means 2 has no reciprocal.

questions.stem: The vectors $(1, 1, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 0, 1)$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$. What about over GF(2)?
choices: Independent, because independence doesn't depend on the field
Independent, because no vector is a multiple of another
Dependent, because three vectors in a 3-entry space always are
questions.explanation: Mod 2, $(1, 1, 0) + (0, 1, 1) + (1, 0, 1) = (2, 2, 2) = (0, 0, 0)$, a nontrivial dependence relation. Over $\mathbb{R}$ the same sum is $(2, 2, 2) \ne \mathbf{0}$, and row reduction ends with the pivot 2, which is 0 mod 2. Independence does depend on the field, and three vectors in a 3-entry space can be independent.

questions.stem: Why can a Lights Out strategy be described by a vector $\mathbf{x}$ in $\text{GF}(2)^n$, with $x_j = 1$ meaning "press light $j$"?
choices: The order of presses doesn't matter, and pressing a light twice undoes itself
Each light can only be on or off
Each light may be pressed at most once by the rules of the game
The toggle patterns are linearly independent
questions.explanation: Each press adds a fixed toggle pattern, and addition is commutative, so only which lights are pressed matters, and how many times. Pressing twice adds $\mathbf{a}_j + \mathbf{a}_j = \mathbf{0}$, so only the count mod 2 matters. The rules allow repeated presses; they are just pointless. That the lights are on or off explains why light patterns are mod-2 vectors, not why strategies are.

questions.stem: In Lights Out on a row of five lights, every solvable starting pattern has exactly ___ different solutions (pressing each light at most once).
questions.explanation: The $5 \times 5$ matrix has 4 pivots mod 2, so one free variable. A consistent system mod 2 with $k$ free variables has $2^k$ solutions: here $2^1 = 2$, a solution $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{p}$ plus the quiet pattern $(1, 1, 0, 1, 1)$.

questions.stem: Three lights in a row; only the middle one is on. Which presses turn every light off?
questions.explanation: Solve $A\mathbf{x} = (0, 1, 0)$ with toggle patterns $(1, 1, 0)$, $(1, 1, 1)$, $(0, 1, 1)$. Their sum is $(2, 3, 2) = (0, 1, 0)$ mod 2, so pressing all three works, and since this $A$ has a pivot in every column it is the only solution. Pressing light 2 alone turns lights 1 and 3 on and light 2 off; lights 1 and 3 together give $(1, 0, 1)$.

questions.stem: With five lights in a row, a starting pattern $\mathbf{b}$ is solvable exactly when $b_1 + b_2 + b_4 + b_5 = 0$ mod 2. Which starting patterns are solvable? Select all that apply.
Which press set is a quiet pattern (changes no lights) for a row of five lights?
questions.explanation: Pressing lights 1, 2, 4, 5 toggles light 1 twice (presses 1, 2), light 2 twice (1, 2), light 3 twice (2, 4), light 4 twice (4, 5) and light 5 twice (4, 5): no change. The others change lights: $(1, 0, 1, 0, 1)$ and $(0, 1, 1, 1, 0)$ both produce $(1, 0, 1, 0, 1)$, and pressing all five produces $(0, 1, 1, 1, 0)$.

questions.stem: The $25 \times 25$ matrix of the 5 × 5 Lights Out game has 23 pivot positions mod 2. What fraction of the $2^{25}$ starting patterns can be solved?
questions.explanation: The solvable patterns are the span of the 25 columns. With 23 pivots, 23 of the columns are independent and the rest are combinations of them, so the span has $2^{23}$ vectors: $2^{23}/2^{25} = \tfrac14$ of all patterns. Each solvable one has $2^{25 - 23} = 4$ solutions.

questions.stem: Put the steps for decoding a received Hamming(7,4) word with at most one flipped bit in order.
choices: Read the syndrome as a binary number j
Flip bit j of the received word
Read the data from bits 3, 5, 6 and 7
questions.explanation: The syndrome $H\mathbf{r}$ comes first; if it is the column of $H$ for bit $j$, that column spells $j$ in binary. Flipping bit $j$ restores the codeword, and only then are the data bits correct to read. (If the syndrome is $\mathbf{0}$, skip the flip.)

questions.stem: Using the lesson's $H$ (column $j$ is $j$ in binary, top row the 4s digit), a received word is $\mathbf{r} = (1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0)$ with exactly one flipped bit. Which bit flipped? Give only the bit number.
questions.explanation: Row 1 (bits 4–7): $0 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 0$. Row 2 (bits 2, 3, 6, 7): $1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 1$. Row 3 (bits 1, 3, 5, 7): $1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 1$. The syndrome is $(0, 1, 1)$, binary 011 = 3, so bit 3 flipped. The codeword sent was $(1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0)$.

questions.stem: Match each idea from Lights Out and the Hamming code to its meaning in this module's terms.
left: The syndrome of a word with bit j flipped
choices: A vector in the span of the columns of A
A nonzero solution of a homogeneous system
A pivot in the last column
questions.explanation: $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ is a combination of the columns. A quiet pattern changes nothing: $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}$. Codewords are defined by $H\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$, and $H(\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{e}_j) = H\mathbf{e}_j$, the $j$th column. A pivot in the last column signals an inconsistent system, such as an unsolvable starting pattern.

questions.stem: Why does the Hamming(7,4) code locate any single flipped bit?
choices: The seven columns of $H$ are nonzero and all different
Every codeword has an even number of 1s
$H$ has a pivot in every column
questions.explanation: A flip in bit $j$ makes the syndrome equal column $j$ of $H$. If the columns are nonzero, every single error is noticed; if they are all different, the syndrome names exactly one position. $H$ is $3 \times 7$, so it can't have a pivot in every column, and the count of codewords says nothing about locating errors.

questions.stem: $A$ is a $4 \times 7$ matrix. The transformation $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ has domain $\mathbb{R}^k$ with $k =$ ___ and codomain $\mathbb{R}^j$ with $j =$ ___. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: For $A\mathbf{x}$ to make sense, $\mathbf{x}$ needs one entry per column of $A$, so inputs live in $\mathbb{R}^7$. The output has one entry per row, so it lives in $\mathbb{R}^4$. Inputs match columns, outputs match rows.

questions.stem: This picture shows a transformation $T$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two ovals joined by arrows labeled T. Arrows run from points in the left oval to points inside a dashed region within the right oval. One point of the right oval lies outside the dashed region and receives no arrow. Six parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: Inputs come from the domain (left oval). Outputs are allowed anywhere in the codomain (right oval), but they actually land in the range (dashed region), the set of all images. Each arrow carries an input vector to its image. The point outside the dashed region is in the codomain but no input reaches it, so it is not in the range.

questions.stem: Which of these transformations $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ are linear? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A rule whose output entries are combinations $c_1x_1 + c_2x_2$ with no constants, powers or products is a matrix transformation, so it is linear: $(2x_1 - x_2,\ 0)$, $(x_2,\ x_1)$, and the zero map $(0,\ 0)$, whose matrix is the zero matrix. $(x_1 + x_2,\ x_1 - 1)$ sends $\mathbf{0}$ to $(0, -1)$. $(x_1x_2,\ x_2)$ fixes $\mathbf{0}$ but fails scaling: $T(2, 2) = (4, 2)$ while $2T(1, 1) = (2, 2)$.

questions.stem: $T$ is linear and you know $T(\mathbf{e}_1)$ and $T(\mathbf{e}_2)$. Put the steps for finding $T(3, -2)$ in order.
choices: Scale them and add entry by entry
questions.explanation: First express the input as a combination of $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$; linearity then turns $T$ of the combination into the same combination of the images; only then can you plug in the known images and do the arithmetic.

questions.stem: Match each rule $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ with the right verdict.
choices: Not linear: it moves the zero vector
Not linear, even though it fixes the zero vector
questions.explanation: $(x_1 + 1,\ x_2)$ sends $\mathbf{0}$ to $(1, 0)$, so it can't be linear. $(x_1^2,\ x_2)$ sends $\mathbf{0}$ to $\mathbf{0}$, but $T(2, 0) = (4, 0) \ne 2T(1, 0) = (2, 0)$: passing the $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ test is not enough. $(3x_2,\ x_1 - x_2)$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}$, and the zero map is the zero matrix times $\mathbf{x}$; both are linear. Linearity is a property of the whole map, required for all inputs, so "linear only for positive inputs" makes no sense.

questions.stem: $T: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is linear with $T(\mathbf{e}_1) = (1, 4)$, $T(\mathbf{e}_2) = (0, -2)$ and $T(\mathbf{e}_3) = (5, 3)$. The entry in row 2, column 3 of its standard matrix is ___.
questions.explanation: Column $j$ of the standard matrix is $T(\mathbf{e}_j)$, so column 3 is $(5, 3)$ and its row-2 entry is 3. The full matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 4 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}$. Writing the images as rows instead would give the wrong answer (and a $3 \times 2$ matrix).

questions.stem: Each panel shows the unit square (dashed) and its image (shaded) under a transformation, with the arrows $T(\mathbf{e}_1)$ and $T(\mathbf{e}_2)$. Name the transformation in each numbered panel.

image.alt: Four numbered panels. Panel 1: T(e₁) points straight up and T(e₂) points left, and the square has turned to the upper left. Panel 2: T(e₁) is unchanged and T(e₂) points down, and the square has flipped below the axis. Panel 3: T(e₁) is unchanged and T(e₂) is (1, 1), and the square leans into a parallelogram. Panel 4: T(e₁) is unchanged and T(e₂) is the zero vector, and the square is flattened onto the axis.

choices: Reflection across the line x₂ = x₁
questions.explanation: Read the columns from the arrows. Panel 1: $\mathbf{e}_1 \mapsto (0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 \mapsto (-1, 0)$, the $90^\circ$ counterclockwise rotation. Panel 2: $\mathbf{e}_1$ stays and $\mathbf{e}_2 \mapsto (0, -1)$, the reflection across the $x_1$-axis. Panel 3: $\mathbf{e}_1$ stays and $\mathbf{e}_2 \mapsto (1, 1)$, the horizontal shear $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. Panel 4: $\mathbf{e}_2 \mapsto \mathbf{0}$, the projection onto the $x_1$-axis. A reflection across $x_2 = x_1$ would swap $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$; a dilation by 2 would double both.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the standard matrix of a linear $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ in order.
choices: Place $T(\mathbf{e}_j)$ as column $j$ of an $m \times n$ matrix
Check that $A\mathbf{x} = T(\mathbf{x})$ for a test vector $\mathbf{x}$
questions.explanation: The theorem says $A = [\,T(\mathbf{e}_1) \;\cdots\; T(\mathbf{e}_n)\,]$: you need the basis vectors, then their images, then you assemble the columns. A final check on one other vector catches slips such as putting images in rows.

questions.stem: Which of these transformations of $\mathbb{R}^2$ leave $\mathbf{e}_1$ where it is? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The first column of the standard matrix is $T(\mathbf{e}_1)$, so look for first column $(1, 0)$. The reflection $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$, the horizontal shear $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and the projection $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ all have it. The rotation sends $\mathbf{e}_1$ to $(0, 1)$ and the vertical shear sends it to $(1, 3)$.

questions.stem: Match each standard matrix with its transformation of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
choices: Reflection across the line x₂ = x₁
questions.explanation: Read each matrix by its columns. $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ sends $\mathbf{e}_1 \mapsto \mathbf{e}_2$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 \mapsto -\mathbf{e}_1$: counterclockwise by $90^\circ$ (clockwise would send $\mathbf{e}_1$ to $-\mathbf{e}_2$). $\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ flips $x_1$ only: reflection across the $x_2$-axis. $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ sends $(x_1, x_2)$ to $(x_1,\ 3x_1 + x_2)$: a vertical shear. $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ keeps only $x_2$: projection onto the $x_2$-axis.

questions.stem: Each numbered arrow diagram shows a map from a domain (left) to a codomain (right). Name the property of each.

image.alt: Four numbered arrow diagrams. Diagram 1: three inputs go to three different outputs and a fourth output gets no arrow. Diagram 2: four inputs go to three outputs; every output gets an arrow and the top output gets two. Diagram 3: three inputs are paired one each with three outputs. Diagram 4: the top two inputs both go to the top output, the third input goes to the bottom output, and the middle output gets no arrow.

questions.explanation: Onto: every output gets at least one arrow. One-to-one: no output gets more than one arrow. Diagram 1 misses an output but never doubles up; diagram 2 hits every output but one output twice; diagram 3 pairs everything up; diagram 4 both doubles up and misses an output. Every input has exactly one arrow in all four, so each one is a function.

questions.stem: $A$ is a $3 \times 5$ matrix with 3 pivot positions, and $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The columns of $A$ are linearly independent
questions.explanation: Three pivots in three rows means a pivot in every row: $T$ is onto and the columns span $\mathbb{R}^3$. But only 3 of the 5 columns have pivots, so there are 2 free variables: $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has nontrivial solutions, the columns are dependent, and $T$ is not one-to-one.

questions.stem: $A$ is a $5 \times 8$ matrix with a pivot in every row, so $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ is onto $\mathbb{R}^5$. How many free variables does $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ have? ___
questions.explanation: A pivot in each of the 5 rows uses 5 of the 8 columns. The other $8 - 5 = 3$ columns give free variables, which is why a wide matrix can never be one-to-one.

questions.stem: Match each matrix description with the properties of $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$.
questions.explanation: Compare the pivot count with the number of rows (onto needs a pivot in every row) and with the number of columns (one-to-one needs a pivot in every column). $4 \times 6$ with 4 pivots: every row, not every column. $6 \times 4$ with 4 pivots: every column, not every row. $4 \times 4$ with 4: both. $4 \times 4$ with 3: neither, as square matrices always have both or neither.

questions.stem: $T$ is linear and only $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ satisfies $T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$. Put the steps of the proof that $T$ is one-to-one in order.
choices: So $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$: no output is hit twice
questions.explanation: Start from two inputs with the same output, use linearity to turn that into an input that maps to $\mathbf{0}$, apply the hypothesis, and conclude the two inputs were equal.

questions.stem: What is the standard matrix of the projection onto the line $x_2 = 3x_1$?
questions.explanation: With $m = 3$, $P = \dfrac{1}{1 + m^2}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & m \\ m & m^2\end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{bmatrix}$. Check: $P(1, 3) = \tfrac{1}{10}(10, 30) = (1, 3)$, so points on the line stay put. Without the $\tfrac{1}{10}$, $(1, 3)$ would go to $(10, 30)$. The matrix with 9 in the top left projects onto $x_2 = \tfrac13 x_1$, and $\tfrac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} -8 & 6 \\ 6 & 8\end{bmatrix}$ is the reflection across $x_2 = 3x_1$.

questions.stem: Reflect $(5, 0)$ across the line $x_2 = 2x_1$. Where does it land?
questions.explanation: $P = \tfrac15\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}$ gives $P(5, 0) = (1, 2)$, the foot of the perpendicular. Then $R\mathbf{x} = 2P\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} = (2, 4) - (5, 0) = (-3, 4)$. Check: the midpoint of $(5, 0)$ and $(-3, 4)$ is $(1, 2)$, on the line, and both have length 5. $(1, 2)$ is the projection, not the reflection.

questions.stem: Which matrix reflects $\mathbb{R}^2$ across the line through the origin at angle $60^\circ$?
questions.explanation: The reflection matrix uses the doubled angle: $\begin{bmatrix} \cos 120^\circ & \sin 120^\circ \\ \sin 120^\circ & -\cos 120^\circ\end{bmatrix}$ with $\cos 120^\circ = -\tfrac12$ and $\sin 120^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Using $60^\circ$ itself gives the reflection across the $30^\circ$ line; the matrix with $-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ in the top right is the rotation by $120^\circ$; and the one with quarters is the projection onto the $60^\circ$ line.

questions.stem: Reflect across the line at angle $20^\circ$, then across the line at angle $65^\circ$ (both through the origin). What is the result?
questions.explanation: Two reflections, first across the line at $\alpha$ and then the line at $\beta$, make the rotation by $2(\beta - \alpha) = 2(65^\circ - 20^\circ) = 90^\circ$, counterclockwise because $\beta > \alpha$. The angle is twice the angle between the lines, not $45^\circ$. Clockwise $90^\circ$ would be the answer for the opposite order. Two reflections never make a reflection.

questions.stem: Rotate by $90^\circ$ counterclockwise, then reflect across the $x_1$-axis. What single transformation is this?
questions.explanation: Rotation by $\gamma$ then reflection across the line at $\beta$ is the reflection across the line at $\beta - \tfrac{\gamma}{2} = 0^\circ - 45^\circ = -45^\circ$, the line $x_2 = -x_1$. Check with the basis: $\mathbf{e}_1 \mapsto (0, 1) \mapsto (0, -1)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 \mapsto (-1, 0) \mapsto (-1, 0)$, so the matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, which swaps the coordinates and changes both signs. A rotation combined with a reflection is always a reflection, never a rotation.

questions.stem: What does $T(\mathbf{x}) = \dfrac{1}{13}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 12 \\ 12 & -5\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}$ do?
questions.explanation: The matrix has the reflection pattern $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & -a\end{bmatrix}$ with $a^2 + b^2 = \tfrac{25 + 144}{169} = 1$. A reflection fixes its line: $T(3, 2) = \tfrac{1}{13}(15 + 24,\ 36 - 10) = (3, 2)$, so the line is $x_2 = \tfrac23 x_1$. (From $\tfrac{1 - m^2}{1 + m^2} = \tfrac{5}{13}$ you get $m^2 = \tfrac49$, and $\tfrac{2m}{1 + m^2} = \tfrac{12}{13} > 0$ picks $m = \tfrac23$.) A rotation would have the pattern $\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}$, and a projection matrix has no negative diagonal entry.

questions.stem: $P$ is the projection onto a line $L$ through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which description is correct?
choices: An isometry, one-to-one but not onto $\mathbb{R}^2$
An involution, neither one-to-one nor onto $\mathbb{R}^2$
questions.explanation: Projecting twice is the same as projecting once ($P$ is idempotent). All outputs lie on $L$, so $P$ is not onto $\mathbb{R}^2$, and every vector perpendicular to $L$ goes to $\mathbf{0}$, so it is not one-to-one. It is not an involution ($P$ twice is $P$, not the identity) and not an isometry (it shortens vectors off the line).

questions.stem: The reflection across the line $x_2 = 3x_1$ has standard matrix $\dfrac{1}{1 + m^2}\begin{bmatrix} 1 - m^2 & 2m \\ 2m & m^2 - 1\end{bmatrix}$ with $m = 3$. Its entry in row 1, column 1 is ___. Give an exact fraction or a decimal.
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{1 - 9}{1 + 9} = \dfrac{-8}{10} = -\dfrac45$. The whole matrix is $\tfrac15\begin{bmatrix} -4 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}$; check that it fixes $(1, 3)$: $\tfrac15(-4 + 9,\ 3 + 12) = (1, 3)$.

questions.stem: Reflecting across the $x_1$-axis and then across the line through the origin at angle $\beta$ (with $0^\circ \le \beta < 180^\circ$) gives the counterclockwise rotation by $100^\circ$. $\beta =$ ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The $x_1$-axis is the line at $\alpha = 0^\circ$, so the rotation angle is $2(\beta - 0^\circ) = 100^\circ$ and $\beta = 50^\circ$. The rotation is twice the angle between the mirrors.

questions.stem: Put the steps for reflecting a vector $\mathbf{x}$ across the line $x_2 = mx_1$ in order, using $R\mathbf{x} = 2P\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}$.
choices: Note that $(1, m)$ lies on the line
Compute $P\mathbf{x}$, the foot of the perpendicular from $\mathbf{x}$
Check that $P\mathbf{x}$ is the midpoint of $\mathbf{x}$ and $R\mathbf{x}$
questions.explanation: The direction $(1, m)$ gives the projection matrix; the projection gives the foot of the perpendicular; doubling it and subtracting $\mathbf{x}$ gives the reflection; and the midpoint check can only come once $R\mathbf{x}$ is known.

questions.stem: The picture shows a vector, a line through the origin, and two vectors made from them. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Coordinate axes with a steep line through the origin. An arrow from the origin points to the lower right of the line, a second arrow points to the upper left, and a dashed segment joins their tips, crossing the line at a right angle at a marked point. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The line is the mirror. The projection is the foot of the perpendicular from the original vector's tip, on the line. The reflection is the same distance on the other side, so the projection is the midpoint of the dashed segment joining the original vector and its reflection. (In the lesson the line is $x_2 = 2x_1$, the vector is $(3, 1)$, its projection $(1, 2)$ and its reflection $(-1, 3)$.)

questions.stem: Which of these linear maps of $\mathbb{R}^2$ preserve the length of every vector? Select all that apply.
choices: A reflection followed by a rotation
questions.explanation: Rotations and reflections are isometries, and doing one isometry after another keeps every length, so a reflection followed by a rotation is one too (in fact it is another reflection). The projection sends $\mathbf{e}_2$ to $\mathbf{0}$, and the shear sends $\mathbf{e}_2$ (length 1) to $(1, 1)$ (length $\sqrt2$).

questions.stem: Match each matrix pattern with the map it describes. Here $a^2 + b^2 = 1$.
questions.explanation: A rotation by $\gamma$ has $a = \cos\gamma$, $b = \sin\gamma$. A reflection across the line at $\theta$ has $a = \cos 2\theta$, $b = \sin 2\theta$; the minus sign in the bottom right is what distinguishes it. The projection onto $x_2 = mx_1$ has the slope form shown. The shear adds $k$ times $x_2$ to $x_1$. A dilation would be $r$ times the identity.

questions.stem: Let $T(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}$. What is the image of the line $(1, 0) + t(1, -2)$?
choices: The line through the origin in the direction $(2, -2)$
questions.explanation: The image of $\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{d}$ is $T(\mathbf{p}) + t\,T(\mathbf{d})$. Here $T(1, 0) = (2, -2)$ and $T(1, -2) = (2 - 2,\ -2 + 2) = (0, 0)$, so every point of the line goes to $(2, -2)$. A line is sent to a line only when $T(\mathbf{d}) \ne \mathbf{0}$; a linear map can never spread a line over the whole plane.

questions.stem: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$, what is the preimage of $\mathbf{b} = (3, 1)$ under $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$?
questions.explanation: With $x_3 = t$: $x_2 = 1 - 3t$ and $x_1 = 3 - 2x_2 = 1 + 6t$, so the preimage is $(1, 1, 0) + t(6, -3, 1)$. Check: $A(1, 1, 0) = (3, 1)$ and $A(6, -3, 1) = (0, 0)$. The free variable makes it a line, not a point. $A(3, 1, 0) = (5, 1)$, not $\mathbf{b}$, and $A(-6, 3, 1) = (0, 6)$, not $\mathbf{0}$.

questions.stem: $A$ is $2 \times 3$ with 2 pivot positions. What do the preimages of $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ look like?
choices: Lines in $\mathbb{R}^3$, all through the origin
questions.explanation: A pivot in both rows means every $\mathbf{b}$ is reached, so no preimage is empty. One of the three columns has no pivot, so $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has one free variable and its solutions form a line through the origin. Every other preimage is a parallel copy of that line, shifted off the origin (only the preimage of $\mathbf{0}$ passes through it).

questions.stem: $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and $S: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^p$ are linear, and "first $T$, then $S$" is onto $\mathbb{R}^p$. Which must be true?
questions.explanation: Every $\mathbf{c}$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ is $S(T(\mathbf{x}))$ for some $\mathbf{x}$, so it is the image under $S$ of $T(\mathbf{x})$: $S$ is onto. Nothing forces the others. With $T(x) = (x, 0)$ and $S(y_1, y_2) = y_1$, the composite is onto $\mathbb{R}$, yet $T$ is not onto $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $S$ is not one-to-one.

questions.stem: $A$ is a $5 \times 3$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent. What size is a left inverse $C$ of $A$?
questions.explanation: $CA = I_3$ needs $C$ to have 5 columns (to multiply the 5 rows of $A$) and 3 rows (so the product is $3 \times 3$). A one-sided inverse of an $m \times n$ matrix is always $n \times m$.

questions.stem: Which matrix has a right inverse?
questions.explanation: A right inverse exists exactly when there is a pivot in every row. $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ has pivots in both rows; for example $D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ works. The $3 \times 2$ matrix is tall, so it can't have a pivot in all 3 rows. In the other two, the second row is twice the first, so row reduction leaves a zero row.

questions.stem: Which matrix $C$ is a left inverse of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}$?
questions.explanation: Rows 2 and 3 of $A$ form $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ with $B^{-1} = \tfrac16\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac12 & -\tfrac16 \\ 0 & \tfrac13\end{bmatrix}$. Put it in columns 2 and 3 of $C$ and zeros in column 1: $CA = I_2$. Multiplying out the others gives $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ (the top block, not its inverse), $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}$, none of them $I_2$.

questions.stem: $A$ is $3 \times 2$ with a left inverse $C$, and for some $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, $C\mathbf{b} = (1, 2)$. What can you conclude?
choices: Any solution must be $(1, 2)$, but there may be none
questions.explanation: If $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, then $\mathbf{x} = CA\mathbf{x} = C\mathbf{b} = (1, 2)$, so a solution can only be $(1, 2)$; check whether $A(1, 2) = \mathbf{b}$. But a $3 \times 2$ matrix is never onto, and when $\mathbf{b}$ is outside the range, $C\mathbf{b}$ is still some vector that solves nothing. Since $A$ is one-to-one, there are never infinitely many solutions.

questions.stem: $A$ is $4 \times 7$ and has a right inverse $D$, so $AD = I_4$. $D$ has ___ rows and ___ columns.
questions.explanation: $AD$ needs $D$ to have as many rows as $A$ has columns (7), and $AD = I_4$ needs $D$ to have 4 columns. So $D$ is $7 \times 4$, the reverse of $A$'s size.

questions.stem: $T: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^5$ and $S: \mathbb{R}^5 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ are linear, and "first $T$, then $S$" is one-to-one. How many pivot positions must the $5 \times 3$ standard matrix of $T$ have? ___
questions.explanation: If the composite is one-to-one, the first map $T$ is one-to-one, so its standard matrix has a pivot in every column: 3 pivots. (It can't have more, since there are only 3 columns.)

questions.stem: $CA = I$ and $AD = I$. Put the steps of the proof that $C = D$ in order.
questions.explanation: The chain $C = CI = C(AD) = (CA)D = ID = D$ uses each hypothesis once, with associativity in the middle to move the brackets. So a matrix with inverses on both sides has only one, the inverse $A^{-1}$.

questions.stem: Match each fact about the pivots of a matrix $A$ with the one-sided inverses $A$ has.
left: Pivot in every column but not in every row
Pivot in every row but not in every column
Pivot in every row and every column
Fewer pivots than its rows and than its columns
choices: Left inverses only, no right inverse
Right inverses only, no left inverse
One inverse that works on both sides
Many left inverses and many right inverses
questions.explanation: Pivot in every column means one-to-one, which is equivalent to having a left inverse; pivot in every row means onto, equivalent to a right inverse. With pivots in every column but not every row, $A$ is tall and has left inverses only; in every row but not every column, it is wide and has right inverses only. With a pivot in every row and column, $A$ is square and has both kinds, and they are the same matrix, $C = D = A^{-1}$, so there is exactly one. With pivots missing from some row and some column, $A$ is neither one-to-one nor onto, so it has neither kind. No matrix has many left inverses and many right inverses: having both forces a single inverse $A^{-1}$.

questions.stem: $A$ is $3 \times 2$ and $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ is one-to-one. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Every nonempty preimage is a single point
Some vectors $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ have an empty preimage
questions.explanation: One-to-one gives a left inverse and makes every nonempty preimage a single point. A $3 \times 2$ matrix has at most 2 pivots, so some row has none: it is not onto, some $\mathbf{b}$ are never reached, and there is no right inverse. Left inverses are not unique: the lesson found two different ones for $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}$, and every tall one-to-one matrix has infinitely many.

questions.stem: $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ and $S: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ are linear, and $S(T(\mathbf{x})) = \mathbf{x}$ for every $\mathbf{x}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which must be true?
questions.explanation: The composite "first $T$, then $S$" is the identity, which is both one-to-one and onto. So the first map, $T$, is one-to-one, and the last map, $S$, is onto. $T$ can't be onto (a $3 \times 2$ standard matrix has no pivot in some row) and $S$ can't be one-to-one (a $2 \times 3$ matrix has a free column), so neither is invertible.

questions.stem: The picture shows a product $AB$ with $A$ of size $3 \times 4$ and $B$ of size $4 \times 2$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A 3 by 4 matrix A with its middle row shaded, a 4 by 2 matrix B with its second column shaded, and the 3 by 2 product AB with its middle-right entry shaded. Below, the sizes (3 × 4) and (4 × 2) are joined by a short inner arc and a longer outer arc. Five numbered markers sit on the shaded row, the shaded column, the shaded entry, the inner arc and the outer arc.

choices: Outer sizes (give the size of AB)
questions.explanation: Entry $(2, 2)$ of $AB$ (3) is row 2 of $A$ (1) times column 2 of $B$ (2): four products added up, one for each entry of the row. The product exists because the inner sizes agree, $4 = 4$ (4), and the outer sizes $3$ and $2$ give $AB$ its size, $3 \times 2$ (5).

questions.stem: If $A$ is $5 \times 3$ and the product $AB$ is $5 \times 7$, then $B$ must be ___ $\times$ ___.
questions.explanation: For $AB$ to exist, $B$ must have as many rows as $A$ has columns: 3. The product then has as many columns as $B$: 7. So $B$ is $3 \times 7$, and $(5 \times 3)(3 \times 7) = 5 \times 7$.

questions.stem: A graphics program must rotate an object $90^\circ$ about the point $(2, 1)$, but its rotation matrix rotates about the origin. Put the moves in the order they are applied to the object.
choices: Translate by $(-2, -1)$, so that $(2, 1)$ moves to the origin
Translate by $(2, 1)$, so that the center goes back to $(2, 1)$
questions.explanation: Move the center of rotation to the origin, rotate there, then move it back. The single matrix that does all three is the product with the first move on the right: $T_{(2,1)}\,R\,T_{(-2,-1)}$ in homogeneous coordinates. The point $(2, 1)$ itself stays fixed, as it should.

questions.stem: Which equations are true for all $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$ and $C$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The transpose rule and the distributive law always hold. The other two quietly assume $AB = BA$: $(AB)^2 = ABAB$, which is $A^2B^2$ only if the middle $BA$ can be swapped, and $(A + B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2$, which has $AB + BA$, not $2AB$.

questions.stem: $A$ is $2 \times 3$ and $B$ is $3 \times 4$. Match each expression to its size.
questions.explanation: $(2 \times 3)(3 \times 4) = 2 \times 4$. Transposing swaps the sizes, so $A^T$ is $3 \times 2$. $B^TA^T = (AB)^T$ is $(4 \times 3)(3 \times 2) = 4 \times 2$. $AA^T$ is $(2 \times 3)(3 \times 2) = 2 \times 2$. $BA$ is $(3 \times 4)(2 \times 3)$, and $4 \ne 2$, so it doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ and write $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s\end{bmatrix}$. Then $p =$ ___, $q =$ ___, $r =$ ___ and $s =$ ___.
questions.explanation: $ad - bc = 4 \cdot 2 - 7 \cdot 1 = 1$, so $A^{-1} = \dfrac11\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$: swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two. Check: $AA^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 - 7 & -28 + 28 \\ 2 - 2 & -7 + 8\end{bmatrix} = I$.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the inverse algorithm for an invertible $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ in order.
choices: Row-reduce, applying every operation to whole rows, until the left block is $I$
questions.explanation: Put $I$ beside $A$, row-reduce the whole $3 \times 6$ matrix until the left block is $I$, and the right block is then $A^{-1}$. Checking a product at the end catches arithmetic slips. (If a zero row had appeared in the left block, $A$ would be singular.)

questions.stem: $A$ and $B$ are invertible $n \times n$ matrices. Which of these must also be invertible? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$, $(A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T$ and $(3A)^{-1} = \tfrac13A^{-1}$. A sum of invertible matrices can be singular: with $B = -A$, $A + B = 0$.

questions.stem: $A$ and $B$ are invertible $n \times n$ matrices. Match each expression to an equal matrix.
questions.explanation: The inverse of a product reverses the order (socks and shoes), so $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$, not $A^{-1}B^{-1}$. Transposing $AA^{-1} = I$ gives $(A^{-1})^TA^T = I$. Undoing an undo gives $A$ back. And $(2A)(\tfrac12A^{-1}) = I$, so the scalar is inverted too.

questions.stem: The shear $S = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ sends the unit square to a parallelogram, moving the corner $(1, 1)$ to $(2, 1)$. Which matrix moves the parallelogram back onto the square?
questions.explanation: Undoing the shear means multiplying by $S^{-1}$. Here $ad - bc = 1$, so $S^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, which shifts each point left by its height: $(2, 1) \mapsto (1, 1)$. Negating every entry ($-S$) is not the inverse, and applying $S$ again would shear twice as far.

questions.stem: Put the steps for writing an invertible matrix $A$ as a product of elementary matrices in order.
choices: Row-reduce $A$ to $I$, keeping a list of the row operations
Write the elementary matrix $E_i$ of each operation, so that $E_k\cdots E_1A = I$
Find each $E_i^{-1}$, the elementary matrix of the reverse operation
questions.explanation: From $E_k\cdots E_1A = I$, multiply on the left by $E_k^{-1}$, then $E_{k-1}^{-1}$, and so on, to get $A = E_1^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1}$. Each $E_i^{-1}$ is easy to write down because it just undoes one row operation.

questions.stem: Match each $3 \times 3$ elementary matrix to the row operation it performs when it multiplies a matrix on the left.
questions.explanation: Each matrix is $I$ after one row operation, and multiplying by it on the left does that operation. The entry $-4$ sits in row 3, column 1: row 3 gets $-4$ times row 1. The entry 2 in row 2, column 3 means row 2 gets 2 times row 3 (the distractor has the rows backwards).

questions.stem: $A$ is a $4 \times 4$ matrix whose columns are linearly dependent. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
choices: The columns of $A$ do not span $\mathbb{R}^4$
$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for every $\mathbf{b}$
questions.explanation: Dependent columns make the IMT statements false, so $A$ is singular, and every statement in the theorem fails: $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ has nontrivial solutions, the columns don't span $\mathbb{R}^4$, $A$ is not row equivalent to $I$, and $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is inconsistent for some $\mathbf{b}$.

questions.stem: The matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & k\end{bmatrix}$ fails every statement of the invertible matrix theorem when $k =$ ___. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: It is singular when $ad - bc = k - 6 = 0$, so $k = 6$. Then column 2 is twice column 1, the columns are dependent, and by the IMT every other statement fails too.

questions.stem: $E$ is the $3 \times 3$ elementary matrix for $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 + 7R_1$. The $(3, 1)$ entry of $E^{-1}$ is ___.
questions.explanation: $E^{-1}$ undoes the operation: $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 7R_1$. That is $I$ with $-7$ in row 3, column 1. (The $(3, 1)$ entry of $E$ itself is $+7$.)

questions.stem: The picture shows the pattern of $A = LU$ for a $4 \times 4$ matrix that needs no row swaps. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two 4 by 4 grids side by side after A =, labeled L and U. In L, the diagonal cells are shaded green and the cells below the diagonal blue; the cells above are blank. In U, the diagonal cells are shaded yellow and the cells above the diagonal purple; the cells below are blank. Six numbered markers: a blue cell of L, a green diagonal cell of L, a blank cell above the diagonal of L, a yellow diagonal cell of U, a blank cell below the diagonal of U, and a purple cell above the diagonal of U.

choices: Other entries of the echelon form
Entries of the inverse of A
questions.explanation: $L$ is unit lower triangular: 1s on the diagonal (2), zeros above it (3), and below it the multipliers $\ell_{ij}$ recorded while clearing each entry (1). $U$ is the echelon form found by row reduction: its pivots on the diagonal (4), zeros below (5), and the remaining entries of the reduced rows above (6).

questions.stem: Put the steps for solving $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with an LU factorization in order.
choices: Reduce $A$ to an echelon form $U$ with row replacements, storing each multiplier in $L$
questions.explanation: The factorization comes first. Then $A\mathbf{x} = L(U\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}$: find $\mathbf{y} = U\mathbf{x}$ from $L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}$ (top row down), then $\mathbf{x}$ from $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$ (bottom row up). For a new $\mathbf{b}$, only the two substitutions are repeated.

questions.stem: In the LU factorization of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 6 & 5\end{bmatrix}$ (with $L$ unit lower triangular), $\ell_{21} =$ ___ and $u_{22} =$ ___.
questions.explanation: The multiplier is $\ell_{21} = 6/3 = 2$, and $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ gives $[\,0 \;\; 5 - 2\,] = [\,0 \;\; 3\,]$, so $u_{22} = 3$. Check: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 6 & 5\end{bmatrix}$.

questions.stem: Which matrices have an LU factorization ($L$ unit lower triangular, no row interchanges)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The first reduces with $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ to $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. The last is already unit lower triangular: $L$ is the matrix itself and $U = I$. The second has 0 in the first pivot position with a nonzero entry below it, so a swap is needed. In the third, clearing column 1 leaves rows $[\,0 \;\; 0 \;\; {-1}\,]$ and $[\,0 \;\; {-1} \;\; {-2}\,]$: a zero in the second pivot position with $-1$ below it, so again a swap is needed.

questions.stem: Match each part of the LU method to its description.
choices: Solves Ly = b from the top row down
Solves Ux = y from the bottom row up
Entry of L below the diagonal
questions.explanation: $L$ is lower triangular, so its system is solved from the first equation down; $U$ is upper triangular, so its system is solved from the last equation up. Multipliers fill $L$ below the diagonal, and the pivots sit on the diagonal of $U$. The diagonal entries of $L$ are always 1.

questions.stem: What is the inverse of the permutation matrix $P = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$?
questions.explanation: For a permutation matrix, $P^{-1} = P^T$: the transpose turns rows into columns, giving $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$. $P$ lists rows in the order 2, 3, 1 and $P^T$ in the order 3, 1, 2, which undoes it. $P$ itself is not its own inverse here, because it is not a single swap.

questions.stem: $P$ is a $3 \times 3$ permutation matrix other than $I$ and $A$ is $3 \times 3$. What does the product $AP$ do to $A$?
questions.explanation: Column $j$ of $AP$ is $A$ times column $j$ of $P$, and that column is some $\mathbf{e}_k$, so column $j$ of $AP$ is column $k$ of $A$. Multiplying on the left, $PA$, is what reorders rows.

questions.stem: There are ___ different $4 \times 4$ permutation matrices (including $I$).
questions.explanation: A permutation matrix is $I$ with its rows in some order, and 4 rows can be ordered in $4! = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24$ ways.

questions.stem: Why does $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ have no factorization $LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular?
choices: Comparing entries forces $u_{11} = 0$, and then the $(2, 1)$ entry of $LU$ is $\ell_{21}u_{11} = 0$, not 1
The matrix is singular, and singular matrices never have LU factorizations
Its determinant is negative, and $LU$ always has a positive determinant
It is symmetric, and symmetric matrices need $LDL^T$ instead
questions.explanation: The $(1, 1)$ entry of $LU$ is $1 \cdot u_{11}$, so $u_{11} = 0$; then the $(2, 1)$ entry is $\ell_{21}u_{11} = 0 \ne 1$. The matrix is invertible (determinant $-1$), so singularity isn't the reason, and plenty of singular matrices do have LU factorizations; the sign of the determinant doesn't matter either. Swapping the rows fixes the problem: $PA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for handling one column with partial pivoting in order.
choices: Find the entry of largest absolute value at or below the pivot position
Swap its row into the pivot position, carrying that row's stored multipliers with it
Divide each entry below the pivot by the pivot to get the multipliers
Subtract each multiplier times the pivot row from its row, and store the multiplier in $L$
questions.explanation: The pivot is chosen first (largest in absolute value, so every multiplier has $|\ell| \le 1$), then moved into place with the swap recorded in $P$. Only then are the multipliers computed from the new pivot and used to clear the column.

questions.stem: Row-reducing $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \\ 4 & 6 & 8\end{bmatrix}$ uses $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 4R_1$, then swaps rows 2 and 3 because of a zero pivot. In $PA = LU$, what is $L$?
questions.explanation: After column 1, row 2 is $[\,0 \;\; 0 \;\; 3\,]$ (multiplier 2) and row 3 is $[\,0 \;\; 2 \;\; 4\,]$ (multiplier 4). The swap moves the rows and their multipliers together, so row 2 of $L$ gets 4 and row 3 gets 2; nothing is left to clear in column 2, so $\ell_{32} = 0$. Check: row 2 of $LU$ is $4(1, 1, 1) + (0, 2, 4) = (4, 6, 8)$, the second row of $PA$. Leaving the multipliers unswapped is the mistake in the first choice; the second has the sign error.

questions.stem: You have $PA = LU$. To solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, which triangular system do you solve first?
questions.explanation: Multiply $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by $P$: $PA\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{b}$, that is $L(U\mathbf{x}) = P\mathbf{b}$. So solve $L\mathbf{y} = P\mathbf{b}$ by forward substitution, then $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$. The right-hand side must be reordered the same way as the rows of $A$.

questions.stem: With partial pivoting, what is always true of the multipliers $\ell_{ij}$?
choices: They are all at least 1 in absolute value
They are all at most 1 in absolute value
questions.explanation: Each multiplier is (entry being cleared) ÷ (pivot), and partial pivoting makes the pivot the largest entry in absolute value among those rows, so $|\ell_{ij}| \le 1$. That is why no row is ever multiplied by a huge number. Signs can be anything, and fractions are normal.

questions.stem: Column 1 of a $3 \times 3$ matrix is $(2, -5, 4)$. Which entry does partial pivoting choose as the first pivot?
choices: The 2 in row 1, since it is already in place
The 4 in row 3, the largest entry
Any of them, since none is zero
questions.explanation: Partial pivoting compares absolute values: $|-5| = 5$ is the largest, so row 2 is swapped to the top. Then the multipliers are $2/(-5) = -0.4$ and $4/(-5) = -0.8$, both at most 1 in size. In exact arithmetic any nonzero pivot would work, but on a computer the largest is safest.

questions.stem: Write $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}$ as $LDU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular, $D = \begin{bmatrix} d_1 & 0 \\ 0 & d_2\end{bmatrix}$ and $U$ unit upper triangular. Then $d_1 =$ ___, $d_2 =$ ___, and the $(1, 2)$ entry of $U$ is ___.
questions.explanation: Elimination: $\ell_{21} = \tfrac12$, and $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - \tfrac12R_1$ leaves $[\,0 \;\; 5 - 3\,] = [\,0 \;\; 2\,]$. So the echelon form is $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ with pivots $d_1 = 2$, $d_2 = 2$. Dividing row 1 by its pivot gives $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, so the $(1, 2)$ entry is 3.

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The inverse of a unit lower triangular matrix is unit lower triangular
Every permutation matrix is its own inverse
If $A$ is symmetric and elimination without row swaps gives nonzero pivots, then $A = LDL^T$
Every invertible matrix has an LU factorization without row swaps
questions.explanation: The first fact is used in the uniqueness proof. The third is the symmetric case of the LDU theorem: uniqueness forces the unit upper factor to be $L^T$. A permutation matrix satisfies $P^{-1} = P^T$, which equals $P$ only for special ones such as a single swap. And $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is invertible but needs a swap.

questions.stem: Match each square-matrix factorization to the most general situation in which it is guaranteed to exist.
choices: Any matrix; rows may need reordering first
Symmetric with nonzero pivots and no swaps
questions.explanation: $PA = LU$ always exists. Plain $A = LU$ works when elimination meets no zero pivot. If in addition $A$ is symmetric, uniqueness of LDU gives $A = LDL^T$, and if all those pivots are positive, splitting $\sqrt{D}$ between the factors gives Cholesky.

questions.stem: For the symmetric matrix $S = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}$, write $S = LDL^T$. What is $D$?
