questions.explanation: $\ell_{21} = 2/4 = \tfrac12$, and the second pivot is $5 - \tfrac12 \cdot 2 = 4$. So $D = \operatorname{diag}(4, 4)$ and $L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \tfrac12 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. Check the $(2, 2)$ entry: $(\tfrac12)^2 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 4 = 5$. Using the diagonal of $S$ (4 and 5) skips the elimination step.

questions.stem: The uniqueness proof for LDU reaches $L_2^{-1}L_1 = D_2U_2U_1^{-1}D_1^{-1}$. Why must both sides equal $I$?
choices: The left side is unit lower triangular and the right side is upper triangular, so both are diagonal with 1s on the diagonal
Both sides are products of invertible matrices, and every invertible matrix is $I$
Both sides are symmetric, so they must be diagonal
The right side contains $D_1^{-1}$, which cancels $D_2$
questions.explanation: A matrix that is both lower and upper triangular is diagonal, and the left side has 1s on its diagonal, so it is $I$. Then $L_1 = L_2$, and the rest of the argument gives $D_1 = D_2$ and $U_1 = U_2$. Nothing in the setup is symmetric, and $D_1^{-1}$ and $D_2$ don't cancel unless we already know $D_1 = D_2$.

questions.stem: For $\mathbf{u} = (1, 2)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (3, -1, 4)$, the outer product $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$ is a ___ $\times$ ___ matrix, and its $(2, 3)$ entry is ___.
questions.explanation: $\mathbf{u}$ is $2 \times 1$ and $\mathbf{v}^T$ is $1 \times 3$, so $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$ is $2 \times 3$, with $(i, j)$ entry $u_iv_j$: $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 & 4 \\ 6 & -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}$. The $(2, 3)$ entry is $u_2v_3 = 2 \cdot 4 = 8$.

questions.stem: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$. Which sum of outer products equals $AB$?
questions.explanation: The column–row expansion pairs column $k$ of $A$ with row $k$ of $B$: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 6 & 2\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 7 & 4\end{bmatrix} = AB$. The second choice uses the rows of $A$ as if they were columns.

questions.stem: Assuming compatible block sizes, what is $\begin{bmatrix} I & B \\ 0 & I\end{bmatrix}^{-1}$?
questions.explanation: Multiply: $\begin{bmatrix} I & B \\ 0 & I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} I & -B \\ 0 & I\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} I & -B + B \\ 0 & I\end{bmatrix} = I$. It is the block triangular formula with $A = D = I$, and the block version of undoing a row replacement.

questions.stem: $A$ and $D$ are invertible square blocks. What is the upper-right block of $\begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & D\end{bmatrix}^{-1}$?
questions.explanation: Solving the block equations gives $Z = 0$, $W = D^{-1}$, $X = A^{-1}$ and $AY + BD^{-1} = 0$, so $Y = -A^{-1}BD^{-1}$. The order matters: $A^{-1}$ multiplies on the left because $A$ was on the left of $Y$. ($B$ need not be square, so $B^{-1}$ may not even exist.)

questions.stem: Partition $M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}$ with $A$ the upper-left $2 \times 2$ block. The Schur complement $S = D - CA^{-1}B$ is the $1 \times 1$ matrix $[\,s\,]$ with $s =$ ___. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $A = \operatorname{diag}(2, 3)$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$, $C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $D = [\,6\,]$. Then $A^{-1}B = (1, 1)$ and $CA^{-1}B = 1 + 1 = 2$, so $S = 6 - 2 = 4$. Since $S \ne 0$, $M$ is invertible.

questions.stem: For an $n \times n$ matrix with $a_{11} \ne 0$, what is the Schur complement of the $1 \times 1$ block $a_{11}$?
choices: The $(n - 1) \times (n - 1)$ block left in rows and columns 2 to $n$ after clearing column 1
The first row of an echelon form
The matrix with row 1 and column 1 deleted, unchanged
questions.explanation: $S = D - \frac{1}{a_{11}}\mathbf{c}\mathbf{b}^T$ subtracts $\frac{c_i}{a_{11}}$ times the rest of row 1 from each lower row: exactly one step of elimination. Ordinary row reduction is a chain of Schur complements. Deleting row 1 and column 1 without updating gives $D$, not $S$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for solving $A\mathbf{x}_1 + B\mathbf{x}_2 = \mathbf{f}$, $C\mathbf{x}_1 + D\mathbf{x}_2 = \mathbf{g}$ by block elimination in order ($A$ invertible).
choices: Form the Schur complement $S = D - CA^{-1}B$
questions.explanation: Each step needs the one before: $S$ needs $A^{-1}B$, the equation for $\mathbf{x}_2$ needs $S$ and $A^{-1}\mathbf{f}$, and $\mathbf{x}_1$ needs $\mathbf{x}_2$. It is substitution, with blocks in place of single unknowns.

questions.stem: $M = \begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D\end{bmatrix}$ with $A$ square and invertible, and $S = D - CA^{-1}B$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: $M$ is invertible exactly when $S$ is invertible
$M = \begin{bmatrix} I & 0 \\ CA^{-1} & I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & S\end{bmatrix}$
$S$ always has the same size as $A$
If $S$ is singular, $M$ can still be invertible
questions.explanation: The block LU factorization is the second statement (multiply it out: the lower-left block is $CA^{-1}A = C$ and the lower-right is $CA^{-1}B + S = D$). From it, $M$ is invertible exactly when $S$ is; a null vector $\mathbf{z}$ of $S$ gives the null vector $(-A^{-1}B\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z})$ of $M$. $S$ has the size of $D$, not $A$.

questions.stem: Let $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{u} = (1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (0, 1)$. What is the Sherman–Morrison denominator $1 + \mathbf{v}^TA^{-1}\mathbf{u}$ for $A + \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$?
questions.explanation: $A^{-1}\mathbf{u}$ is column 1 of $A^{-1}$, $(2, 1)$, and $\mathbf{v}^T(2, 1) = 1$ picks its second entry. So the denominator is $1 + 1 = 2$, nonzero, and $A + \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$ is invertible. (Forgetting the 1 gives 1; using $(A^{-1})_{11} = 2$ gives 3.)

questions.stem: Use the Sherman–Morrison formula with $A = I_2$, $\mathbf{u} = (1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (0, 2)$ to find $(I + \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T)^{-1}$.
questions.explanation: $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $1 + \mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{u} = 1 + 0 = 1$, so the inverse is $I - \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. Check: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} = I$. The third choice has $\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}^T$ in place of $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$.

questions.stem: $A$ is invertible. The updated matrix $A + \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$ is singular exactly when $1 + \mathbf{v}^TA^{-1}\mathbf{u} =$ ___.
questions.explanation: When the denominator is nonzero, the Sherman–Morrison formula produces an inverse. When it is 0, the vector $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{u}$ (nonzero, since $\mathbf{u} \ne \mathbf{0}$ here) satisfies $(A + \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{v}^TA^{-1}\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$, so the updated matrix is singular.

questions.stem: $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (columns). Match each product to what it is.
questions.explanation: Column times row is the $3 \times 3$ outer product; row times column is the $1 \times 1$ inner product. In $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{u})$ the bracket is a number, so the result is that number times $\mathbf{u}$; likewise $(\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{u})\mathbf{v}^T$ is a number times $\mathbf{v}^T$. Associativity lets you group the factors either way.

questions.stem: Updating a known inverse with Sherman–Morrison takes on the order of $n^2$ operations, while computing a new inverse from scratch takes on the order of $n^3$. For $n = 1000$, about how many times less work is the update (ignoring constant factors)?
questions.explanation: $n^3/n^2 = n = 1000$. The real ratio depends on the constants in front of $n^2$ and $n^3$, but the update wins by roughly a factor of $n$, which is why it is used whenever a matrix changes a little at a time.

questions.stem: What is the Schur complement of the $1 \times 1$ block $a_{11} = 2$ in $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 4 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}$?
questions.explanation: $S = D - \tfrac12\mathbf{c}\mathbf{b}^T = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix} - \tfrac12\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 - 2 & 1 + 2 \\ 2 + 1 & 6 - 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{bmatrix}$, the rows left after clearing column 1 in the LU lesson. Adding instead of subtracting gives the third choice; $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ is the finished $U$ block, one step further.

questions.stem: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 10\end{bmatrix}$, the cofactor $C_{23}$ is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Delete row 2 and column 3: the minor is $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 7 & 8\end{vmatrix} = 8 - 14 = -6$. Position $(2, 3)$ has sign $(-1)^{2+3} = -1$, so $C_{23} = -(-6) = 6$. The minor $-6$ is not the cofactor.

questions.stem: The picture shows how the minor for one entry of a $4 \times 4$ matrix is formed. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A 4 by 4 grid of cells with its second row shaded and crossed out by a dashed line and its third column shaded and crossed out by a dashed line. The cell where they meet is boxed. An arrow points to a separate 3 by 3 grid. Marker 1 is on the crossed-out row, marker 2 on the crossed-out column, marker 3 on the boxed cell and marker 4 on the 3 by 3 grid.

choices: Smaller matrix whose determinant is the minor
questions.explanation: To find the minor of the entry in row 2, column 3 (marker 3), delete its row (1) and its column (2). The entries left over, in their original order, form the $3 \times 3$ matrix $A_{23}$ (4); its determinant is the minor, and the cofactor attaches the sign $(-1)^{2+3} = -1$.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a cofactor expansion in order.
choices: Choose the row or column with the most zeros
For each nonzero entry in it, delete that entry's row and column
Compute each minor (the determinant of the smaller matrix) and attach the checkerboard sign $(-1)^{i+j}$ to get its cofactor
Multiply each entry by its cofactor and add the results
questions.explanation: Pick the line to expand along first, since that decides which entries you use. Each entry's minor comes from deleting its row and column; the minor with its sign is the cofactor (the sign can be written down before or after the minor is computed, so the two go in one step); and the determinant is the sum of entry times cofactor.

questions.stem: Match each matrix to its determinant.
questions.explanation: $ad - bc$ each time: $6 - 0 = 6$ (lower triangular, so also the product of the diagonal); $4 - 4 = 0$ (the rows are proportional); $0 - 1 = -1$; $-3 - 1 = -4$. The distractor 4 comes from subtracting the wrong way round, $bc - ad = 1 - (-3)$, in the last matrix.

questions.stem: For which kinds of square matrix is the determinant simply the product of the diagonal entries? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Expanding a triangular matrix down its first column (upper) or along its first row (lower) leaves one term each time, so the determinant is the product of the diagonal; a diagonal matrix is both. A symmetric matrix needn't be: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $1 - 4 = -3$, not $1$.

questions.stem: Expanding a $5 \times 5$ determinant along a row with no zero entries produces ___ determinants of size $4 \times 4$.
questions.explanation: One cofactor for each of the 5 entries in the row, and each cofactor needs a $4 \times 4$ determinant. Each of those needs four $3 \times 3$ determinants, and so on, which is why the work grows like $n!$.

questions.stem: $A$ is $3 \times 3$ with $\det A = 6$. Then $\det(2A^{-1}) =$ ___. Give an exact fraction.
questions.explanation: $\det(2M) = 2^3\det M$ for a $3 \times 3$ matrix, and $\det A^{-1} = 1/\det A = 1/6$. So $\det(2A^{-1}) = 8 \cdot \tfrac16 = \tfrac43$. Getting $\tfrac13$ means using $2$ instead of $2^3$.

questions.stem: $A$ is $3 \times 3$. Match each change to $A$ with its effect on $\det A$.
left: Multiply every entry of A by 5
questions.explanation: A swap flips the sign, a replacement changes nothing, and scaling one row scales the determinant by the same factor. Multiplying the whole $3 \times 3$ matrix by 5 scales all three rows, so the factor is $5^3 = 125$. No row operation adds a constant to the determinant.

questions.stem: Which of these force $\det A = 0$ for a square matrix $A$? Select all that apply.
choices: One column of $A$ is a multiple of another column
A zero appears on the main diagonal of $A$
questions.explanation: Equal rows: subtracting one from the other makes a zero row without changing the determinant. A column that is a multiple of another makes the columns dependent (and the column version of the same argument applies, since $\det A^T = \det A$). A zero row gives 0 by expanding along it. A zero on the diagonal does not: $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $-1$. Only for a triangular matrix does a diagonal zero force $\det = 0$.

questions.stem: $A$ is $3 \times 3$ with $\det A = 2$. Put these determinants in order from smallest to largest.
Use row reduction to find $\det\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 8 & 1\end{bmatrix} =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The first pivot position holds 0, so swap $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$ (one swap): $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. Then $R_3 - 2R_1 = [\,0 \;\; 2 \;\; -3\,]$ and $R_3 - R_2 = [\,0 \;\; 0 \;\; -7\,]$. The diagonal product is $1 \cdot 2 \cdot (-7) = -14$, and one swap flips the sign: $\det = 14$.

questions.stem: The volume of this parallelepiped is (area of base) × (height) $= |\det[\,\mathbf{u} \;\; \mathbf{v} \;\; \mathbf{w}\,]|$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A slanted box drawn from a corner point, with three arrows leaving that corner: one to the right along the bottom, one going back along the bottom, and one rising up and to the right. The bottom face is shaded and a dashed vertical line drops from the tip of the rising arrow to the bottom face. Marker 1 is on the shaded bottom face, marker 2 on the dashed vertical line, marker 3 on the rising arrow and marker 4 on the corner point.

choices: Base parallelogram spanned by u and v
questions.explanation: The two arrows along the bottom are $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$; they span the shaded base (1). The rising arrow is $\mathbf{w}$ (3), and the dashed line is the height (2), the perpendicular distance from the tip of $\mathbf{w}$ down to the base, which is generally shorter than $\mathbf{w}$ itself. All three edges start at the origin (4). No diagonal is drawn, and the top face is not marked.

questions.stem: Use Cramer's rule on $3x_1 + 2x_2 = 7$, $x_1 + 4x_2 = 9$. Then $x_2 =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\det A = 3 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 1 = 10$. Replace column 2 by $\mathbf{b} = (7, 9)$: $\det\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 7 \\ 1 & 9\end{bmatrix} = 27 - 7 = 20$. So $x_2 = 20/10 = 2$ (and $x_1 = (28 - 18)/10 = 1$; check: $3 + 4 = 7$, $1 + 8 = 9$).

questions.stem: Match each matrix $A$ with what $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ does to areas and orientation in the plane.
choices: Flattens every region onto a line
questions.explanation: The determinants are $6$, $-1$, $1$ and $0$. Area is multiplied by $|\det A|$, and a negative determinant reverses orientation: the swap matrix is a reflection across $y = x$ ($\det = -1$), the shear keeps both ($\det = 1$), and the singular matrix sends the plane onto a line (area 0).

questions.stem: Which pairs of vectors span a parallelogram of area 10? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Area $= |\det[\,\mathbf{u} \;\; \mathbf{v}\,]|$: $2 \cdot 5 - 1 \cdot 0 = 10$; $5 - 5 = 0$ (parallel vectors, no area); $3(-3) - 1 \cdot 1 = -10$, area 10; $4 \cdot 3 - 2 \cdot 1 = 10$; $2 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 4 = 2$.

questions.stem: The triangle with vertices $(1, 2)$, $(5, 3)$ and $(2, 6)$ has area ___.
questions.explanation: Translate $(1, 2)$ to the origin: the edge vectors are $(4, 1)$ and $(1, 4)$. Then area $= \tfrac12\left|\det\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\right| = \tfrac12(16 - 1) = 7.5$. Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ gives 15.

questions.stem: How many terms does the permutation formula have for a $5 \times 5$ determinant?
questions.explanation: One term per permutation of $1, \dots, 5$: $5! = 120$. $5^5 = 3125$ would allow any column in each row, including repeated columns, which the formula excludes.

questions.stem: The permutation $(2, 5, 1, 4, 3)$ has ___ inversions.
questions.explanation: Count smaller entries to the right: 2 has 1 (the 1); 5 has 3 (1, 4, 3); 1 has none; 4 has 1 (the 3); 3 has none. Total $1 + 3 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 5$, so the permutation is odd.

questions.stem: With what sign does $a_{14}a_{23}a_{31}a_{42}$ appear in the permutation formula for a $4 \times 4$ determinant?
questions.explanation: The columns used by rows 1 to 4 give $\sigma = (4, 3, 1, 2)$. Smaller entries to the right: 4 has 3, 3 has 2, 1 has 0, so $3 + 2 + 0 + 0 = 5$ inversions. Five is odd, so the sign is minus. (6 would be the count for $(4, 3, 2, 1)$, where every pair is out of order.)

questions.stem: The shaded cells pick out one term of the permutation formula for a $4 \times 4$ determinant. What sign does that term get?

image.alt: A 4 by 4 grid with one shaded cell in each row: row 1 in column 4, row 2 in column 1, row 3 in column 3, row 4 in column 2.

questions.explanation: Reading the shaded column in each row gives $\sigma = (4, 1, 3, 2)$. Smaller entries to the right: 4 has 3, 1 has 0, 3 has 1 (the 2), 2 has 0, so 4 inversions and the sign is plus. (Reading the shaded row in each column instead gives the inverse permutation $(2, 4, 3, 1)$, which also has 4 inversions: a permutation and its inverse always have the same sign.)

questions.stem: Match each permutation of $1, 2, 3$ with its inversion count and parity.
questions.explanation: $(2, 1, 3)$: only the pair $2, 1$. $(2, 3, 1)$: $2, 1$ and $3, 1$. $(3, 2, 1)$: every pair is out of order, $3$ pairs. A 3-cycle such as $(2, 3, 1)$ is even even though it moves every entry.

questions.stem: Which products are terms (up to sign) of the permutation formula for a $4 \times 4$ determinant? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A term uses each row once and each column once. The first, second and fourth do (columns $1, 2, 3, 4$; $2, 1, 4, 3$; $4, 3, 2, 1$). $a_{11}a_{21}a_{33}a_{44}$ uses column 1 twice, and $a_{13}a_{22}a_{31}a_{43}$ uses column 3 twice; neither uses every column.

questions.stem: What is $\det\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$?
questions.explanation: This is the permutation matrix of $\sigma = (2, 3, 1)$ (row $i$ has its 1 in column $\sigma(i)$). Only one term is nonzero, equal to $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma$. $(2, 3, 1)$ has 2 inversions, so it is even and $\det = 1$. (It takes two row swaps to turn the matrix into $I$.)

questions.stem: Which defining property of the determinant says that swapping two rows multiplies it by $-1$?
questions.explanation: That is the alternating property. Multilinear means linear in each row with the others fixed, and normalized means $\det I = 1$. The multiplicative property $\det(AB) = \det A\det B$ is a consequence, not one of the three defining properties.

questions.stem: Using only the three defining properties, why does a matrix with two equal rows have determinant 0?
choices: Swapping the two equal rows leaves the matrix unchanged but must flip the sign, so $\det A = -\det A$
Its rows are linearly dependent, so by the invertible matrix theorem $\det A = 0$
Linearity in a row means that row can be multiplied by 0 without changing anything
The permutation formula has no terms for such a matrix
questions.explanation: The alternating property applied to the two equal rows gives $\det A = -\det A$, so $\det A = 0$. The invertible-matrix route is true but uses more than the three properties. Scaling a row by 0 does change the determinant (to 0), and the permutation formula still has all its terms; they cancel in pairs.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the proof that $\det(AB) = \det A\det B$ (when $\det B \neq 0$) in order.
choices: Check that $D$ is multilinear and alternating in the rows of $A$, with $D(I) = 1$
Conclude by uniqueness that $D(A) = \det A$ for every $A$
questions.explanation: The function has to be defined before its properties can be checked; the uniqueness theorem applies only once all three properties are known; and the product rule is the last line, $\det(AB) = D(A)\det B = \det A\det B$.

questions.stem: $\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 5 & 25\end{bmatrix} =$ ___. (It is a Vandermonde determinant.)
questions.explanation: The rows are $(1, x, x^2)$ for $x = 0, 2, 5$, so $\det = (2 - 0)(5 - 0)(5 - 2) = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 3 = 30$. Direct check, expanding along row 1: $1 \cdot (2 \cdot 25 - 4 \cdot 5) = 50 - 20 = 30$.

questions.stem: Rows $\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \mathbf{r}_3$ form a matrix with determinant 4, and the matrix with rows $\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \mathbf{s}$ has determinant $-1$. What is the determinant of the matrix with rows $\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, 2\mathbf{r}_3 + \mathbf{s}$?
questions.explanation: The determinant is linear in row 3 when rows 1 and 2 are fixed: $2 \cdot 4 + (-1) = 7$. Answer 3 forgets the factor 2; $-8$ multiplies instead of adding.

questions.stem: When is $\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2\end{bmatrix}$ equal to 0?
choices: Exactly when two of $a, b, c$ are equal
questions.explanation: The determinant is $(b - a)(c - a)(c - b)$, which is 0 exactly when some pair is equal (two equal rows). If $a, b, c$ are distinct it is nonzero, even when they add to 0, for example $-1, 0, 1$ give $(1)(2)(1) = 2$.

questions.stem: A permutation $\sigma$ of $1, \dots, n$ has $\sigma(1) = j$. How many of its inversions involve position 1?
questions.explanation: The values $1, \dots, j - 1$ are all smaller than $j$ and all sit to the right of position 1, so each makes an inversion with it: $j - 1$ in all. That is where the cofactor sign $(-1)^{1+j} = (-1)^{j-1}$ comes from.

questions.stem: Why does the rule of Sarrus (three down-right diagonal products minus three down-left ones) fail for $4 \times 4$ matrices?
choices: A $4 \times 4$ determinant has 24 terms, and the diagonals give only 8 of them
The signs of the diagonals alternate differently for even sizes
It works, but only for symmetric $4 \times 4$ matrices
A $4 \times 4$ determinant has 16 terms, one per entry
questions.explanation: Sarrus lists the $3! = 6$ terms of a $3 \times 3$ determinant. A $4 \times 4$ determinant has $4! = 24$ terms, and the 8 wrapped diagonals miss 16 of them (some diagonal products also get the wrong sign).

questions.stem: For $\mathbf{u} = (2, 0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (1, 3, -1)$, the components of $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$ are ___, ___ and ___ (in order).
Two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ lie in the horizontal plane, and their cross product $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$ points straight up. Use the right-hand rule to name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A horizontal plane drawn in perspective. Two arrows start at the same point in the plane: one points to the right and one points back and to the right; the parallelogram they span is shaded. A third arrow rises straight up from the same point. A small curved arrow turns from the right-pointing arrow toward the back-pointing one. Marker 1 is on the upward arrow, marker 2 on the shaded parallelogram, marker 3 on the right-pointing arrow and marker 4 on the back-pointing arrow.

choices: Parallelogram spanned by u and v
questions.explanation: The cross product is perpendicular to both vectors, so it is the upward arrow (1); its length equals the area of the shaded parallelogram (2). With your thumb pointing up, your right hand's fingers curl counterclockwise as seen from above, from the right-pointing arrow toward the back-pointing one, so the right-pointing arrow is $\mathbf{u}$ (3) and the other is $\mathbf{v}$ (4). $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u}$ would point straight down.

questions.stem: Find the area of the triangle with two edges $\mathbf{u} = (2, 0, 0)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (0, 3, 4)$ from the same corner.
questions.explanation: $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = (0 \cdot 4 - 0 \cdot 3,\; 0 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot 4,\; 2 \cdot 3 - 0 \cdot 0) = (0, -8, 6)$, with length $\sqrt{64 + 36} = 10$. That is the parallelogram; the triangle is half, 5. (Also: $\mathbf{u}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}$, so the triangle is right-angled with legs 2 and 5.)

questions.stem: How is $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u}$ related to $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$?
questions.explanation: Swapping $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ swaps two rows of the determinant that defines the cross product, which flips the sign of every component. Same length, opposite direction.

questions.stem: Why is $\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}) = 0$ for all $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$?
choices: It equals a determinant with two equal rows
Because the dot product is commutative
It only holds when $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are perpendicular
questions.explanation: $\mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v})$ is the determinant with rows $\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$. With $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u}$ two rows are equal, so it is 0 for every $\mathbf{v}$. That is why $\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{u}$. ($\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ is true but is a different statement.)

questions.stem: Find the volume of the tetrahedron with corners $(0, 0, 0)$, $(2, 0, 0)$, $(0, 3, 0)$ and $(1, 1, 4)$.
questions.explanation: The edges from the origin give $\det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24$ (triangular). The tetrahedron is $\tfrac16$ of that box: $24/6 = 4$. 24 is the parallelepiped; 12 uses $\tfrac12$ (the triangle factor); 8 uses $\tfrac13$.

questions.stem: If $\det[\,\mathbf{u} \;\; \mathbf{v} \;\; \mathbf{w}\,] = -5$, what is $\mathbf{v} \cdot (\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{w})$?
questions.explanation: $\mathbf{x} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = \det[\,\mathbf{a} \;\; \mathbf{b} \;\; \mathbf{x}\,]$, so $\mathbf{v} \cdot (\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{w}) = \det[\,\mathbf{u} \;\; \mathbf{w} \;\; \mathbf{v}\,]$. That is $[\,\mathbf{u} \;\; \mathbf{v} \;\; \mathbf{w}\,]$ with its last two columns swapped, so it equals $-(-5) = 5$.

questions.stem: Which sets of three points lie on one line? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Compute $D = \det[\,\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p} \;\; \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{p}\,]$ for each: $\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix} = 0$; $\det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} = 2$; $\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix} = 0$; $\det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4\end{bmatrix} = 0$; $\det\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} = -3$. Zero means collinear.

questions.stem: For $\mathbf{p} = (0, 0)$, $\mathbf{q} = (4, 1)$, $\mathbf{r} = (1, 3)$, which way does the path $\mathbf{p} \to \mathbf{q} \to \mathbf{r}$ turn?
choices: It doesn't turn: the points are collinear
questions.explanation: $D = \det\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} = 12 - 1 = 11 > 0$, so the turn is to the left and the triangle $\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{r}$ is listed counterclockwise. 13 comes from adding $1 \cdot 1$ instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: The quadrilateral with corners $(0, 0)$, $(5, 0)$, $(4, 3)$, $(1, 4)$, in that (counterclockwise) order, has area ___.
Put the steps of the shoelace formula in order.
choices: List the corners in counterclockwise order around the boundary
Repeat the first corner at the end of the list
For each consecutive pair, compute $x_iy_{i+1} - x_{i+1}y_i$
questions.explanation: The corners must be in order around the boundary first; repeating the first corner supplies the last pair; each pair gives twice a signed triangle area; the total is twice the polygon's area, so it is halved at the end.

questions.stem: Match each expression to the quantity it gives ($\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}$ are edge vectors from one corner).
choices: Area of the parallelogram on u and v
Area of the triangle on u and v
Volume of the parallelepiped on u, v, w
Volume of the tetrahedron on u, v, w
Volume of the pyramid on a square base
questions.explanation: The cross product's length is the parallelogram's area, and a triangle is half of it. The triple product's absolute value is the box volume, and a tetrahedron (a pyramid on a triangular base) is $\tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac16$ of the box.

questions.stem: A student applies the shoelace formula to a pentagon but lists the corners clockwise. What happens?
choices: The result is the area with a minus sign
The result is twice the area
questions.explanation: Reversing the order turns every term $x_iy_{i+1} - x_{i+1}y_i$ into its negative (each pair is now taken the other way round), so the formula gives $-(\text{area})$. Take the absolute value, or list the corners counterclockwise.

questions.stem: Setting $\begin{vmatrix} x & y & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 7 & 1\end{vmatrix} = 0$ gives the line through $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 7)$. Which equation is it?
Each panel shows a set in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Say whether it is a subspace, and if not, which condition it fails.

image.alt: Four small coordinate planes, numbered. One shows a line through the origin; one shows a line that misses the origin, with the origin drawn as a hollow dot; one shows both axes highlighted, with u on the x-axis, v on the y-axis and a dashed u + v pointing between them; one shows the shaded first quadrant with u inside it and a dashed −u pointing out of it.

choices: Does not contain the zero vector
questions.explanation: The line through the origin is $\operatorname{Span}$ of one vector, so it is a subspace. The line that misses the origin fails at once: it doesn't contain $\mathbf{0}$. The union of the axes contains $\mathbf{0}$ and every multiple of an axis vector stays on that axis, but $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$ lands off both axes, so it is not closed under addition. The first quadrant is closed under addition, but $(-1)\mathbf{u}$ leaves it, so it is not closed under scalar multiplication.

questions.stem: Write $H = \{(a - 2b,\ b,\ 3a) : a, b \text{ real}\}$ as a span: $H = \operatorname{Span}\{(1, 0, 3),\ (x, 1, y)\}$, where $x =$ ___ and $y =$ ___. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: Split by parameter: $(a - 2b, b, 3a) = a(1, 0, 3) + b(-2, 1, 0)$. So $x = -2$ and $y = 0$. Since $H$ is a span, it is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

questions.stem: Test each set in the order: zero vector, then closure under addition, then closure under scalar multiplication. Match each set with the first test it fails (or with "Subspace" if it passes all three).
questions.explanation: $y = 5x$ is a line through the origin, the span of $(1, 5)$. The zero polynomial has value 0 at $t = 2$, not 1, so the second set fails the first test. $xy = 0$ is the union of the two axes: it contains $(0, 0)$, but $(1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1)$ has $xy = 1$. The upper half-plane $y \ge 0$ contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under addition (two nonnegative $y$'s add to a nonnegative one), but $(-1)(0, 1) = (0, -1)$ leaves it.

questions.stem: Which of these sets are subspaces of $\mathbb{P}_3$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $p(0) = 0$ and $p(1) - p(2) = 0$ are conditions that survive adding and scaling (each side is linear in $p$), and the zero polynomial satisfies both, so both sets are subspaces. "Degree exactly 3" misses the zero polynomial, and $t^3 + (-t^3 + t)$ has degree 1. $p(0) \ge 0$ fails under multiplication by $-1$: $p = 1$ is in the set but $-1$ is not.

questions.stem: Which subset of $M_{2\times 2}$ is a subspace?
choices: The matrices whose two diagonal entries add to 0
The matrices whose entries are all $\ge 0$
questions.explanation: $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$ with $a + d = 0$: the zero matrix qualifies, and if $a + d = 0$ and $a' + d' = 0$ then $(a + a') + (d + d') = 0$ and $ka + kd = 0$. The determinant-0 matrices are not closed under addition: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} = I$. The invertible matrices don't contain the zero matrix. Nonnegative matrices aren't closed under multiplication by $-1$.

questions.stem: The picture shows the subspaces of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two panels, inputs R² on the left and outputs R³ on the right, joined by an arrow. The left panel shows a line through the origin. The right panel shows three axes, a line through the origin, and a hollow point on the x₃-axis that is off that line. The line in each panel, the arrow and the hollow point are numbered.

choices: A vector not in Col A
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{Nul} A$ lives among the inputs: it is the line $\operatorname{Span}\{(-2, 1)\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. $\operatorname{Col} A$ lives among the outputs: the line $\operatorname{Span}\{(1, 2, -1)\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, because column 2 is twice column 1. The arrow is the map $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$. The hollow point $(0, 0, 2)$ is not a multiple of $(1, 2, -1)$, so it is not in $\operatorname{Col} A$, and $A\mathbf{x} = (0, 0, 2)$ has no solution.

questions.stem: Let $A$ be a $4 \times 6$ matrix. Then $\operatorname{Nul} A$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n =$ ___, and $\operatorname{Col} A$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$ with $m =$ ___.
questions.explanation: Null-space vectors are inputs $\mathbf{x}$ with $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$; they have one entry per column, 6. Column-space vectors are outputs $A\mathbf{x}$; they have one entry per row, 4.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding a spanning set for $\operatorname{Nul} A$ in order.
choices: Identify the free variables (the non-pivot columns)
Solve for each pivot variable in terms of the free variables
Write the solution $\mathbf{x}$ in parametric vector form
Take the vector multiplying each free variable
questions.explanation: You need the reduced echelon form to see the pivots, the pivots to know which variables are free, the free variables before you can solve for the others, and the solved equations before you can write $\mathbf{x}$ as a combination of vectors. The vectors in that combination, one per free variable, span $\operatorname{Nul} A$.

questions.stem: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}$. Which vectors are in $\operatorname{Nul} A$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Row 2 is twice row 1, so $\mathbf{x}$ is in $\operatorname{Nul} A$ exactly when $x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = 0$. Check each: $1 - 1 + 0 = 0$ ✓; $-2 - 0 + 2 = 0$ ✓; $1 + 1 + 0 = 2$ ✗; $2 - 0 + 2 = 4$ ✗. Testing membership in a null space is just multiplying by $A$.

questions.stem: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}$. Is $\mathbf{b} = (2, 5)$ in $\operatorname{Col} A$?
choices: No: $(2, 5)$ is not a multiple of $(1, 2)$
Yes: every vector of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is in the column space of a $2 \times 2$ matrix
questions.explanation: Column 2 is $3 \times$ column 1, so $\operatorname{Col} A = \operatorname{Span}\{(1, 2)\}$, a line. $(2, 5)$ is not on it ($2 \cdot 2 \ne 5$), so $A\mathbf{x} = (2, 5)$ is inconsistent. $A(2, 0) = (2, 4)$, not $(2, 5)$. A $2 \times 2$ matrix has $\operatorname{Col} A = \mathbb{R}^2$ only when it has two pivots. Computing $A\mathbf{b}$ tests the null space, not the column space.

questions.stem: The picture shows $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ and its reduced echelon form. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: The matrix A beside its reduced echelon form, joined by an arrow labeled row-reduce. In A, columns 1 and 3 are shaded. In the reduced echelon form, two entries equal to 1 are circled, the last column is outlined with a dashed box, and the bottom row of zeros is shaded. Four parts are numbered.

choices: Pivot column of A, part of a basis for Col A
Pivot column of the RREF to use for Col A
questions.explanation: The reduced echelon form has pivots in columns 1 and 3 (the circled 1s), so columns 1 and 3 of $A$ itself, $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(-1, 1, 0)$, are a basis for $\operatorname{Col} A$. Column 4 has no pivot: it is a combination of the pivot columns. The bottom row became all zeros, so $A$ has rank 2. The RREF's own pivot columns $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 0)$ are not even in $\operatorname{Col} A$.

questions.stem: The reduced echelon form of $A$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. A basis for $\operatorname{Nul} A$ is $\{(a, b, 1, 0)\}$, where $a =$ ___ and $b =$ ___. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: Pivots are in columns 1, 2 and 4, so $x_3$ is the only free variable. The rows say $x_1 + 2x_3 = 0$, $x_2 - x_3 = 0$ and $x_4 = 0$. So $\mathbf{x} = x_3(-2, 1, 1, 0)$: $a = -2$, $b = 1$.

questions.stem: Match each subspace with where a basis for it comes from after one row reduction of $A$.
choices: The pivot columns of A itself
The nonzero rows of an echelon form
The vectors in the parametric vector form of Ax = 0
The pivot columns of the echelon form
questions.explanation: Row operations keep the dependence relations among the columns but change the columns themselves, so the pivot columns tell you which columns of the original $A$ to keep for $\operatorname{Col} A$. Row operations do preserve the row space, so the nonzero rows of an echelon form are a basis for $\operatorname{Row} A$ (the rows of $A$ may be dependent). The parametric vector form gives one null-space basis vector per free variable.

questions.stem: Which sets are bases of $\mathbb{R}^2$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$ are not multiples of each other, so they are independent and span $\mathbb{R}^2$; the same goes for $(0, 5)$ and $(2, 0)$. Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ are always dependent, so $\{(1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)\}$ spans but is not a basis. $(3, -6) = -3(-1, 2)$, so that pair is dependent and spans only a line.

questions.stem: Which set is a basis for $\mathbb{P}_2$?
questions.explanation: In coordinates relative to $\{1, t, t^2\}$, the last set is $(1, 1, 0)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 0, 1)$. Row-reducing the matrix with these columns gives three pivots, so they are independent and span $\mathbb{P}_2$. $\{1, t^2\}$ can't produce $t$. $2 + 2t = 2(1 + t)$, so that set is dependent. $t^3$ is not in $\mathbb{P}_2$ at all.

questions.stem: The slanted grid is built from $\mathbf{b}_1 = (2, 1)$ and $\mathbf{b}_2 = (-1, 1)$. Give the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates $(c_1, c_2)$ of each numbered point.

image.alt: A slanted grid drawn over the standard axes, with the arrows b₁ and b₂ starting at the origin. Four grid points are numbered.

questions.explanation: Count grid steps along $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$. Point 1 is $2\mathbf{b}_1 + 3\mathbf{b}_2 = (1, 5)$: its standard coordinates are $(1, 5)$, but its $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates are $(2, 3)$. Point 2 is $\mathbf{b}_1 + 2\mathbf{b}_2 = (0, 3)$. Point 3 is $2\mathbf{b}_1 - \mathbf{b}_2 = (5, 1)$. Point 4 is $-\mathbf{b}_1 + \mathbf{b}_2 = (-3, 0)$.

questions.stem: Let $\mathcal{B} = \{(1, 1), (1, -1)\}$ and $\mathbf{x} = (5, 1)$. Then $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = (c_1, c_2)$ with $c_1 =$ ___ and $c_2 =$ ___.
You know $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ and want $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}$, for two bases of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Put the steps in order.
choices: Row-reduce until the left block is $I$
questions.explanation: The target basis $\mathcal{C}$ goes on the left. When the left block becomes $I$, the right block holds the columns $[\mathbf{b}_j]_{\mathcal{C}}$, which is $P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}$. Only then can you multiply it by $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$.

questions.stem: Let $\mathcal{B} = \{\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $P_{\mathcal{B}} = [\,\mathbf{b}_1 \;\; \mathbf{b}_2\,]$. Which statements are true for every $\mathbf{x}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $P_{\mathcal{B}}[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1 + c_2\mathbf{b}_2 = \mathbf{x}$, and multiplying by $P_{\mathcal{B}}^{-1}$ reverses it. $P_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbf{x}$ goes the wrong way: it treats the standard coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ as if they were $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates. $\mathbf{b}_1 = 1\mathbf{b}_1 + 0\mathbf{b}_2$, so its coordinate vector is $(1, 0)$.

questions.stem: Find the coordinate vector of $p(t) = 4 + 3t - t^2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B} = \{1,\ 1 + t,\ t^2\}$ of $\mathbb{P}_2$.
questions.explanation: Write $p = c_1 \cdot 1 + c_2(1 + t) + c_3t^2$. Matching $t^2$: $c_3 = -1$. Matching $t$: $c_2 = 3$. Matching constants: $c_1 + c_2 = 4$, so $c_1 = 1$. Check: $1 + 3(1 + t) - t^2 = 4 + 3t - t^2$. $(4, 3, -1)$ is the coordinate vector in the standard basis; $(7, 3, -1)$ adds $c_2$ instead of subtracting it; $(1, -1, 3)$ lists the weights in the wrong order.

questions.stem: An $m \times n$ matrix $A$ has rank $r$. Name the four subspaces in the picture, using their dimensions and where they live.

image.alt: Two regions: Rⁿ (inputs, n = number of columns) and Rᵐ (outputs, m = number of rows), joined by an arrow labeled A. Each region holds two numbered ovals. In Rⁿ the ovals have dimension r and n − r, and a dashed arrow labeled sent to 0 runs from the second one to the zero vector of Rᵐ. In Rᵐ the ovals have dimension r and m − r.

questions.explanation: Among the inputs: $\operatorname{Row} A$ has dimension $r$ (the number of pivots) and $\operatorname{Nul} A$ has dimension $n - r$ (the number of free variables); $\operatorname{Nul} A$ is the part sent to $\mathbf{0}$. Among the outputs: $\operatorname{Col} A$ has dimension $r$, and $\operatorname{Nul} A^T$ has dimension $m - r$ by the rank theorem applied to the $n \times m$ matrix $A^T$, which also has rank $r$.

questions.stem: A $6 \times 9$ matrix $A$ has rank 4. Then $\dim\operatorname{Nul} A =$ ___ and $\dim\operatorname{Nul} A^T =$ ___.
questions.explanation: Rank theorem for $A$ (9 columns): $\dim\operatorname{Nul} A = 9 - 4 = 5$. $A^T$ is $9 \times 6$ with the same rank 4, so $\dim\operatorname{Nul} A^T = 6 - 4 = 2$.

questions.stem: Match each vector space with its dimension.
questions.explanation: $\mathbb{P}_4$ has basis $1, t, t^2, t^3, t^4$: five vectors (count the constant). $M_{2\times 3}$ has one basis matrix per entry: 6. A plane through the origin is spanned by two independent vectors, even though its vectors have three entries. $\mathbb{R}^4$ has the standard basis of 4 vectors.

questions.stem: A $5 \times 5$ matrix $A$ has $\dim\operatorname{Nul} A = 0$. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
choices: The columns of $A$ are linearly dependent
questions.explanation: By the rank theorem, $\operatorname{rank} A = 5 - 0 = 5$, so $\operatorname{Col} A$ is a 5-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^5$, which is all of $\mathbb{R}^5$. Five pivots in a $5 \times 5$ matrix means $A$ is invertible, and its columns are independent, not dependent.

questions.stem: What is the smallest possible value of $\dim\operatorname{Nul} A$ for a $4 \times 7$ matrix $A$?
questions.explanation: The rank is at most the number of rows, 4, so the rank theorem gives $\dim\operatorname{Nul} A = 7 - \operatorname{rank} A \ge 7 - 4 = 3$. A $4 \times 7$ matrix always has at least three free variables. 0 would need rank 7, which is impossible with 4 rows.

questions.stem: A vector space $V$ is spanned by 5 vectors. Which statement must be true?
choices: Every linearly independent set in $V$ has at most 5 vectors
Every spanning set of $V$ has exactly 5 vectors
Every set of 5 vectors in $V$ is a basis
questions.explanation: The exchange lemma says an independent set is never larger than a spanning set. The spanning set may be redundant, so $\dim V$ could be less than 5 (for example, five vectors spanning a plane). Then other spanning sets can be smaller, and five vectors in $V$ cannot all be independent.

questions.stem: In the proof of the exchange lemma, $\mathbf{u}_k = a_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \cdots + a_{k-1}\mathbf{u}_{k-1} + c_k\mathbf{w}_k + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{w}_n$. Why must some $c_j$ be nonzero?
choices: Otherwise $\mathbf{u}_k$ would be a combination of $\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_{k-1}$, which contradicts the independence of the $\mathbf{u}$'s
Because $\mathbf{u}_k$ is not the zero vector
questions.explanation: If every $c_j$ were 0, the equation would write $\mathbf{u}_k$ using only earlier $\mathbf{u}$'s, a dependence relation among independent vectors. The $\mathbf{w}$'s are only assumed to span, not to be independent. $\mathbf{u}_k \ne \mathbf{0}$ is true but not enough: a nonzero vector could still be a combination of $\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_{k-1}$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for extending a linearly independent set $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_p\}$ to a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ in order.
choices: Make $\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_p$ the first columns of a matrix
Row-reduce to find the pivot columns
Keep the pivot columns of the original matrix as the basis
questions.explanation: The given vectors must come first: independent vectors at the front are always pivot columns, so they all survive. The standard vectors are added so the columns span $\mathbb{R}^n$. Row reduction finds the pivot columns, and, as for any column space, the basis is made of the original columns in those positions.

questions.stem: The vector $\mathbf{u} = (0, 2, 1, 0)$ is to be swapped into the spanning set $\{\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3, \mathbf{e}_4\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$. Which $\mathbf{e}_j$ could it replace, so that the new set still spans $\mathbb{R}^4$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\mathbf{u} = 0\mathbf{e}_1 + 2\mathbf{e}_2 + 1\mathbf{e}_3 + 0\mathbf{e}_4$. The exchange works for any $\mathbf{e}_j$ with a nonzero coefficient: $\mathbf{e}_2 = \tfrac12(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{e}_3)$ and $\mathbf{e}_3 = \mathbf{u} - 2\mathbf{e}_2$. Replacing $\mathbf{e}_1$ or $\mathbf{e}_4$ fails: $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3$ and the remaining one all have a 0 in that slot, so the removed vector can't be rebuilt.

questions.stem: $H$ and $K$ are subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^6$ with $\dim H = \dim K = 4$. What is the smallest possible value of $\dim(H \cap K)$?
questions.explanation: $H + K$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^6$, so $\dim(H + K) \le 6$. The dimension formula gives $\dim(H \cap K) = 4 + 4 - \dim(H + K) \ge 8 - 6 = 2$. It can equal 2: take $H = \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_4\}$ and $K = \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{e}_3, \dots, \mathbf{e}_6\}$, which meet in $\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{e}_3, \mathbf{e}_4\}$.

questions.stem: Two 3-dimensional subspaces $H$ and $K$ of $\mathbb{R}^5$ meet in a 2-dimensional subspace. Then $\dim(H + K) =$ ___.
questions.explanation: $\dim(H + K) = \dim H + \dim K - \dim(H \cap K) = 3 + 3 - 2 = 4$.

questions.stem: In $\mathbb{R}^3$, let $H = \operatorname{Span}\{(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)\}$ and $K = \operatorname{Span}\{(1, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)\}$. What is $H \cap K$?
questions.explanation: $H$ is the plane $x_3 = 0$ and $K$ is the plane $x_1 = x_2$. A vector in both has $x_3 = 0$ and $x_1 = x_2$, so it is a multiple of $(1, 1, 0)$. Check with the formula: the two planes are different, so $H + K = \mathbb{R}^3$ and $\dim(H \cap K) = 2 + 2 - 3 = 1$. $(0, 0, 1)$ is in $K$ but not $H$; $\{\mathbf{0}\}$ is impossible for two planes in $\mathbb{R}^3$; the last plane is $H$ itself.

questions.stem: Let $H$ and $K$ be subspaces of a finite-dimensional space $V$. Which statements are always true? Select all that apply.
choices: $H + K$ is the smallest subspace that contains both $H$ and $K$
questions.explanation: The intersection contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under both operations, because each of $H$ and $K$ is. Any subspace containing $H$ and $K$ contains every sum $\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{k}$, so $H + K$ is the smallest. The union of the two axes in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not a subspace. The dimension formula subtracts $\dim(H \cap K)$, which is 0 only for a direct sum.

questions.stem: $H$ is a plane through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and $\mathbb{R}^3 = H \oplus K$. What can $K$ be?
choices: Any line through the origin that does not lie in $H$
Only the line through the origin perpendicular to $H$
Any plane through the origin other than $H$
questions.explanation: A direct sum needs $H \cap K = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ and $\dim H + \dim K = 3$, so $K$ is a line meeting $H$ only at $\mathbf{0}$: any line through the origin not lying in $H$. The perpendicular line is one choice among many. A second plane meets $H$ in a line, so the sum isn't direct, and a line inside $H$ adds nothing.

questions.stem: Match each pair of subspaces $H$, $K$ with $\dim(H + K)$.
left: A line $H$ lying inside a plane $K$, both through $\mathbf{0}$
questions.explanation: Use $\dim(H + K) = \dim H + \dim K - \dim(H \cap K)$. Two different lines meet only at $\mathbf{0}$: $1 + 1 - 0 = 2$ (they span a plane). Two different planes in $\mathbb{R}^3$ meet in a line: $2 + 2 - 1 = 3$. A line inside a plane: $H \cap K = H$, so $1 + 2 - 1 = 2$, the plane itself. A direct sum of two planes in $\mathbb{R}^4$: $2 + 2 - 0 = 4$.

questions.stem: To extend $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2\}$ with $\mathbf{u}_1 = (1, 1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{u}_2 = (0, 1, 1)$ to a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$, you row-reduce $[\,\mathbf{u}_1 \;\; \mathbf{u}_2 \;\; \mathbf{e}_1 \;\; \mathbf{e}_2 \;\; \mathbf{e}_3\,]$ and find pivots in columns 1, 2 and 3. Which basis does the method give?
questions.explanation: Keep the original columns in the pivot positions 1, 2, 3: $\mathbf{u}_1$, $\mathbf{u}_2$ and $\mathbf{e}_1$. This contains the given vectors, as an extension must. Two vectors can't span $\mathbb{R}^3$, and four vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are dependent. The standard basis is a basis but doesn't contain $\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2$.

questions.stem: $L_1$, $L_2$, $L_3$ are three different lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^2$. What is $\dim(L_1 + L_2 + L_3)$?
questions.explanation: Any two different lines through the origin already span $\mathbb{R}^2$, so the sum is $\mathbb{R}^2$, of dimension 2. Adding dimensions and subtracting pairwise intersections (all $\{\mathbf{0}\}$) would wrongly give 3: the two-subspace formula does not extend to three subspaces like inclusion–exclusion.

questions.stem: Subspaces $H$ and $K$ of $\mathbb{R}^7$ have $\dim H = 3$, $\dim K = 5$ and $H + K = \mathbb{R}^7$. Then $\dim(H \cap K) =$ ___.
questions.explanation: $\dim(H \cap K) = \dim H + \dim K - \dim(H + K) = 3 + 5 - 7 = 1$.

questions.stem: Which of these statements needs the space $V$ to be finite-dimensional?
choices: The intersection of two subspaces of $V$ is a subspace
A span of vectors in $V$ is a subspace
A subspace $H$ of $V$ with $\dim H = \dim V$ equals $V$
questions.explanation: The other three are true in every vector space. The last one fails in infinite dimensions: the polynomials with zero constant term are an infinite-dimensional subspace of the space of all polynomials, yet not the whole space. In finite dimensions, a basis of $H$ is an independent set of $\dim V$ vectors, so by the basis theorem it spans $V$.

questions.stem: $T: V \to W$ is linear, $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V$ (with $n$ vectors) and $\mathcal{C}$ a basis of $W$ (with $m$ vectors), and $M$ is the matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$. Name the numbered maps.

image.alt: A square diagram with boxes V at top left, W at top right, Rⁿ at bottom left and Rᵐ at bottom right. Arrows go from V to W, from Rⁿ to Rᵐ, from V down to Rⁿ, and from W down to Rᵐ, and each arrow is numbered. Beside the boxes are x, T(x), [x] sub B and [T(x)] sub C.

questions.explanation: $T$ goes straight from $V$ to $W$. Taking $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates turns $\mathbf{x}$ into $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and taking $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates turns $T(\mathbf{x})$ into $[T(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{C}}$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$. The bottom arrow is multiplication by $M$, because $[T(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{C}} = M[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$: both routes from $V$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ agree.

questions.stem: Let $T: \mathbb{P}_4 \to \mathbb{P}_2$ be linear. What size is the matrix of $T$ relative to bases of $\mathbb{P}_4$ and $\mathbb{P}_2$?
questions.explanation: The matrix is $\dim W \times \dim V$: one column per input basis vector and one row per output coordinate. $\dim\mathbb{P}_4 = 5$ and $\dim\mathbb{P}_2 = 3$, so it is $3 \times 5$. The sizes with 4 and 2 forget that $\dim\mathbb{P}_n = n + 1$; $5 \times 3$ has rows and columns swapped.

questions.stem: Find the matrix of differentiation $D: \mathbb{P}_2 \to \mathbb{P}_1$, $D(p) = p'$, relative to the standard bases $\{1, t, t^2\}$ and $\{1, t\}$.
questions.explanation: $D(1) = 0$, $D(t) = 1$, $D(t^2) = 2t$, with coordinates $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(0, 2)$ in $\{1, t\}$. These are the three columns of a $2 \times 3$ matrix. The $3 \times 2$ choice writes them as rows; $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ drops the zero column for $D(1)$ and shifts the others; the $3 \times 3$ matrix uses $\mathbb{P}_2$ as the output space.

questions.stem: Let $T: \mathbb{P}_2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$, $T(p) = (p(0), p(3))$. Its kernel is spanned by one polynomial $t^2 + bt + c$, where $b =$ ___ and $c =$ ___.
questions.explanation: The matrix relative to $\{1, t, t^2\}$ is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 9\end{bmatrix}$. Its null space: $x_1 = 0$ and $3x_2 + 9x_3 = 0$, so $(0, -3, 1)x_3$. That is the polynomial $-3t + t^2 = t(t - 3)$, which vanishes at 0 and 3. So $b = -3$ and $c = 0$.

questions.stem: A linear map $T: M_{2\times 2} \to \mathbb{P}_2$ is onto. What is $\dim(\ker T)$?
questions.explanation: Onto means the range is all of $\mathbb{P}_2$, of dimension 3. Rank–nullity: $\dim M_{2\times 2} = 4 = \dim\ker T + 3$, so $\dim\ker T = 1$. 0 would need $\dim V = \dim W$; 3 confuses the range's dimension with the kernel's.

questions.stem: For which of these could a linear map be one-to-one? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: One-to-one means $\ker T = \{\mathbf{0}\}$, so $\dim V = \dim\operatorname{range} T \le \dim W$. $\mathbb{P}_3 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ has $4 \le 4$ (the coordinate mapping works) and $\mathbb{R}^2 \to M_{2\times 2}$ has $2 \le 4$. $M_{2\times 2} \to \mathbb{R}^3$ has $4 > 3$ and $\mathbb{P}_5 \to \mathbb{P}_4$ has $6 > 5$, so those kernels are at least 1-dimensional.

questions.stem: Which vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}_5$?
questions.explanation: Finite-dimensional spaces are isomorphic exactly when their dimensions agree. $\dim\mathbb{P}_5 = 6$ and $\dim M_{2\times 3} = 6$. The others have dimensions 5, 4 and 7.

questions.stem: Match each linear map with its kernel.
questions.explanation: A derivative is 0 exactly for constants. $A^T = 0$ only when $A = 0$, so the transpose is one-to-one. A quadratic vanishing at 1 and 2 is a multiple of $(t - 1)(t - 2)$ (Example 2 of the lesson). $p(0)$ is the constant term, so the kernel is $\{a_1t + a_2t^2\}$, a 2-dimensional subspace, matching rank–nullity: $3 = 2 + 1$.

questions.stem: $T: U \to V$ has a $3 \times 4$ matrix $M_T$ (bases $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{B}$) and $S: V \to W$ has a $2 \times 3$ matrix $M_S$ (bases $\mathcal{B}$, $\mathcal{C}$). What is the matrix of $S \circ T$ relative to $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{C}$?
questions.explanation: $[S(T(\mathbf{x}))]_{\mathcal{C}} = M_S[T(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{B}} = M_SM_T[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{A}}$. The first map applied is written on the right, as with standard matrices. $(2 \times 3)(3 \times 4)$ is $2 \times 4$: $\dim W \times \dim U$. $M_TM_S$ isn't even defined ($4 \ne 2$), and matrices of different sizes can't be added.

questions.stem: Let $S(p)(t) = p(t + 1)$ on $\mathbb{P}_2$, with matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ relative to $\{1, t, t^2\}$. For $q(t) = 1 + 2t + t^2$, $S(q) = a + bt + t^2$ with $a =$ ___ and $b =$ ___.
The matrix $M$ of a linear operator $T: V \to V$ relative to a basis $\mathcal{B}$ is invertible. What follows?
choices: $T$ is an isomorphism of $V$ onto itself
$T$ is one-to-one but may not be onto
questions.explanation: $\ker T$ corresponds to $\operatorname{Nul} M = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ and $\operatorname{range} T$ to $\operatorname{Col} M$, which is everything, so $T$ is one-to-one and onto. Its inverse has matrix $M^{-1}$. The transpose on $M_{2\times 2}$ is an example that is invertible but not the identity, and its matrix is not $I$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for building the matrix of $T: V \to W$ relative to bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ in order.
choices: List the basis vectors $\mathbf{b}_1, \dots, \mathbf{b}_n$ of $V$ in order
Use $[T(\mathbf{b}_j)]_{\mathcal{C}}$ as column $j$ of the matrix
questions.explanation: The order of the input basis fixes the order of the columns; each column is the output of one basis vector, and it must be converted to $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates before it can be written down as a column of numbers.

questions.stem: Let $T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{P}_1$, $T(a, b) = a + bt$. Find its matrix relative to the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the basis $\mathcal{C} = \{1 + t,\ 1 - t\}$ of $\mathbb{P}_1$.
questions.explanation: $T(\mathbf{e}_1) = 1 = \tfrac12(1 + t) + \tfrac12(1 - t)$, so column 1 is $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$. $T(\mathbf{e}_2) = t = \tfrac12(1 + t) - \tfrac12(1 - t)$, so column 2 is $(\tfrac12, -\tfrac12)$. The identity is what you'd get by forgetting to convert to $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates; $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ lists the vectors of $\mathcal{C}$ themselves; the remaining matrix would make $T(\mathbf{e}_2) = \tfrac12(1 + t) + \tfrac12(1 - t) = 1$.

questions.stem: Why does every linear map $T: \mathbb{P}_3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ send some nonzero polynomial to $\mathbf{0}$?
choices: Because constant polynomials are always sent to $\mathbf{0}$
questions.explanation: Rank–nullity: the range is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$, so its dimension is at most 3, leaving at least 1 dimension for the kernel. Constants need not go to $\mathbf{0}$ (e.g. $T(p) = (p(0), p(1), p(2))$ sends 1 to $(1, 1, 1)$). $\mathbb{P}_3$ is finite-dimensional. And $T$ can be onto (that same evaluation map is).

questions.stem: With nodes $0, 1, 2$, what is the coordinate vector of $p(t) = t^2$ relative to the Lagrange basis $\{L_0, L_1, L_2\}$?
questions.explanation: Lagrange coordinates are the values at the nodes: $(p(0), p(1), p(2)) = (0, 1, 4)$, so $t^2 = 0L_0 + 1L_1 + 4L_2$. $(0, 0, 1)$ is the coordinate vector in the standard basis $\{1, t, t^2\}$.

questions.stem: With nodes $0, 1, 3$, the Lagrange polynomial $L_1$ is $L_1(t) = \dfrac{t(t - 3)}{(1 - 0)(1 - 3)}$. Then $L_1(2) =$ ___.
questions.explanation: $L_1(2) = \dfrac{2(2 - 3)}{(1)(-2)} = \dfrac{-2}{-2} = 1$. Note that 2 is not a node, so nothing forces $L_1(2)$ to be 0 or 1; it just happens to be 1 here. At the nodes, $L_1(0) = 0$, $L_1(1) = 1$ and $L_1(3) = 0$.

questions.stem: Find the polynomial of degree at most 2 through $(0, 2)$, $(1, 0)$ and $(2, 0)$.
Let $E: \mathbb{P}_2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$, $E(p) = (p(t_0), p(t_1), p(t_2))$, for three different nodes. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The same map would still be one-to-one if $t_0 = t_1$
questions.explanation: Evaluation respects sums and multiples, so $E$ is linear. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most 2 has at most two roots, so only $p = 0$ vanishes at three different nodes: $E$ is one-to-one, and with equal dimensions (3 and 3) it is onto. If $t_0 = t_1$, the nonzero polynomial $(t - t_0)(t - t_2)$ is sent to $\mathbf{0}$.

questions.stem: For three different nodes, $V$ is the Vandermonde matrix with rows $(1, t_i, t_i^2)$. Which matrix has as its columns the standard coordinate vectors of $L_0, L_1, L_2$?
questions.explanation: $V$ turns standard coordinates into values at the nodes, which are Lagrange coordinates: $V = P_{\mathcal{L} \leftarrow \mathcal{S}}$. The matrix whose columns are $[L_i]_{\mathcal{S}}$ is $P_{\mathcal{S} \leftarrow \mathcal{L}}$, the inverse. (For nodes $0, 1, 2$ the lesson checked that its first column is $(1, -\tfrac32, \tfrac12)$, the coefficients of $L_0$.)

questions.stem: What is the dimension of the space of sequences that satisfy $y_{k+2} - 3y_{k+1} + 2y_k = 0$ for all $k \ge 0$?
questions.explanation: The map $y \mapsto (y_0, y_1)$ is an isomorphism from the solution space onto $\mathbb{R}^2$: any starting pair can be continued in exactly one way. So the dimension is 2, with basis $\{1^k, 2^k\}$ here. The space of all sequences is infinite-dimensional, but the solutions form only a plane inside it.

questions.stem: The auxiliary equation of $y_{k+2} - 7y_{k+1} + 10y_k = 0$ has roots $r =$ ___ and $r =$ ___. Give the smaller root first.
questions.explanation: Substituting $y_k = r^k$ gives $r^2 - 7r + 10 = (r - 2)(r - 5) = 0$. So the basis is $\{2^k, 5^k\}$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for solving $y_{k+2} + a\,y_{k+1} + b\,y_k = 0$ with given $y_0$ and $y_1$ in order.
choices: Write the auxiliary equation $r^2 + ar + b = 0$
Choose a basis of two solutions and write the general solution
Use $y_0$ and $y_1$ to solve for the two weights
questions.explanation: The roots come from the auxiliary equation, and the basis ($r_1^k, r_2^k$ or $r^k, k\,r^k$) depends on the roots. The initial values can only pin down the weights once the general solution is written.

questions.stem: Solve $y_{k+2} = 5y_{k+1} - 6y_k$ with $y_0 = 2$ and $y_1 = 5$.
questions.explanation: $r^2 - 5r + 6 = (r - 2)(r - 3)$, so $y_k = c_12^k + c_23^k$ with $c_1 + c_2 = 2$ and $2c_1 + 3c_2 = 5$, giving $c_2 = 1$, $c_1 = 1$. Check: $y_2 = 5 \cdot 5 - 6 \cdot 2 = 13 = 4 + 9$. The negative roots come from a sign slip in the auxiliary equation (they give $y_1 = -5$); $2 \cdot 2^k + 3^k$ has $y_0 = 3$; $5^k + 1$ has $y_1 = 6$.

questions.stem: Which sequences satisfy $y_{k+2} - 4y_{k+1} + 4y_k = 0$ for all $k$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The auxiliary equation $(r - 2)^2 = 0$ has the repeated root 2, so $\{2^k, k\,2^k\}$ is a basis and every combination of them is a solution, including $3 \cdot 2^k - k\,2^k$. $(-2)^k$ gives $(-2)^k(4 + 8 + 4) \ne 0$. $k^2\,2^k$ gives $2^k\big[4(k + 2)^2 - 8(k + 1)^2 + 4k^2\big] = 8 \cdot 2^k \ne 0$.

questions.stem: The sequences $u_k = 3^k$ and $v_k = 3^{k+1}$ both solve $y_{k+2} - 5y_{k+1} + 6y_k = 0$. Are they linearly independent?
choices: Yes: their Casorati matrix is invertible
No: their Casorati matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{bmatrix}$ is singular, and in fact $v = 3u$
It cannot be decided from the first two terms
questions.explanation: The Casorati matrix has columns $(u_0, u_1) = (1, 3)$ and $(v_0, v_1) = (3, 9)$; its determinant is $9 - 9 = 0$. For solutions of the same recurrence, the first two terms decide independence, because $y \mapsto (y_0, y_1)$ is an isomorphism. Different sequences can still be dependent: $v = 3u$.

questions.stem: Match each recurrence with a basis for its solution space.
questions.explanation: Auxiliary equations: $r^2 - 5r + 6 = (r - 2)(r - 3)$; $r^2 - 6r + 9 = (r - 3)^2$, a repeated root, so the second basis vector is $k\,3^k$; $r^2 - r - 6 = (r - 3)(r + 2)$; $r^2 - 4 = (r - 2)(r + 2)$. The distractor $(-3)^k, 2^k$ would come from $r^2 + r - 6$.

questions.stem: Which describes every solution of $y_{k+2} - 6y_{k+1} + 8y_k = 9$?
questions.explanation: Try a constant $y_k = c$: $c - 6c + 8c = 3c = 9$, so $c = 3$ is a particular solution. The homogeneous part has $r^2 - 6r + 8 = (r - 2)(r - 4)$. Every solution is particular plus homogeneous: $3 + c_12^k + c_24^k$. Without the 3 you get only the homogeneous solutions; 9 is the right-hand side, not a solution ($9 - 54 + 72 = 27$); the negative roots are a sign slip.

questions.stem: The recurrence $y_{k+2} = y_{k+1} + 2y_k$ with $y_0 = 0$, $y_1 = 3$ has solution $y_k = c_1 2^k + c_2(-1)^k$, where $c_1 =$ ___ and $c_2 =$ ___.
questions.explanation: The auxiliary equation $r^2 - r - 2 = (r - 2)(r + 1)$ gives the basis $\{2^k, (-1)^k\}$. Then $c_1 + c_2 = 0$ and $2c_1 - c_2 = 3$, so $3c_1 = 3$: $c_1 = 1$, $c_2 = -1$. Check: the recurrence gives $y_2 = 3 + 0 = 3$, and $4 - 1 = 3$.

questions.stem: $\mathbf{v} = (2, 1)$ is an eigenvector of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}$. Its eigenvalue is ___. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $A\mathbf{v} = (5 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 1,\ 2 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 1) = (12, 6) = 6(2, 1)$, so the eigenvalue is 6.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding a basis of the eigenspace of $A$ for a given eigenvalue $\lambda$ in order.
choices: Subtract $\lambda$ from each diagonal entry to form $A - \lambda I$
Write the solutions of $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ in parametric vector form
Take the vectors multiplying the free variables as the basis
questions.explanation: The eigenspace is $\operatorname{Nul}(A - \lambda I)$, so it is found exactly like any null space: form the matrix, row-reduce it, read off the free variables, write the general solution in parametric vector form, and keep the vectors that multiply the free variables.

questions.stem: Which of these are eigenvectors of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $A(1, 1) = (2, 2)$, twice $(1, 1)$: eigenvalue 2. $A(-4, -2) = (-16 + 4,\ -4 - 2) = (-12, -6) = 3(-4, -2)$: eigenvalue 3 (it is a multiple of the eigenvector $(2, 1)$). $A(1, 0) = (4, 1)$ is not a multiple of $(1, 0)$. The zero vector is never an eigenvector, even though $A\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$.

questions.stem: The picture shows the reflection $T$ across the line $x_2 = x_1$. Solid arrows are vectors and dashed arrows are their images. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Coordinate axes with a dashed green line through the origin at 45 degrees. A blue arrow lies along the line. A second blue arrow points down and to the right, perpendicular to the line, with a dashed blue arrow pointing the opposite way labeled Tv. An orange arrow points right and slightly up, with a dashed orange image labeled Tw pointing up and slightly right.

choices: Vector that is not an eigenvector
questions.explanation: 1 is the mirror line $x_2 = x_1$. 2 lies on the mirror, so the reflection leaves it unchanged: eigenvalue 1. 3 is perpendicular to the mirror, so its image (dashed) points the opposite way: eigenvalue $-1$. 4 is sent to a vector in a different direction (its dashed image), so it is not an eigenvector. A reflection never has eigenvalue 0 (it is invertible) or 2 (it doesn't change lengths).

questions.stem: Match each transformation of the plane to its real eigenvalues.
left: Reflection across a line through the origin
Projection onto a line through the origin
questions.explanation: A reflection keeps vectors on the mirror (1) and flips those perpendicular to it ($-1$). A projection keeps vectors on the line (1) and sends perpendicular ones to $\mathbf{0}$ (0). A $90^\circ$ rotation turns every nonzero vector, so no real eigenvector exists (its eigenvalues are $\pm i$). Scaling by 3 makes every nonzero vector an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3.

questions.stem: The characteristic polynomial of $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$ is $\lambda^2 - b\lambda + c$ with $b =$ ___ and $c =$ ___. (Give only the numbers.)
questions.explanation: For a $2 \times 2$ matrix the characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$. Here $\operatorname{tr} A = 5 + 4 = 9$ and $\det A = 20 - 2 = 18$, so it is $\lambda^2 - 9\lambda + 18 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda - 6)$.

questions.stem: Match each matrix to its characteristic polynomial.
questions.explanation: Use $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$. First matrix: trace 5, determinant $4 - 6 = -2$. Rotation: trace 0, determinant 1. Triangular matrix: trace 4, determinant 4. Diagonal matrix: trace 2, determinant $-3$. The distractor has the wrong sign on the middle term.

questions.stem: $B = P^{-1}AP$ for an invertible matrix $P$. Which must $A$ and $B$ have in common? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\det(B - \lambda I) = \det P^{-1}\det(A - \lambda I)\det P = \det(A - \lambda I)$, so the characteristic polynomials agree, and with them the eigenvalues, their sum (the trace) and their product (the determinant). Eigenvectors generally change: if $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, then $B(P^{-1}\mathbf{v}) = \lambda P^{-1}\mathbf{v}$, so the eigenvectors of $B$ are $P^{-1}$ times those of $A$. The diagonal entries can differ too; only their sum is fixed.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the eigenvalues of a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ by hand in order.
choices: Subtract $\lambda$ from each diagonal entry to get $A - \lambda I$
Expand $\det(A - \lambda I)$ along a row or column with many zeros
Set the characteristic polynomial equal to 0 and factor it
Check that the roots add up to the trace of $A$
questions.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is $\det(A - \lambda I)$, so first form $A - \lambda I$, then expand the determinant (choosing a row or column with zeros keeps it short), then solve the characteristic equation. The trace check comes last because it needs the roots.

questions.stem: A $2 \times 2$ matrix has trace 7 and determinant 10. Its larger eigenvalue is ___.
questions.explanation: The characteristic equation is $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 5) = 0$, so the eigenvalues are 2 and 5. Check: $2 + 5 = 7$ and $2 \cdot 5 = 10$.

questions.stem: $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$. Then $A^5 = PD^5P^{-1}$, where $D^5$ has diagonal entries ___ and ___ (in order).
questions.explanation: A power of a diagonal matrix just raises each diagonal entry to that power: $2^5 = 32$ and $(-1)^5 = -1$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for diagonalizing an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ in order.
choices: Find a basis for each eigenspace
Check that there are $n$ independent eigenvectors in all
Form $P$ from the eigenvectors and $D$ from the matching eigenvalues
questions.explanation: Eigenvectors are found from the eigenvalues, and only after counting them do you know whether $A$ is diagonalizable at all. Then build $P$ and $D$ (in matching order) and confirm with $AP = PD$, which avoids computing $P^{-1}$.

questions.stem: Which of these matrices are diagonalizable using real matrices $P$ and $D$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The first matrix is triangular with distinct eigenvalues 2 and 3, so it is diagonalizable. The all-ones matrix has trace 2 and determinant 0, so its eigenvalues are 2 and 0, also distinct. $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalue 2 twice but only a 1-dimensional eigenspace. The rotation has eigenvalues $\pm i$, which are not real.

questions.stem: Match each $3 \times 3$ matrix description to the conclusion.
choices: Diagonalizable only if it is invertible
questions.explanation: Three distinct real eigenvalues guarantee three independent eigenvectors. With a repeated eigenvalue, compare the eigenspace dimension with the multiplicity: 1 is less than 2 (not diagonalizable), 2 equals 2 (diagonalizable, $2 + 1 = 3$ eigenvectors). Non-real eigenvalues rule out a real $D$. Invertibility has nothing to do with diagonalizability.

questions.stem: For $S = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}$, the eigenspace for $\lambda = 3$ has dimension ___.
questions.explanation: $S - 3I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ has one pivot, so it has $3 - 1 = 2$ free variables. The geometric multiplicity is 2, less than the algebraic multiplicity 3, so $S$ is not diagonalizable.

questions.stem: The matrix $C = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -12 \\ 12 & 5\end{bmatrix}$ rotates every vector and multiplies its length by ___.
questions.explanation: $C$ has the form $\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}$ with $a = 5$, $b = 12$, so its eigenvalues are $5 \pm 12i$ and the scale factor is $r = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$.

questions.stem: The picture shows a complex eigenvalue $\lambda = a + bi$ of a real $2 \times 2$ matrix, plotted in the complex plane. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Horizontal real axis and vertical imaginary axis. A point labeled lambda up and to the right of the origin, joined to the origin by a blue segment. An arc marks the angle between that segment and the real axis. An orange segment runs along the real axis from 0 to directly below lambda, and a green dashed segment runs up from there to lambda. A second point lies the same distance below the real axis, joined to the origin by a dashed line.

questions.explanation: 1: the distance from 0 to $\lambda$ is $r = |\lambda| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, the factor by which the matrix scales lengths. 2: the angle of $(a, b)$ is the rotation angle. 3 and 4: $\lambda$ sits at the point $(a, b)$, so the horizontal leg is the real part and the vertical leg the imaginary part. 5: complex eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs, and $a - bi$ is the mirror image of $a + bi$ across the real axis. (The trace is $2a$, not a part of the picture.)

questions.stem: Match each matrix to the transformation it performs.
choices: Rotation by about 53° with no scaling
questions.explanation: Each matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{bmatrix}$: it scales by $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and rotates by the angle of the point $(a, b)$. $(0, 1)$: $r = 1$, angle $90^\circ$. $(1, 1)$: $r = \sqrt2$, angle $45^\circ$. $(0, 2)$: $r = 2$, angle $90^\circ$. $(0.6, 0.8)$: $r = 1$, angle $\tan^{-1}(0.8/0.6) \approx 53.1^\circ$.

questions.stem: A real $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has eigenvalue $1 + 2i$. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs, so the eigenvalues are $1 \pm 2i$. Their product is $1 + 4 = 5 = \det A$ and their sum is $2 = \operatorname{tr} A$, not 1. A real $2 \times 2$ matrix whose eigenvalues are both non-real has no real eigenvector: every real vector is turned.

questions.stem: The steady-state vector of $P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.7 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.8\end{bmatrix}$ has first entry ___ and second entry ___. (Give decimals or fractions.)
Put the steps for finding the steady-state vector of a regular stochastic matrix $P$ in order.
choices: Divide $\mathbf{x}$ by the sum of its entries to get $\mathbf{q}$
questions.explanation: The steady state is an eigenvector for eigenvalue 1, so solve $(P - I)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, pick a nonzero solution, and scale it into a probability vector. The check uses the finished $\mathbf{q}$, so it comes last.

questions.stem: Which of these are regular stochastic matrices? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: All four are stochastic (columns sum to 1). The first and last already have all entries positive ($k = 1$). The swap matrix alternates between itself and $I$, so every power has zeros. In $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}$ state 1 is never left, so the bottom-left entry of every power is 0 (for example $P^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.75 \\ 0 & 0.25\end{bmatrix}$).

questions.stem: A $2 \times 2$ system $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A\mathbf{x}_k$ has the given eigenvalues. Match each to the behavior at the origin.
questions.explanation: For discrete systems the absolute value decides: both $|\lambda| < 1$ is an attractor, both $|\lambda| > 1$ a repeller, one of each a saddle point. A negative eigenvalue like $-0.8$ makes that component flip sign each step, but $|{-0.8}| < 1$ still shrinks it.

questions.stem: Each panel shows trajectories of $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A\mathbf{x}_k$ near the origin, one dot per step, with arrows showing the direction of motion. Name the behavior of the origin in each panel.

image.alt: Three square panels with axes through the origin. Panel 1: dotted paths from the edges step inward and end at the origin. Panel 2: dotted paths start near the origin and step outward to the edges. Panel 3: dotted paths come in along the vertical axis toward the origin, then turn and leave along the horizontal axis.

questions.explanation: 1: every path moves toward the origin, an attractor (both $|\lambda| < 1$). 2: every path moves away, a repeller (both $|\lambda| > 1$). 3: paths approach along one eigenvector direction and leave along the other, a saddle point (one $|\lambda| < 1$, one $|\lambda| > 1$). A center (closed loops) belongs to differential equations with purely imaginary eigenvalues.

questions.stem: For $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ___ (the larger) and ___.
questions.explanation: $\operatorname{tr} A = 2$ and $\det A = 1 - 9 = -8$, so $\lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 8 = (\lambda - 4)(\lambda + 2) = 0$. Solutions are combinations of $e^{4t}(1, 1)$ and $e^{-2t}(1, -1)$; with eigenvalues of opposite signs the origin is a saddle point.

questions.stem: Put the steps for solving $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with a given $\mathbf{x}(0)$ in order ($A$ is $2 \times 2$ with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2$).
choices: Check that the formula gives $\mathbf{x}(0)$ at $t = 0$
questions.explanation: Eigenvectors need the eigenvalues; the weights need the eigenvectors; the formula needs all three; and the check needs the formula.

questions.stem: For which matrices $A$ does every solution of $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ tend to $\mathbf{0}$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The test is trace negative and determinant positive. $\operatorname{diag}(-2, -5)$: eigenvalues $-2$, $-5$, a sink. $\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}$: trace $-2$, determinant 5, eigenvalues $-1 \pm 2i$, a spiral sink. $\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $1 - 9 = -8 < 0$ (eigenvalues 2 and $-4$), a saddle. The rotation has eigenvalues $\pm i$: a center, whose solutions circle forever without approaching $\mathbf{0}$.

questions.stem: Match the eigenvalues of a real $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ to the behavior of $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ at the origin.
questions.explanation: For differential equations the sign of the real part decides. Both negative: sink. Opposite signs: saddle point. Complex with negative real part: spiral sink. Real part 0: center (closed loops). A source or spiral source would need positive real parts.

questions.stem: The picture shows the trace–determinant plane for $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$, with $\operatorname{tr} A$ across and $\det A$ up. Name the numbered regions (region 6 is the positive vertical axis).

image.alt: Axes labeled trace (horizontal) and determinant (vertical). A dashed parabola opens upward from the origin. Region 1 is inside the parabola on the left, region 2 inside it on the right, region 3 outside it on the left above the axis, region 4 outside it on the right above the axis, region 5 is everything below the horizontal axis, and 6 marks the positive vertical axis.

questions.explanation: The eigenvalues satisfy $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \operatorname{tr} A$ and $\lambda_1\lambda_2 = \det A$. Below the axis ($\det A < 0$) they are real with opposite signs: saddle (5).
